# Six Ladders: everything needed for machine learning, at six levels

_September 2026. Supersedes `22_LEARNING_PATH_ML.md` and `23_LESSONS_SIX_LEVELS.md`; companion to `21_PLAN_M1_TRAFFIC_MODEL.md`._

**Everything needed for machine learning, told six times: twelve phases, thirty-nine lessons and 140 free books, courses and papers, each with its own study guide, from age five to a PhD at Apple.**

The Fremont traffic model is the spine: you build it stage by stage and learn each idea the week it is needed. Around that spine the course covers the rest of the field, from SQL and regression to transformers, reinforcement learning, causal inference and fairness, so nothing needed for real machine-learning work is left out. Every lesson, topic and resource is explained at six levels, every resource is free, and every resource carries a study guide that teaches its content here, so the course can be learned from this page alone. Pick a level with the switcher and read the whole course at that height, or turn on every level and watch one idea gain precision rung by rung. Tick things off as you go; progress is saved in this browser.

The six levels, in order: Age 5, Middle school, High school, Stanford undergrad, Stanford grad, PhD at Apple. Every lesson, topic and resource below carries all six, and every resource has a study guide (what it covers, key ideas, formulas, takeaways, practice) so the content can be learned from this document before opening the link. Every walkthrough step explains its tools, terms and commands before it asks anything, and reads its code line by line; the glossary at the end defines every word the course uses. Links were checked in September 2026.

## Six rules

- **The project is the syllabus.** Every topic in the first seven phases is here because a stage of the traffic model needs it, and you learn it the week you build that stage. The later phases cover the rest of machine learning with the same discipline: each topic ends in something that runs.
- **Build it twice.** First with the library, so it works. Then the core from scratch in numpy, the way `03_train_from_scratch.py` does, so you know what the library hides. Then back to the library, faster.
- **Evaluate before you model.** Baselines, metrics and leakage come before any algorithm past logistic regression. A number without a baseline next to it is not a result.
- **Math just in time.** Linear algebra, calculus and probability in the amounts the stage needs, derived once by hand. Depth comes in the final phase, when you know what it is for.
- **Write it down.** A lab notebook every week, a README per stage, a write-up per phase. If you cannot explain it in plain words you do not have it yet.
- **Checkpoints are things that run.** Each phase ends with code that produces a number or a file, not with a quiz.

### What really good looks like

- **Framing.** Turn a fuzzy question into a unit, a target, a horizon and a metric, and say what the answer cannot mean.
- **Data.** Build the pipeline from raw files or a database, know its failure modes, and measure its memory and time.
- **Models.** Know the whole toolbox, from logistic regression to transformers and graph networks, well enough to say which wins on which data and why, and to implement the core of any of them from a paper.
- **Evaluation.** Design a split that cannot leak, pick metrics the imbalance cannot fool, put a baseline next to every number, and calibrate what you ship.
- **Engineering.** Ship one implementation used by training and serving, containerize it, schedule it, monitor it, retrain it, and roll it back.
- **Acting.** Know what changes when a model's output is a decision: causal questions, feedback loops, fairness and privacy.
- **Reading.** Read a new paper in an evening and say what it would change in your system and what it would not fix.
- **Explaining.** Describe all of the above to a smart person outside the field without hiding behind jargon.

## The project, laid out

Every file the course asks you to make, in one place, before any phase asks for it. Read this page once now and come back whenever a Build page names a file: the folder it lives in, who writes it, what it reads and what it writes are all here, and the twelve Build pages hold the contract for each file in full. If a Build page and this page ever disagree, this page is wrong; tell someone.

The repository on GitHub holds four documents and nothing else: the plan (`21_PLAN_M1_TRAFFIC_MODEL.md`), two superseded drafts of this course (`22_LEARNING_PATH_ML.md`, `23_LESSONS_SIX_LEVELS.md`) and the course itself (`24_APPRENTICESHIP_SIX_LEVELS.md`). Every script, module, test and folder below is yours to write, in the phase named beside it. Nothing is assumed to exist that this page does not say you will create.

### The machine, the accounts and the time

- A Mac with Apple silicon. The plan budgets a 16 GB M1 Mac mini and every number in it is measured against those 16 GB. An 8 GB machine gets through phase 4 on three months of data; an Intel Mac runs everything except the GPU lessons in phases 7 and 8, which fall back to the processor.
- macOS with Apple's Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`) and Homebrew (from brew.sh), which is only needed once, for `brew install libomp`, the OpenMP runtime LightGBM cannot ship.
- Native arm64 Python 3.11 or newer from miniforge or python.org, and a virtual environment at `.venv` inside the project. Rosetta Python runs at half speed and cannot use the GPU.
- Google Chrome, installed the normal way. Phase 3 drives it with Selenium to download PeMS files; nothing else uses it.
- VS Code with Microsoft's Python extension, and a GitHub account holding your own copy of Traffic1.
- Two free accounts and one key. A 511.org token (511.org/open-data/token; it arrives by email) for the incident feed, from phase 0. A PeMS account (pems.dot.ca.gov, free registration, approved by hand within a day or two) for the detector history, from phase 3. Open-Meteo, the weather source in phase 6, needs no account.
- Disk. Raw PeMS is about 16 GB per year; the cleaned Parquet is 100 to 150 MB per year. Keep 25 GB free or put `data/pems_raw/` on an external SSD. Five gigabytes is enough through phase 4 on three months of data.
- Ten hours a week. The hours on each phase page assume a beginner.

### The one convention every file follows

- Numbered scripts, `NN_name.py`, are runners. Each one parses its command line, calls one module, writes its files and prints one log line. Their names start with a digit so `ls` shows the pipeline in order, and that is also why Python cannot import them: `import 02_collect_events` is a syntax error. Nothing imports a runner.
- The code that does the work lives in plain modules with importable names: `common.py`, `collector.py`, `logreg.py`, `pems.py`, `labels.py`, `incidents.py`, `weather.py`, `features.py`, `split.py`, `evaluate.py`, `stnet.py`. Tests import these. The serving loop imports these. There is one implementation of every feature, and it is in `features.py`.
- Every runner answers `python NN_name.py --help`. Runners that work on history take `--month YYYY-MM` and default to every month present. Every runner writes to a `.tmp` path and renames it into place at the end, so a crash never leaves a half-written file that the next stage would read.
- Every runner ends with the line `stage=<name> seconds=<n> rss_gb=<n> rows=<n>` from `common.log_stage()`, on the screen and appended to `logs/pipeline.log`. The plan's memory budgets are checked against these lines, not guessed.
- Every stage has a page in `docs/stages/`, named after its runner: what it reads, what it writes with the column list, how to run it, the numbers from the last run and what surprised you. Phase 9's `make all` fails if a stage has no page.
- Every command in the course is run from the repository root with the venv active: `cd ~/code/Traffic1 && source .venv/bin/activate`. Every path is relative to that root.
- Code, tests, docs, `launchd/`, `sql/`, `studies/`, `serve/`, `bench/`, `notebook/`, `requirements.txt`, `Makefile`, `.gitignore`, `.env.example` and `.vscode/settings.json` are committed. `data/`, `models/`, `output/`, `logs/`, `.venv/` and `.env` never are; `.gitignore` says so and phase 0 proves it with `git ls-files`.
- Model files carry the label definition in their name, `thresh0.6_win3`, and the split they were trained on lives in `models/manifest.json`. A model whose name does not say what it predicts is not kept.
- The numbers that define the problem are written once, in `common.py`, and imported everywhere. They are listed at the bottom of this page.

### The requirements

The setup files, exactly as phase 0 writes them. Later phases append to `requirements.txt` and `.env.example`; the lines they add are listed under each file so the finished versions are also here.

#### `requirements.txt` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ The packages the project needs, one per line with the lowest version that will do. `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs them all into the venv. Loose pins resolve on any day; the exact versions that worked are frozen separately in `requirements.lock.txt`.

_Contents, as phase 0 writes it._

```text
# data
pandas>=2.2            # tables: read, clean, group, join
numpy>=1.26            # arrays and the maths under pandas
pyarrow>=15.0          # lets pandas read and write Parquet files

# getting the data
requests>=2.31         # HTTP calls to the 511 traffic feed
python-dotenv>=1.0     # loads secrets from the .env file

# models
scikit-learn>=1.4      # baselines, metrics, calibration, splits
lightgbm>=4.3          # gradient boosted trees: the production model
torch>=2.2             # PyTorch, the neural networks (large download)
shap>=0.45             # explains which features drove a prediction

# looking at things
matplotlib>=3.8        # plots
jupyterlab>=4.1        # notebooks for exploring

# the rest
pytest>=8.0            # tests
holidays>=0.45         # public holiday calendar for the feature set
psutil>=5.9            # memory and timing for every pipeline stage
duckdb>=0.10           # SQL over Parquet without a database server
tqdm>=4.66             # progress bars for long loops
```

_Lines later phases add._ Each phase's Build page says when.

```text
# phase 3
selenium>=4.18         # drives Chrome to download PeMS files
polars>=0.20           # the faster second pass at cleaning
joblib>=1.3            # saves the category sets and isotonic maps

# phase 5
optuna>=3.5            # hyperparameter search with a budget

# phase 8
torchvision>=0.17      # digits, ResNet and image transforms
transformers>=4.38     # the small pretrained text encoder
sentence-transformers>=2.5   # embeddings for retrieval

# phase 9
fastapi>=0.110         # the prediction service
uvicorn>=0.27          # runs it
httpx>=0.27            # the service's tests call it

# phase 11
pymc>=5.10             # the hierarchical Bayesian model
tables>=3.9            # PyTables, to read the DCRNN benchmark's .h5 speed tables
pyyaml>=6.0            # reads bench/pems_bay/config.yaml
```

_Check._ `pip install -r requirements.txt` finishes without a red line, and the import block in the phase 0 walkthrough prints `arm64` and one version per package. If `import lightgbm` fails naming `libomp`, run `brew install libomp` and open a new terminal.

#### `requirements.lock.txt` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ The exact versions that worked, written by `pip freeze > requirements.lock.txt` once the install is clean. This is what a new machine installs from (`pip install -r requirements.lock.txt`) when it must behave identically; `requirements.txt` is what you edit. Regenerate it whenever `requirements.txt` changes and commit both.

#### `.env` and `.env.example` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ `.env` holds the secrets, one `NAME=value` per line, no quotes, no spaces around the equals sign; `python-dotenv`'s `load_dotenv()` reads it into `os.environ`. It is never committed. `.env.example` has the same names with empty values and is committed, so the list of what a newcomer must supply is documented without revealing anything.

_Contents of `.env.example`, finished._ Phase 0 writes the first line; phase 3 adds the two PeMS lines; phase 9 adds the last three, which have safe defaults and can stay empty.

```text
# copy this file to .env and fill in your own values
TOKEN_511=
PEMS_USERNAME=
PEMS_PASSWORD=
TRAFFIC1_ROOT=          # phase 9: absolute path of the repo for launchd; defaults to the folder .env is in
PREDICT_INTERVAL_S=     # phase 9: seconds between prediction cycles; defaults to 300
ALERT_PRECISION=        # phase 9: the precision the alert must keep; defaults to 0.5
```

_Check._ `python -c "from dotenv import load_dotenv; import os; load_dotenv(); print(bool(os.environ.get('TOKEN_511')))"` prints `True`, and `git ls-files | grep -c '^\.env$'` prints `0`.

#### `.gitignore` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ What git must never record: the secret, the data, everything rebuildable, editor and system litter. It exists before the first commit because history is permanent.

_Contents, verbatim._

```text
# secrets
.env
!.env.example

# data and anything rebuilt from it
data/
models/
output/
logs/

# the environment
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# notebooks and macOS litter
.ipynb_checkpoints/
.DS_Store
```

_Check._ `git status --short` never lists `data/`, `models/`, `.venv/` or `.env`; `git ls-files | grep -c -E '^\.env$|^data/'` prints `0`.

#### `.vscode/settings.json` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ Makes VS Code use the project's venv without asking, activates it in the editor's terminal, trims trailing whitespace and draws a ruler at 100 columns.

_Contents, verbatim._

```json
{
  "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python",
  "python.terminal.activateEnvironment": true,
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "editor.rulers": [100]
}
```

#### `Makefile` · phase 0, finished in phase 9 · repo root

_Purpose._ One word per job, so the whole pipeline is `make all` and nobody has to remember fourteen commands in order. Phase 0 writes `setup`, `check` and `test`; phase 9 adds the rest. Recipes are indented with a tab, never spaces; that is the only trap in a Makefile.

_Targets, finished._

- `setup` · creates `.venv` if missing, upgrades pip, installs `requirements.txt`, runs `brew install libomp` if `brew` exists and libomp is absent.
- `check` · the import block from phase 0: prints the machine type and every package version, and whether MPS is available.
- `test` · `pytest -q`.
- `collect` · one poll of `02_collect_events.py`.
- `pems` · `09_collect_pems_selenium.py` for the months in `MONTHS`, newest first.
- `clean`, `labels`, `incidents`, `features` · runners 10 to 13 for `MONTHS`, in that order, each depending on the one before.
- `baselines`, `train`, `calibrate`, `evaluate` · runners 14, 16, 16b, 18; `train` also runs 15 so the numpy and scikit-learn numbers sit in the same log.
- `all` · `clean labels incidents features baselines train calibrate evaluate`, then checks that `docs/stages/` has a page for every runner and fails if one is missing.
- `predict` · one cycle of `19_predict_live.py --replay`.
- `monitor` · `20_monitor.py`.
- `retrain` · `20_monitor.py --stash` (the live set copied to `models/previous/`), then `features train calibrate evaluate` for the newest month, then `20_monitor.py --promote`, which swaps the model files atomically and records the previous set in `models/manifest.json`. `20_monitor.py --retrain-if-due` is what the monthly launchd job calls; it runs this only when the schedule or the decay rule says so.
- `rollback` · `20_monitor.py --rollback`: the previous set becomes live again.
- `serve` · `uvicorn serve.app:app --port 8000`.
- `MONTHS ?= $(shell ls data/pems_processed | sed 's/.parquet//')` at the top, so every target defaults to every month present and `make features MONTHS=2026-03` does one.

#### `README.md` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ The page a stranger reads first. It must say, in this order: what the project predicts in one sentence (the plan's bold line); the three data sources and where their keys come from; setup in four commands (`git clone`, `python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate`, `pip install -r requirements.txt`, `cp .env.example .env` and fill it in); how to run one poll and how to run everything (`make collect`, `make all`); the tree above, abridged to the folders; the convention that runners are numbered and modules are imported; where the numbers are (`output/evaluation_report.json`) and where the decisions are (`docs/decisions/`). Under 120 lines. Phase 0 writes the first four parts; each later phase adds its line to the run section.

#### `common.py` · phase 0 · repo root

_Purpose._ The one module every other module imports: the paths, the constants that define the problem, and three helpers. Nothing in it does any work on data.

_Must contain._

- `ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent`, and `DATA`, `MODELS`, `OUTPUT`, `LOGS` as `ROOT / 'data'` and so on. Every other file builds paths from these, never from a string.
- The constants listed in the last section of this page, with these exact names, so a Build page can say `common.SLOW_RATIO` and mean one number.
- `log_stage(name, t0, rows=None, **extra)` · prints and appends to `logs/pipeline.log` the line `stage=<name> seconds=<n> rss_gb=<n> rows=<n>` plus any extra key=value pairs; the seconds are `time.time() - t0`, the memory is `psutil.Process().memory_info().rss / 1e9`.
- `atomic_write(df_or_obj, path)` · writes a DataFrame (Parquet), a dict (JSON) or text to `path.with_suffix(path.suffix + '.tmp')`, then `os.replace` into place.
- `RATIO_RULE`, `LEAD_WINDOW_STEPS` and `FALSE_ALARM_STEPS` beside the other constants, so the baseline runner and the evaluator import them rather than defining their own.
- `env(name, default=None, required=False)` · reads `.env` once through `load_dotenv()` and returns the variable, exiting with a one-line message naming it when required and missing.

### The data, the models and the outputs

Every generated file, who writes it and what it holds. Column lists are in the Build page of the runner that writes the file; the plan has the same tables under each stage.

- `data/fremont_events_log.csv` · runner 02, from phase 0. One row per event per poll. Phase 0's columns: `pulled_at, id, event_type, severity, headline, roads, created, updated`. Phase 1 renames `id` to `event_id` and `roads` to `road_names`, and adds `status, directions, lat, lon, geo_missing, first_seen_at, last_seen_at`, which is the plan's stage 2 layout.
- `data/events_raw/YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl` · runner 02, from phase 1. Every poll's raw response, one JSON object per line with `pulled_at` added, so the join rules can change without polling again.
- `data/pems_raw/*.txt.gz`, `manifest.json`, `pems_last_request.json` · runner 09, phase 3. Raw district-4 files, about 45 MB each; the manifest makes reruns skip finished days and catches truncated downloads; the request clock keeps the 305-second gap across runs.
- `data/pems_meta/d04_text_meta_*.txt` and `fremont_stations.parquet` · runner 09 moves the meta file; runner 10 builds the registry from it, about 100 mainline stations with `upstream_id`, `downstream_id`, `lanes`, `length`, `abs_pm`.
- `data/pems_processed/YYYY-MM.parquet` · runner 10. Columns `station_id, timestamp, speed, occ, flow, observed_frac, samples`, float32, one row per station per five-minute UTC slot, no gaps.
- `data/labels/YYYY-MM.parquet` · runner 11. Adds `profile_speed, speed_ratio, ratio_ff, label, label_abs`; the profile itself is a model artifact, `models/profile_<split>.parquet`.
- `data/incidents/YYYY-MM.parquet` · runner 12. The six incident columns keyed by `station_id, timestamp`.
- `data/weather/openmeteo_hourly.parquet` · `weather.py`, phase 6. Hourly `precip_mm` for Fremont, UTC.
- `data/features/YYYY-MM.parquet` · runner 13. About 60 feature columns plus `y_15, y_30, y_60, speed_t30`, keys `station_id, timestamp`; rows whose target is unknown are dropped, never filled. The occupancy column is `occ` from the cleaning stage on, and every feature built from it says `occ` (`occ_lag_3`).
- `models/` · `bottleneck_weights.npz` (03); `profile_<split>.parquet` (11); `profile_rate_<split>.parquet` (13); `logreg_h{h}_thresh0.6_win3.npz` (15); `gbt_h{h}_thresh0.6_win3.txt`, `gbt_h{h}_features.json`, `categorical_dtypes.joblib` (16); `iso_h{h}.joblib`, `calibration.json` (16b); `mlp_h30.pt` (17a); `stnet_thresh0.6_win3.pt` (17b); `manifest.json` and `previous/` (phase 9); `gbt_speed30*.txt` (phase 5); `ranker_h30_thresh0.6_win3.txt` (phase 10); `conformal_h30.json`, `pems_bay_<tag>.pt` (phase 11).
- `output/` · `baselines.json`, `logreg.json`, `lgbm_training.json` (14, 15, 16); `evaluation_report.json` with `reliability_h{h}.png` and `lead_time_hist.png` (18); `predictions_latest.json` and `predictions_log.parquet/` as daily parts (19); `predictions_stnet.parquet` (17b); `monitor/YYYY-WW.json` (20); `studies/<name>.json` and `.png` (every side study). Every prediction row carries `h`, the horizon in minutes (15, 30 or 60), under that name.
- `logs/` · `pipeline.log` (every runner's last line), `collect.log`, `predict.log`, `predict.err`.

### The numbers the whole project shares

Written once in `common.py` and imported everywhere. Each is the plan's value; the Build pages say where each is used and phase 6 is where the label numbers are finally decided with data.

- `FREMONT_BOX = (37.447, 37.612, -122.075, -121.888)` · south, north, west, east; latitude then longitude.
- `ROUTES = {880, 680, 84}` and `LANE_TYPE = 'ML'` · mainline detectors on I-880, I-680 and SR-84 only.
- `FREMONT_ROADS` · the road-name fragments the 511 filter accepts: I-880, I-680, SR-84, CA-84, Mission Blvd, Fremont Blvd, Auto Mall Pkwy, Dumbarton.
- `TZ = 'America/Los_Angeles'`; every stored timestamp is UTC; `tz_localize(TZ, ambiguous='NaT', nonexistent='shift_forward')` is the only allowed conversion.
- `STEP = '5min'`, `STEPS_PER_DAY = 288`.
- `MIN_OBSERVED = 50` · rows with `% Observed` below this are nulled; `MAX_FFILL = 3` · the longest gap forward-filled, in steps.
- `SPEED_RANGE = (0, 100)`, `OCC_RANGE = (0, 100)`, `FLOW_PER_LANE_MAX = 3000` · bounds; anything outside becomes NaN.
- `PROFILE_SMOOTH = 7`, `PROFILE_MIN_N = 20` · the centred rolling median over slots, and the sample count below which a cell falls back to the hourly median.
- `SLOW_RATIO = 0.6`, `SLOW_WINDOW = 3`, `SLOW_ABS_MPH = 35`, `FREE_FLOW_Q = 0.85` · the relative label, its run length, the absolute label, the free-flow percentile.
- `HORIZONS = {15: 3, 30: 6, 60: 12}` · minutes to steps.
- `LAGS = (0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 12)`, `ROLL_STEPS = {30: 6, 60: 12}`.
- `SPLIT_GAP_DAYS = 1` · between train and validation, and between validation and test.
- `INCIDENT_MILES = 1.0`, `INCIDENT_MIN_MINUTES = 20`, `NO_INCIDENT_MILES = 99`, `SEVERITY = {'Unknown': 1, 'Minor': 1, 'Moderate': 2, 'Major': 3}`.
- `LGBM_PARAMS` · `objective='binary', is_unbalance=True, num_leaves=63, min_data_in_leaf=200, learning_rate=0.05, feature_fraction=0.8, bagging_fraction=0.8, bagging_freq=1, lambda_l2=1.0, max_bin=255, num_threads=8, metric='average_precision', verbose=-1`; `LGBM_ROUNDS = 3000`, `LGBM_PATIENCE = 100`.
- `CATEGORICALS = ['station_id', 'fwy', 'dir', 'daytype']`.
- `RATIO_RULE = 0.7` · the speed ratio below which the rule-of-thumb baseline says slow.
- `LEAD_WINDOW_STEPS = 24`, `FALSE_ALARM_STEPS = 12` · how far before an onset an alert counts (two hours), and how far ahead a label must be absent for an alert to be a false alarm (one hour).
- `ALERT_PRECISION = 0.5` · the validation precision `tau_h` must keep; `CHALLENGER_MARGIN = 0.02` · the validation AP gain the net needs to be shipped.
- `PSI_ALERT = 0.2`, `RETRAIN_DROP = 0.2`, `RETRAIN_WEEKS = 2` · drift and decay rules for `20_monitor.py`.
- `POLL_SECONDS = 900`, `PEMS_GAP_SECONDS = 305`, `PREDICT_SECONDS = 300`.

## Phase 0: Setup and habits

_weeks 0–1 · ≈8 h · builds stage 2 runs_

**Goal.** A working machine and a working routine.

### What you need to learn

- The terminal: `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `head`, pipes, environment variables.
- Git: clone, branch, commit, push, diff, `.gitignore`; what a repository and a README are.
- Native arm64 Python on Apple silicon (miniforge or python.org), virtual environments, `pip`, VS Code, Jupyter.
- The shape of this repo: the numbered scripts, `data/`, `models/`, `.env`, and why secrets never get committed.
- What the traffic model predicts, so every later week has a destination.

### Topic: The terminal, git and a Python environment

**Goal.** Talk to the computer by typing, keep every version of your work, and give this project its own toolbox.

**Age 5.**

The computer has a secret room called the terminal where you talk to it by typing instead of clicking.

Git is a magic notebook that remembers every version of your work, so if you mess something up you can go back to yesterday's page.

A Python environment is a toybox where you keep the tools for one project, so they do not get mixed up with another project's tools.

_Try this._ Ask someone to open the terminal and type `ls`. It means 'list', and it shows what is in the folder you are standing in.

**Middle school.**

The terminal runs commands: `cd` moves between folders, `ls` lists files, `cat` shows one, and `python script.py` runs a program.

Git saves snapshots called commits, each with a message saying what changed. `git log` shows the history, and GitHub is where a copy lives online.

A virtual environment (`python -m venv .venv`) is a private folder of installed packages for this project, so upgrading something for one project cannot break another.

_Try this._ Make a folder, put a text file in it, run `git init`, `git add .`, `git commit -m 'first'`. Change the file and run `git diff`. Read what it shows you.

**High school.**

Shell essentials: absolute and relative paths, pipes with `|`, redirects with `>`, environment variables (`export PEMS_USERNAME=...`), `.env` files that scripts load, `which python`.

Git's model: working tree, staging area, repository. Branches are pointers to commits. `git status` before every commit; `.gitignore` keeps `data/` and `.env` out of history forever.

Python on Apple silicon: install a native arm64 Python (miniforge or python.org), check with `python -c 'import platform; print(platform.machine())'` which must print `arm64`, then `pip install -r requirements.txt` inside the venv. VS Code needs to be pointed at that interpreter.

_Try this._ Run the collector once with `python 02_collect_events.py`, then `git status`. The `data/` folder should not appear as untracked. If it does, fix `.gitignore` before anything else.

**Stanford undergrad.**

These tools exist for reproducibility. A venv plus pinned requirements turns 'works on my machine' into 'works on any machine'; git makes every change attributable and reversible; the shell makes procedures scriptable, and a Makefile target is a shell script with declared dependencies.

Know the difference between `pip` and `conda`, between a shell variable and an exported one, and how `PATH` resolves the word `python`. Rosetta versus native is visible through `arch` and `platform.machine()`; native wheels exist for numpy, LightGBM and PyTorch.

Git workflow even when alone: feature branches, small commits, and a pull request you review yourself. Reading your own diff before merging catches most mistakes.

_Try this._ Write a Makefile with `setup`, `collect` and `test` targets, where `test` depends on `setup`. Run `make test` from a fresh clone.

**Stanford grad.**

Environments are dependency graphs: solver conflicts, lock files (pip-tools, uv, conda-lock), and the reason a lock file belongs in the experiment record. Numerical results can change with a BLAS backend or a compiler flag.

Git internals: content-addressed objects (blob, tree, commit), refs, the reflog as a safety net, and `bisect` for finding the commit that broke a metric. Shell as glue: `set -euo pipefail`, and knowing when a task has outgrown the shell and belongs in Python.

On macOS: launchd rather than cron, `caffeinate` for long jobs, and the permission system (Full Disk Access) that silently blocks scheduled jobs from reading files.

_Try this._ Break a metric deliberately in one commit among twenty, then find it with `git bisect` driven by a script. Afterward, delete a branch and recover it from the reflog.

**PhD at Apple.**

At scale, environments become containers and hermetic builds (Nix, Bazel), because ML reproducibility depends on driver versions, BLAS backends and compiler flags that a requirements file does not capture. Git's model does not fit large data and model artifacts, which is why data versioning and model registries grew separate lineage systems.

Security hygiene is part of the craft: secrets in a credential manager, least-privilege tokens, and a scanner that fails the build if a key appears in a diff.

The reproducibility problem in research is mostly this stage done badly. A lock file, a data hash and a hardware note are the minimum for a claim to be checkable a year later.

_Try this._ Write the 'reproduce this result' section of a paper for this repository: exact commands, content hashes for data, versions, hardware, and expected runtime. Then have someone else follow it.

**Guided walkthrough.** This is the one walkthrough where nothing is assumed: no Python, no git, no editor. Every command is typed into the Terminal app, one line at a time, pressing return after each. If a step fails, read the error out loud before doing anything else; the fix is nearly always in the last line of it.

**Step 1.**

_Before you do this._ The Terminal is an app that comes with macOS: press Command and the space bar, type `terminal`, press return. A window opens showing a prompt, a line ending in `%` (or `$`) that means the computer is waiting. You type one command, press return, it runs, and the prompt comes back. That is the entire loop.

Three commands cover ninety percent of moving around. `pwd` means print working directory: it answers 'which folder am I in right now?'. `ls` lists what is in that folder. `cd` means change directory: `cd Documents` goes into a folder named Documents, `cd ..` goes up one level, and `cd ~` goes to your home folder. The `~` character is shorthand for your home folder, `/Users/yourname`.

Two habits that save hours. Press the tab key halfway through a name and the shell completes it for you, which also proves the name exists. And if a command ever hangs or runs away, press Control and C together to stop it.

`mkdir` makes a directory. The `-p` flag means 'make parent folders as needed and do not complain if it already exists', which makes the command safe to run twice.

_Do this._ Open Terminal and make a folder to keep projects in, then go into it.

```bash
pwd
ls
mkdir -p ~/code
cd ~/code
pwd
```

_What each line does._

- `pwd` — prints the folder you are in; it will say /Users/yourname
- `ls` — lists that folder's contents, so you can see Desktop, Documents and the rest
- `mkdir -p ~/code` — creates a folder called code in your home folder, quietly succeeding if it is already there
- `cd ~/code` — moves into it; the prompt now shows code
- `pwd` — confirms the move: /Users/yourname/code

**Step 2.**

_Before you do this._ Git is the tool that records versions of your work, and on a Mac it arrives inside Apple's Command Line Tools, a free download that also includes the compiler some Python packages need. You do not need the full Xcode app, which is many gigabytes; the command line tools are a few hundred megabytes.

Running the install command opens a small dialog box asking you to agree and install. It takes a few minutes. If the tools are already present, the command says so and does nothing, which is fine.

After it finishes, `git --version` should print something like `git version 2.39.5`. Any version above 2.30 is fine for this course.

_Do this._ Install Apple's command line tools, then check that git is there.

```bash
xcode-select --install
git --version
```

_What each line does._

- `xcode-select --install` — opens the installer dialog; click Install and wait, or read the note that they are already installed
- `git --version` — proves git now exists and is on your PATH, the list of folders the shell searches for commands

**Step 3.**

_Before you do this._ macOS ships with a Python, and you must not use it. It belongs to the system, it is often an old version, and installing packages into it can break parts of macOS. Every serious project installs its own Python.

There are two good ways to get one on Apple silicon. Miniforge is a small installer from the conda-forge community that gives you a native Python plus the conda tool; it is the smoothest path on an M-series Mac and is what this walkthrough uses. The other is the official installer from python.org, which is equally fine; if you take that route, download the macOS 64-bit universal2 installer, double-click it, and skip to the next step.

Native matters. Apple silicon runs two kinds of program: native arm64 code, and older Intel code translated on the fly by Rosetta, which runs at roughly half speed and cannot use the Mac's GPU from PyTorch. The check at the end of this step must print `arm64`. If it prints `x86_64`, you have an Intel Python and should uninstall it and start this step again.

The commands below download an installer script, run it, and then tell your shell about the new Python. `curl` fetches a file from the internet; `-L` follows redirects; `-O` saves it under its own name. `bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh -b -p ~/miniforge3` runs the installer in batch mode (`-b`, meaning do not ask questions) into the folder `~/miniforge3` (`-p` for prefix). `conda init zsh` edits your shell's startup file, `~/.zshrc`, so that new terminal windows can find this Python. Because that file is only read when a shell starts, you must close the Terminal window and open a new one before the last line will work.

_Do this._ Install a native arm64 Python, then open a new Terminal window and prove it is native.

```bash
cd ~/Downloads
curl -L -O https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh
bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh -b -p ~/miniforge3
~/miniforge3/bin/conda init zsh

# now quit Terminal (Command-Q), open it again, and run:
python -c "import platform, sys; print(platform.machine(), sys.version)"
which python
```

_What each line does._

- `curl -L -O https://...Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh` — downloads the installer script for Apple silicon into your Downloads folder
- `bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh -b -p ~/miniforge3` — runs it without prompts, installing into a folder called miniforge3 in your home folder
- `~/miniforge3/bin/conda init zsh` — adds a few lines to ~/.zshrc so future terminals find this Python first
- `python -c "...print(platform.machine(), sys.version)"` — runs one line of Python; it must print arm64 followed by a version of 3.11 or newer
- `which python` — shows which file the word python actually runs; it should be inside your miniforge3 folder, not /usr/bin

**Step 4.**

_Before you do this._ A repository, or repo, is a folder whose history git tracks. The course's repo is Traffic1 on GitHub. Cloning it copies the whole folder and its history to your machine.

`git clone URL` creates a folder named after the repo and downloads it. If you have your own copy of Traffic1 on GitHub, use its URL instead. If you have no repo at all yet, take the second block: `git init -b main` turns an ordinary folder into a repo with a first branch called main, which is what GitHub expects.

After cloning, `ls` shows the files. Right now the repo holds the planning documents; the numbered scripts are what you will write during the course, starting with the collector in step 11 of this walkthrough.

_Do this._ Get the project folder onto your machine and go into it.

```bash
cd ~/code
git clone https://github.com/21AG21/Traffic1.git
cd Traffic1
ls

# no repo of your own yet? do this instead:
# mkdir -p ~/code/Traffic1 && cd ~/code/Traffic1 && git init -b main
```

_What each line does._

- `git clone https://github.com/21AG21/Traffic1.git` — downloads the repository and its history into a new folder called Traffic1
- `cd Traffic1` — moves into the project; every command from here on assumes you are in this folder
- `ls` — lists what came down: the plan and lesson documents
- `git init -b main` — the alternative: start a fresh repository in the current folder with main as the first branch

**Step 5.**

_Before you do this._ A virtual environment, or venv, is a private copy of Python and its packages that belongs to one project. Without one, every project shares a single set of packages and they eventually conflict: one project needs an old pandas, another needs a new one, and installing for one breaks the other. With one, each project gets its own, and deleting the folder undoes everything cleanly.

`python -m venv .venv` runs Python's built-in venv tool and creates a folder called `.venv` inside your project. The leading dot means the Finder and `ls` hide it by default; `ls -a` shows hidden files. The name `.venv` is a convention that VS Code recognizes automatically.

Creating it is not enough; you must activate it. `source .venv/bin/activate` changes the current terminal so the word `python` means the one inside `.venv`. You will see `(.venv)` appear at the start of your prompt, which is how you know it is on. Activation lasts only for that terminal window: every new window, and every restart, needs the `source` line again. `deactivate` turns it off.

The `.venv` folder is large and is rebuilt from requirements.txt in one command, so it never goes into git. Step 9 adds it to `.gitignore`.

_Do this._ Create the project's virtual environment, turn it on, and confirm which Python is now in charge.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
which python
python -V
```

_What each line does._

- `python -m venv .venv` — creates the private environment in a hidden folder called .venv
- `source .venv/bin/activate` — switches this terminal into it; your prompt gains a (.venv) prefix
- `which python` — must now print .../Traffic1/.venv/bin/python — inside the project, not miniforge3
- `python -V` — prints the version, which should match the Python you installed

**Step 6.**

_Before you do this._ `requirements.txt` is a plain text file listing the packages the project needs, one per line, so anyone (including you on a new machine) can install all of them with one command. This is the file you asked about, and here is exactly what to put in it.

Each line is a package name and a version rule. `pandas>=2.2` means 'at least 2.2, newer is fine'. Loose rules like that are right while you are setting up, because they always resolve. Once everything works, you freeze the exact versions with `pip freeze > requirements.lock.txt`, and that lock file is what makes a run reproducible months later. Text after `#` is a comment that pip ignores.

Why these packages: pandas and numpy are the table and array libraries; pyarrow lets pandas read and write Parquet; requests fetches the 511 feed; python-dotenv reads your `.env` file; scikit-learn provides the baselines, metrics and calibration; lightgbm is the production model; torch is PyTorch for the neural networks and is the only large download; matplotlib draws the plots; jupyterlab runs notebooks; pytest runs the tests; holidays marks public holidays; psutil measures memory; duckdb runs SQL over Parquet; tqdm draws progress bars; shap explains model predictions.

The command below writes the file using a here-document: `cat > requirements.txt << 'EOF'` means 'take everything up to a line containing EOF and write it into requirements.txt'. The quotes around 'EOF' stop the shell from interpreting anything inside. You can equally create the file in VS Code once step 8 is done, or in TextEdit as plain text; the content is what matters.

_Do this._ Create requirements.txt with exactly these lines.

```bash
cat > requirements.txt << 'EOF'
# data
pandas>=2.2            # tables: read, clean, group, join
numpy>=1.26            # arrays and the maths under pandas
pyarrow>=15.0          # lets pandas read and write Parquet files

# getting the data
requests>=2.31         # HTTP calls to the 511 traffic feed
python-dotenv>=1.0     # loads secrets from the .env file

# models
scikit-learn>=1.4      # baselines, metrics, calibration, splits
lightgbm>=4.3          # gradient boosted trees: the production model
torch>=2.2             # PyTorch, the neural networks (large download)
shap>=0.45             # explains which features drove a prediction

# looking at things
matplotlib>=3.8        # plots
jupyterlab>=4.1        # notebooks for exploring

# the rest
pytest>=8.0            # tests
holidays>=0.45         # public holiday calendar for the feature set
psutil>=5.9            # memory and timing for every pipeline stage
duckdb>=0.10           # SQL over Parquet without a database server
tqdm>=4.66             # progress bars for long loops
EOF

cat requirements.txt
```

_What each line does._

- `cat > requirements.txt << 'EOF'` — starts writing the file; everything until the EOF line goes into it
- `pandas>=2.2` — one requirement: the package name, then the lowest version that will do
- `# tables: read, clean, group, join` — a comment; pip ignores everything after the hash
- `EOF` — ends the here-document and closes the file
- `cat requirements.txt` — prints the file back so you can see it saved correctly

**Step 7.**

_Before you do this._ `pip` is Python's package installer. It reads requirements.txt and downloads each package from PyPI, the public package index. Because your venv is active, everything lands inside `.venv` and nothing touches the rest of your machine.

Upgrade pip itself first; old versions sometimes fail to find the right wheel. A wheel is a pre-built package: if one exists for your Mac, installation is a fast download, and if not, pip compiles from source, which is slow and is where the command line tools from step 2 earn their place. Expect the whole install to take a few minutes, most of it PyTorch.

Then verify by importing everything and asking PyTorch whether it can see the Mac's GPU. MPS stands for Metal Performance Shaders, Apple's GPU interface; `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` printing True means later lessons can train on the GPU. False is not fatal, it just means training runs on the processor.

One known failure on macOS: `import lightgbm` raising an error about `libomp` or OpenMP. LightGBM needs Apple's OpenMP runtime, which is not bundled. The fix is Homebrew, the package manager for macOS: install it from brew.sh with the one line on that page, then run `brew install libomp`, then open a new terminal and try again.

_Do this._ Install everything from the file, then prove each import works.

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt

python - << 'EOF'
import platform, pandas as pd, numpy as np, sklearn, lightgbm as lgb, torch
print("machine      ", platform.machine())
print("pandas       ", pd.__version__)
print("numpy        ", np.__version__)
print("scikit-learn ", sklearn.__version__)
print("lightgbm     ", lgb.__version__)
print("torch        ", torch.__version__)
print("GPU (mps)    ", torch.backends.mps.is_available())
EOF
```

_What each line does._

- `python -m pip install --upgrade pip` — updates the installer itself before it does any real work
- `pip install -r requirements.txt` — reads the file and installs every package into the active venv
- `python - << 'EOF' ... EOF` — runs the block of Python between the markers without saving it to a file
- `print("machine", platform.machine())` — arm64 again: this time it proves the venv's Python is native too
- `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` — True means PyTorch can use the Mac's GPU in the neural network lessons

**Step 9.**

_Before you do this._ `.gitignore` is a list of things git must never record. It has to exist before your first commit, because git history is permanent: a secret committed once stays in the history even if you delete the file in the next commit, and public repositories are scanned by bots within minutes of a push.

Four kinds of thing belong in it. Secrets, meaning `.env`. Data, because the PeMS files are hundreds of megabytes a day and are re-downloadable. Anything rebuildable: `.venv`, trained models, outputs, logs, Python's `__pycache__` folders. And editor or operating system litter such as `.DS_Store`.

Patterns are simple. A name ending in `/` matches a folder, `*.pyc` matches by extension, and a line starting with `!` is an exception that keeps a file which an earlier pattern excluded. The `!.env.example` line below is exactly that: the real `.env` stays out, but a template with empty values stays in, so the next person knows which variables to set.

_Do this._ Write .gitignore before anything is committed.

```bash
cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
# secrets
.env
!.env.example

# data and anything rebuilt from it
data/
models/
output/
logs/

# the environment
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# notebooks and macOS litter
.ipynb_checkpoints/
.DS_Store
EOF

git status --short
```

_What each line does._

- `.env` — the secrets file: never recorded
- `!.env.example` — an exception: the template with blank values is recorded, so the file list is documented
- `data/` — the trailing slash means a folder; everything inside it is ignored
- `*.pyc` — ignores compiled Python files wherever they appear
- `git status --short` — lists what git currently sees as new or changed; data and .venv must not appear

**Step 10.**

_Before you do this._ 511.org is the Bay Area's traveller information service, and its traffic events feed is one of the two data sources for the model. The key is free: go to 511.org/open-data/token, fill in your name and email, and the token arrives by email as a long string of letters, digits and dashes.

A token is a secret. It goes in a file called `.env`, one `NAME=value` per line, with no spaces around the equals sign and no quotes. Nothing else reads that file by magic: the `python-dotenv` package's `load_dotenv()` reads it and puts the values into `os.environ`, the dictionary of environment variables that Python programs can see.

Name the variable `TOKEN_511` rather than `511_TOKEN`, because shell variable names cannot start with a digit and you will eventually want to export it by hand.

Write `.env.example` alongside it with the same names and empty values. It is the documented list of what a newcomer must supply, and it is safe to commit because it contains no secret.

_Do this._ Get a free 511 token, put it in .env, and write the example file beside it.

```bash
cat > .env << 'EOF'
TOKEN_511=paste-your-token-here
EOF

cat > .env.example << 'EOF'
# copy this file to .env and fill in your own values
TOKEN_511=
EOF

python -c "from dotenv import load_dotenv; import os; load_dotenv(); print('token loaded:', bool(os.environ.get('TOKEN_511')))"
```

_What each line does._

- `TOKEN_511=paste-your-token-here` — replace the right-hand side with the token from your email; no quotes, no spaces
- `.env.example with an empty value` — documents the variable without revealing it, and is safe to commit
- `load_dotenv()` — reads .env from the current folder and adds its names to os.environ
- `print('token loaded:', bool(os.environ.get('TOKEN_511')))` — prints True when the token was found; False means the file is misspelt or you are in the wrong folder

**Step 11.**

_Before you do this._ Now the first real script: it asks 511 for the current traffic events near Fremont and appends them to a CSV file, one row per event per poll. Run it every few minutes and you build the incident history the model later joins to the detector data.

What the code uses. `requests.get(url, params={...})` makes the web request and builds the query string for you. The 511 response carries a byte-order mark, an invisible marker at the start of the text that makes a plain `.json()` call fail with a confusing error, so the code decodes the bytes with `utf-8-sig`, which strips it. `.get('key')` on a dictionary returns `None` instead of crashing when a field is missing, which matters because not every event has every field. `csv.DictWriter` writes dictionaries as rows and can write the header line only when the file is new. `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` stamps each row with when we pulled it, in UTC. The `try` and `except` around the request means a network blip prints a message instead of killing the program. And `if __name__ == '__main__':` at the bottom means the file runs when you call it directly but stays importable from other scripts and tests.

Before trusting any of it, the script prints how many events came back and the keys of the first one, so you see the real shape of the data rather than assuming it.

_Do this._ Write 02_collect_events.py, run it once, and look at what it wrote.

```python
# 02_collect_events.py
import csv, os, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

URL = "https://api.511.org/traffic/events"
OUT = Path("data/fremont_events_log.csv")
FIELDS = ["pulled_at", "id", "event_type", "severity", "headline", "roads", "created", "updated"]


def fetch_events(token):
    r = requests.get(URL, params={"api_key": token, "format": "json"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json() if not r.content.startswith(b"\xef\xbb\xbf") else __import__("json").loads(r.content.decode("utf-8-sig"))


def flatten(event, pulled_at):
    roads = event.get("roads") or []
    return {
        "pulled_at": pulled_at,
        "id": event.get("id"),
        "event_type": event.get("event_type"),
        "severity": event.get("severity"),
        "headline": (event.get("headline") or "").replace("\n", " "),
        "roads": "; ".join(r.get("name", "") for r in roads),
        "created": event.get("created"),
        "updated": event.get("updated"),
    }


def main():
    load_dotenv()
    token = os.environ.get("TOKEN_511")
    if not token:
        sys.exit("No TOKEN_511 in .env — see step 10.")

    try:
        payload = fetch_events(token)
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        sys.exit(f"Could not reach 511: {e}")

    events = payload.get("events", [])
    print(f"{len(events)} events came back")
    if events:
        print("fields on the first one:", sorted(events[0].keys()))

    pulled_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    OUT.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    new_file = not OUT.exists()
    with OUT.open("a", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=FIELDS)
        if new_file:
            w.writeheader()
        for e in events:
            w.writerow(flatten(e, pulled_at))
    print(f"wrote {len(events)} rows to {OUT}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

_What each line does._

- `requests.get(URL, params={...}, timeout=30)` — asks 511 for the events; timeout stops it hanging forever
- `r.raise_for_status()` — turns an HTTP error such as 401 (bad token) into a Python exception you can see
- `decode("utf-8-sig")` — strips the invisible byte-order mark that would otherwise break JSON parsing
- `event.get("severity")` — returns None for a missing field instead of crashing
- `datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()` — the moment of this poll, in UTC, as text; the delay between created and pulled_at is the model's blind spot
- `OUT.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` — creates the data folder the first time, and does nothing after that
- `OUT.open("a", ...)` — opens the file in append mode so each run adds to the history
- `if new_file: w.writeheader()` — writes the column names only when the file was just created
- `if __name__ == "__main__": main()` — runs main() when you launch the file, but not when a test imports it

_Before you do this._ Now run it and read the output. Save the file in VS Code (Command and S), then run it from the terminal with the venv active. Three things should happen: a count of events, the field names of the first one, and a line saying rows were written.

Common failures and what they mean. `No TOKEN_511 in .env` means the file is missing, misspelt, or you are in the wrong folder. A 401 error means the token is wrong; copy it again without spaces. `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named requests` means the venv is not active in this terminal, so run `source .venv/bin/activate` and try again.

`head -2` prints the first two lines of a file: the header and one event. `wc -l` counts lines. Run the script twice, a minute apart, and the line count grows while the header stays single, which is the append working correctly.

- `wc -l ...csv` — counts the lines; run the script again and this number grows

**Step 13.**

_Before you do this._ Time to record the work. Git has three places: the working tree (your files), the staging area (what the next commit will contain), and the repository (the permanent history). `git add` moves changes into staging, `git commit` writes them into history with a message, `git push` sends them to GitHub.

Check before you commit, every time. `git status --short` lists what will go in: `??` means untracked, `A` means added, `M` means modified. If `data/` or `.env` appear here, stop and fix `.gitignore` first, because after a commit and push it is too late and the honest fix becomes rotating the token.

`git ls-files` lists what git is actually tracking, which is the strongest check available: piping it through `grep` and counting should give zero for both the environment file and the data folder.

If you cloned from GitHub, `git push` already knows where to send things. If you started with `git init`, create an empty repository on GitHub first, then add it as the remote named origin, as the commented lines show. `-u` on the first push links your local main to the remote one so later pushes are just `git push`.

_Do this._ Check what is staged, commit, and push, proving no secret went with it.

```bash
git status --short
git ls-files | grep -c -E '^\.env$|^data/' || echo "0 secrets tracked — good"

git add -A
git status --short
git commit -m "Set up the environment and the 511 collector"

# only if you started with git init:
# git remote add origin https://github.com/YOURNAME/Traffic1.git

git push -u origin main
git log --oneline -3
```

_What each line does._

- `git status --short` — the pre-commit check: two-letter codes beside every file that changed
- `git ls-files | grep -c -E '^\.env$|^data/'` — counts tracked secrets and data files; anything but zero means fix .gitignore now
- `git add -A` — stages every change in the folder, respecting .gitignore
- `git commit -m "..."` — writes the staged changes into history with a message saying why
- `git push -u origin main` — sends the commits to GitHub and remembers the destination
- `git log --oneline -3` — shows the last three commits, newest first, one line each
