### Done when

- `pytest -q` prints all green, and the count includes the 9 tests of `tests/test_labels.py`, the 11 of `tests/test_incidents.py`, the 9 of `tests/test_features.py` (with the perturbed-future leakage test among them) and the 7 of `tests/test_split.py`.
- `python 11_build_labels.py && python 12_join_incidents.py && python 13_feature_engineering.py` on every month present ends with three `stage=` lines in `logs/pipeline.log`, each with `rss_gb` under 3, and `ls data/labels data/incidents data/features` shows one file per month in each folder with the same row count in labels and incidents.
- `python 13_feature_engineering.py --check 20` passes the leakage assert on every month, and `python -c "import pandas as pd; d=pd.read_parquet('data/features/2026-03.parquet'); print(d.dtypes.value_counts())"` shows no float64 and no object.
- `python 14_train_baselines.py` writes `output/baselines.json` with persistence AP falling from 15 to 60 minutes, and `python 15_train_logreg.py` prints coefficient rows that agree to two decimals for all three horizons.
- `python 16_train_lgbm.py && python 16b_calibrate_select.py` produce `models/gbt_h{15,30,60}_thresh0.6_win3.txt`, three feature lists, `categorical_dtypes.joblib`, three `iso_h{h}.joblib` and `calibration.json` with a `tau` below 1.0 at every horizon.
- One table: `python 18_evaluate_lead_time.py` (validation) prints persistence, profile rate, logistic and LightGBM at 15, 30 and 60 minutes on the chronological validation split, and the same table is in `docs/stages/18_evaluate_lead_time.md`; LightGBM's AP beats persistence at 30 and 60 minutes, and you have written whether it clears the plan's bar (twice persistence at 30 minutes).
- A reliability diagram near the diagonal after calibration: `output/reliability_h30.png` from the test run shows the calibrated curve within the bin noise of the diagonal, and `ece` for `lightgbm` in `output/evaluation_report.json` is below the plan's 0.05, or the page says by how much it misses.
- `python studies/leakage_experiment.py` has written `output/studies/leakage_experiment.json`, and the notebook has the gap and two sentences on why it exists; `output/studies/shap_summary.png` exists and the notebook says which features the gain and SHAP rankings disagree on.
- You explained every number in the table to someone else, and they could repeat it: for each of the twelve cells, what the metric is, what split it was computed on, what the baseline in the same column is, and why the horizon changes it. Write their name and the date in the notebook.

### Pitfalls

- Judging by accuracy. With 3 to 10 % positives, a model that never alerts is 90 % accurate. The report has no accuracy column on purpose; `evaluate.row_metrics()` does not compute it, and the headline is average precision beside prevalence.
- Tuning on the test split, even once. Any choice made after looking at a test number makes that number a validation number, and there is no third split left. `18` defaults to `--split validation`; run `--split test` once, at the end, and write the date in the notebook and the stage page.
- Celebrating an AUC that persistence also gets. At 15 minutes the ROC-AUC of persistence is high because speed five minutes ago is an excellent forecast; a model with the same number has learned nothing. Every model row in the table has `skill_vs_persistence`; the plan's bar is twice persistence at 30 minutes, and a horizon with no skill is dropped, not decorated.
- The profile leaks. If `fit_profile()` is given rows after `train_end`, test-period speeds shape training labels and every metric moves up a little for a reason you will never find. `11` filters on `split_dates().train_end` before fitting, `test_profile_uses_training_rows_only` checks it, and the profile file carries the split name.
- Missing speeds become label 0. `rolling(3).sum() == 3` reads a NaN window as "not slow", so a dead detector looks free-flowing and the model learns that gaps are safe. `labels.apply_profile()` writes `label_known`, `features.add_targets()` turns the target to NaN where it is 0, and `13` drops those rows.
- The target shifted the wrong way. `shift(6)` looks back; `shift(-6)` looks forward. With the sign wrong the model predicts the past, scores an AP near 1, and `test_targets_shift_forward` fails. That test exists for this line alone.
- Lags cross a station boundary. A `shift()` without `groupby('station_id')` gives the first rows of station B the last speeds of station A. `add_history()` asserts the sort and groups every shift; `test_lag_equals_row_k_back_within_station` checks the first three rows of every station are NaN.
- The first hour of every month vanishes. Without the apron, lags at the start of a month and targets at its end are NaN and get dropped, and the row after midnight looks like a station returning from an outage. `load_month_with_apron()` reads twelve steps on each side and trims after building.
- Zeros in the incident columns for months before the poller. The model learns that "no incident" means "an old month" and the incident features look useless or harmful. The stage 7 page names the first polled day; train once with `--drop-incidents` on the polled era and report the difference instead of guessing.
- Category codes that mean different stations in training and serving. Casting with a fresh `CategoricalDtype` at serving time renumbers the stations and the trees split on the wrong ids without an error. `16` saves `categorical_dtypes.joblib`; `16b`, `18` and phase 9 cast with it and never build their own.
- The calibration looks perfect because it was judged on the rows it was fit on. `16b`'s ECE is in-sample for the map; the diagram that counts is `18`'s on the test split. Phase 6 adds the first-half, second-half check to `16b`.
- A threshold of 0.5. `tau_h` is whatever calibrated probability keeps `ALERT_PRECISION` on validation and it differs by horizon; it lives in `calibration.json`, and no file in the repository compares a probability with a literal 0.5.
- `profile_label_rate` is a target encoding. On training rows it contains the row's own label, one part in n per cell, which with `PROFILE_MIN_N` samples is small but not zero. If it tops the SHAP ranking at 15 minutes, compute it leave-one-out or drop it, and say which in the stage 8 page.
- Early stopping that never stops. A `best_iteration` equal to `LGBM_ROUNDS` means validation AP was still rising, or the metric name is wrong and LightGBM is watching something else. Check `metric='average_precision'` in `common.LGBM_PARAMS` and that `valid_sets` is the validation set, not training.
- float64 creeping in. A `merge` with a float64 rate table or a `np.sin` without a cast doubles the feature table and the training memory. `build_features()` casts every float column to float32 at the end, and the Done when checks `dtypes.value_counts()`.

## Phase 5: Classical machine learning, the rest

_weeks 22–28 · ≈50 h · builds a regression twin, station clusters, a tuned model_

**Goal.** The rest of the classical toolbox: regression and its metrics, other classifiers and multiclass, unsupervised learning, tuning done honestly, and the information theory under it all.

### What you need to learn

- Regression: least squares, ridge and lasso, quantile regression; MAE, RMSE, MAPE, R², residual plots.
- k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines and kernels; softmax and multiclass metrics; ordinal targets.
- Clustering (k-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN), principal components, anomaly detection; how to judge unsupervised results.
- Hyperparameter search: grid, random, Bayesian, early stopping of trials; selection bias and nested validation.
- Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, mutual information; information gain in trees; feature selection.
- Feature scaling, encoding and pipelines in scikit-learn.

### Topic: Regression: predicting a number, and the metrics that judge it

**Goal.** Predict the speed itself, not only whether it will be slow, and know how to score a numeric forecast.

**Age 5.**

Sometimes the question is not 'will it be slow?' but 'how fast will the cars go?' The answer is a number, like 32 miles per hour.

Guessing a number is called regression. You are right when your number is close, and you can measure how far off you were.

_Try this._ Guess how tall your friend is in centimeters, then measure. How far off were you? That distance is your error.

**Middle school.**

A regression model predicts a number from clues. The simplest is a line: speed in 30 minutes ≈ a + b × speed now. Fitting the line means choosing a and b so the guesses are as close as possible to what happened.

How close is close? Mean absolute error is the average distance between guess and truth. Root mean squared error punishes big misses more. R² says how much better you did than just guessing the average every time.

_Try this._ Take ten (speed now, speed 30 minutes later) pairs from one station and plot them. Draw the line you think fits best. Compute the average distance from the line to the points.

**High school.**

Linear regression minimizes the sum of squared errors; with several clues it is y ≈ w·x + b, fit by least squares. Metrics: MAE (robust, in mph), RMSE (sensitive to outliers), MAPE (percent, undefined at zero), R² (fraction of variance explained). Residual plots show where the model fails.

Regularization: ridge (L2) shrinks weights, lasso (L1) zeroes some, both fight overfitting when clues are many or correlated. Quantile regression predicts the 10th or 90th percentile instead of the mean, which is what a 'worst plausible speed' needs.

Trees and networks do regression too: LightGBM with `objective='regression'` or `quantile`, the same features as the classifier, a different target (`speed_t30`).

_Try this._ Train LightGBM to predict `speed_t30` and report MAE against persistence (speed now) and against the profile. Which stations have the largest errors, and at what hour?

**Stanford undergrad.**

Least squares as maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise; the normal equations and their geometry (projection onto the column space); Gauss-Markov; heteroscedasticity and why MAE or quantile losses are preferable when noise scales with level. Bias-variance for regression; ridge as a Bayesian prior; lasso and sparsity; elastic net.

Evaluation subtleties: RMSE decomposition into bias and variance, MASE (scaled by a naive forecast) for comparability across series, and the pinball loss for quantiles. Multi-output regression (three horizons at once) versus three models.

_Try this._ Show that minimizing squared error yields the conditional mean and minimizing absolute error yields the conditional median, and explain which the traffic product should report.

**Stanford grad.**

Generalized linear models unify regression targets (Gaussian, Poisson for counts such as flow, Gamma for positive skewed durations). Heteroscedastic and distributional regression (predict mean and variance, or full quantile sets) are the bridge to uncertainty. Regression under dependence: errors autocorrelated in time, spatially correlated across stations, and what that does to standard errors and to cross-validation.

Trees regress piecewise-constantly and cannot extrapolate; linear models extrapolate linearly and can be wildly wrong; networks are in between. Monotone and shape constraints in gradient boosting encode physics.

_Try this._ Fit a Poisson GLM to flow counts with calendar features and compare its calibration of predicted variance with a squared-error model. Then fit quantile boosting at 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 and check pinball loss and crossing.

**PhD at Apple.**

Production forecasting is regression at scale: hierarchical targets, reconciliation across levels (station, route, city), distributional outputs for downstream optimization, and metrics chosen by the decision they serve (ETA error weighted by trips, not by rows). Research threads: distribution-free intervals for regression, multi-horizon coherence, and losses aligned with downstream utility.

_Try this._ Propose the regression target and metric for a route-level travel-time product built on station speeds, and say how station-level errors compound along a route.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why is RMSE larger than MAE on the same data?</summary>

Squaring weights large errors more; RMSE is at least MAE and the gap grows with outliers.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does R² = 0 mean?</summary>

The model does no better than predicting the mean every time. It can be negative when the model is worse than that.

</details>

### Topic: Other classifiers and multiclass: k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines, softmax

**Goal.** Know the rest of the classical toolbox, when each wins, and how two-class methods extend to many classes.

**Age 5.**

There are many ways to sort things into groups. One way: look at the things nearest to you and copy their label. Another: count how often each clue shows up in each group. Another: draw the widest possible gap between the groups.

_Try this._ Sort a pile of leaves into trees by looking at each leaf's closest match among leaves you already know. That is nearest neighbors.

**Middle school.**

k-nearest neighbors predicts by finding the k most similar past rows and voting. Naive Bayes multiplies the chance of each clue given each class, assuming clues are independent, which is naive but often works. A support vector machine finds the boundary with the widest margin between classes.

When there are more than two classes (light, moderate, heavy congestion), softmax turns scores into probabilities that add to one, and the loss is cross-entropy over all classes.

_Try this._ With five past rows labelled slow or fine and their speeds, classify a new row using k = 3 nearest neighbors by speed. Change k to 1 and 5; does the answer change?

**High school.**

k-NN: no training, all the cost at prediction; needs scaled features and a distance; works when similar inputs have similar outputs and data are plentiful. Naive Bayes: fast, works with counts and text, calibrates badly. SVM: maximize margin, use kernels to draw curved boundaries, strong on small clean data, slow on millions of rows.

Multiclass: one-vs-rest, one-vs-one, or native softmax (logistic regression and networks). Metrics generalize: per-class precision and recall, macro versus micro averages, the confusion matrix as the primary picture. Ordinal classes (light < moderate < heavy) deserve ordinal losses or a regression on the ratio.

_Try this._ Turn the speed ratio into three classes (above 0.8, 0.6 to 0.8, below 0.6) and train a softmax logistic regression; print the 3 × 3 confusion matrix and macro F1.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Bayes-optimal classification and what each method approximates: k-NN estimates the posterior locally (consistent as k grows with n, cursed by dimension); naive Bayes is a generative model with a factorized likelihood; the SVM is a large-margin discriminative model whose dual reveals the kernel trick and support vectors. Hinge loss versus logistic loss; kernels as inner products in a feature space; the representer theorem.

Softmax regression as the multinomial logit; its gradient generalizes p − y to a vector. Calibration in multiclass (temperature scaling). Cost-sensitive learning and thresholding per class.

_Try this._ Derive the dual of the soft-margin SVM and identify the support vectors; then show that kernel k-NN and kernel SVM use the same similarity in different ways.

**Stanford grad.**

Where each method still matters: k-NN as a retrieval baseline and in nearest-neighbor search at scale (approximate methods, vector databases); naive Bayes as a fast text baseline; SVMs in small-sample scientific settings and as the origin of kernel methods leading to Gaussian processes. Structured prediction and sequence labelling as multiclass over structured outputs.

Metric choice under class imbalance in multiclass, hierarchical classification, and label noise. The relation between margin theory (SVMs, boosting) and generalization.

_Try this._ Implement a kernelized ridge classifier and a linear SVM on the same features; compare margins and calibration, and explain why the boosted trees still win on this data.

**PhD at Apple.**

Nearest-neighbor retrieval is now infrastructure (embeddings plus approximate search underlie retrieval-augmented systems and recommenders); kernel methods live on in theory (neural tangent kernels) and in Gaussian processes. The practical multiclass problems at scale are extreme classification (millions of labels) and hierarchical, cost-sensitive decisions.

_Try this._ Design an approximate nearest-neighbor index over per-station day embeddings to find 'days like today' as a forecasting baseline, and state its failure modes.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why does k-NN need scaled features?</summary>

Distance mixes units; an unscaled flow in vehicles swamps a speed in mph, so the neighbors are chosen by one feature only.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does softmax guarantee?</summary>

A vector of positive numbers that sum to one, so the outputs can be read as class probabilities.

</details>

### Topic: Unsupervised learning: clustering, principal components and anomaly detection

**Goal.** Find structure with no labels: groups of similar stations or days, compact descriptions of many columns, and rows that look wrong.

**Age 5.**

Sometimes nobody tells you the answers, and you just sort things into piles that look alike. That is unsupervised learning: finding groups on your own.

It can also spot the odd one out, like the one sensor that says cars are going 200 miles per hour.

_Try this._ Dump out a box of buttons and sort them into piles however makes sense to you. Now find the button that fits no pile.

**Middle school.**

Clustering groups similar rows: k-means picks k centers and assigns each row to the nearest one, then moves the centers, and repeats. Days could cluster into 'normal weekday', 'holiday', 'crash day'.

Principal component analysis finds the few directions along which the data vary most, so sixty columns can be summarized by a handful. Anomaly detection flags rows far from everything else, which is how you catch a broken detector.

_Try this._ Take one station's daily speed profiles (288 numbers per day) for a month and run k-means with k = 3. Which days landed together? Look at the odd cluster.

**High school.**

k-means (choose k with the elbow or silhouette), hierarchical clustering (a tree of merges), DBSCAN (density, no k, finds noise). PCA: center, take the top eigenvectors of the covariance, project; explained variance tells how many to keep. Anomaly detection: distance from the profile, isolation forests, or reconstruction error.

Uses here: cluster stations by their weekly profile to find station types; PCA on the 288-slot daily profile to get a few 'shape' features; anomaly scores to flag detector faults before they poison training.

_Try this._ Run PCA on daily speed profiles across all stations and plot the first two components colored by weekday. What does component one measure?

**Stanford undergrad.**

Clustering as optimization (k-means as coordinate descent on within-cluster variance; Gaussian mixtures and EM as its probabilistic version), the meaning of a 'good' clustering (no ground truth; stability and downstream utility), and the curse of dimensionality for distances. PCA as the best low-rank approximation (Eckart-Young), its relation to the SVD, and its limits (linear, variance is not always signal). Nonlinear reduction (t-SNE, UMAP) for visualization only.

Anomaly detection formally: density estimation and its thresholds; one-class methods; the distinction between point, contextual and collective anomalies (a detector stuck at 65 mph is contextual).

_Try this._ Implement k-means and EM for a Gaussian mixture from scratch in numpy on the daily profiles, and show that k-means is the limit of EM as the variances shrink.

**Stanford grad.**

Representation learning as the modern form of unsupervised learning: autoencoders, contrastive methods, and the fact that most 'unsupervised' structure now comes from pretext tasks. Mixture models and latent-variable models for regime detection on the fundamental diagram; hidden Markov models for congestion states over time. Evaluation of unsupervised methods through downstream tasks and through stability under resampling.

Anomaly detection under distribution shift: what counts as anomalous changes with roadwork; contextual detection using the profile and neighbors.

_Try this._ Fit a hidden Markov model with three states to a station's speed and occupancy and compare the inferred states with the relative and absolute labels; where do they disagree?

**PhD at Apple.**

Unsupervised structure at scale underlies embeddings, retrieval, and pretraining; the research frontier is in self-supervised objectives, in identifiability of latent variables, and in detection of anomalies and drift without labels in streaming systems. For sensor networks, unsupervised detector-health models are a product in their own right.

_Try this._ Propose a self-supervised pretraining task on unlabeled PeMS history for all of California and argue what representation it would learn and how you would test transfer to Fremont.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why is there no accuracy for clustering?</summary>

There are no labels to compare with. You judge clusters by stability, by interpretability, and by whether they help a downstream task.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does the first principal component of daily profiles usually capture?</summary>

Overall level, how slow or fast the whole day was. Shape differences come in the later components.

</details>

### Topic: Hyperparameter tuning and model selection

**Goal.** Choose settings and models with a budget and without fooling yourself.

**Age 5.**

A learning machine has dials, like how many questions a tree may ask. Turning the dials changes how well it learns. Finding good dial settings is tuning, and you check each setting on a quiz the machine has not seen.

_Try this._ Set a kitchen timer to different times for cooking rice. Which time gives the best rice? That is tuning one dial.

**Middle school.**

Hyperparameters are settings you choose, not things the model learns: number of leaves, learning rate, how many lags to use. Tuning tries settings and keeps the best by the validation score. Grid search tries every combination; random search tries random ones and is usually better for the same effort.

The trap: if you try a thousand settings and pick the best on validation, the validation score is now too optimistic. That is why the test split stays untouched until the end.

_Try this._ Train LightGBM with learning rates 0.01, 0.05, 0.2 and leaves 15, 63, 255. Make a 3 × 3 table of validation AP. Is the best corner where you expected?

**High school.**

Search strategies: grid, random, Bayesian optimization (build a model of score versus settings and pick the most promising next point), and early-stopping-based methods such as successive halving that kill bad trials early. Tools: Optuna. Rules: tune few things (learning rate, leaves, min data in leaf, feature fraction), on the chronological validation split, with a fixed budget of trials, and log every trial.

Model selection is the same problem one level up: which model family to ship. Use the same validation protocol, compare against baselines, and prefer the simpler model unless the gain is clear and reproducible across folds.

_Try this._ Run 30 Optuna trials over four LightGBM parameters with early stopping, plot validation AP against trial number, and check how much the best trial beats the defaults.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Why random beats grid (most dials matter little, so sampling explores the important ones more densely); Bayesian optimization with Gaussian processes or tree-structured estimators; multi-fidelity methods (Hyperband). The selection bias of picking the maximum of many noisy scores, and nested cross-validation as the honest fix. Learning curves to decide whether more data or more capacity helps.

For time series: tuning on rolling-origin folds, reporting the spread, and re-tuning cadence when retraining monthly.

_Try this._ Simulate selecting the best of N random models with pure-noise validation scores and plot the expected 'best' score against N; then explain what nested cross-validation changes.

**Stanford grad.**

AutoML as automated pipeline search; its wins on benchmarks and its costs in compute and interpretability. Hyperparameter importance analysis (which dials mattered) as a research tool. Transfer of hyperparameters across tasks and scales, and scaling laws as principled tuning for large models. The reproducibility problem: reported gains within tuning noise.

_Try this._ Fit a functional ANOVA on your tuning trials to estimate each parameter's importance, and use it to prune the search space for the monthly retrain.

**PhD at Apple.**

At scale, tuning is an engineering system: distributed trials, early stopping, warm starts from previous versions, and budgets set by cost. The research frontier includes learning-rate-free methods, tuning under distribution shift, and using scaling laws to extrapolate from small runs.

_Try this._ Design the tuning policy for the monthly retrain: what is re-tuned, what is inherited, how many trials, and the statistical test that decides whether the new configuration replaces the old.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why does random search often beat grid search?</summary>

Most parameters matter little; random search spends its trials exploring more distinct values of the ones that matter.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why must the test split stay untouched during tuning?</summary>

Any choice made by looking at a score on a split makes that score optimistic; the test split is the one score you never chose on.

</details>

### Topic: Information theory in machine learning: entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, mutual information

**Goal.** See why cross-entropy is the loss, what KL divergence measures, and how mutual information screens features.

**Age 5.**

Information is surprise. If I tell you the sun rose today, that is no surprise, so little information. If I tell you it snowed in Fremont, that is a big surprise.

A learning machine is trying to be less surprised by what happens. Its score is how surprised it was.

_Try this._ Play twenty questions and count how many yes-or-no questions you need. Fewer questions means the answer carried less surprise.

**Middle school.**

Entropy measures how unpredictable something is: a fair coin has one bit of entropy, a coin that always lands heads has zero. Cross-entropy measures how surprised your model is by the truth: if you said 90 % slow and it was slow, small surprise; if you said 5 % and it was slow, big surprise.

Training minimizes the average surprise, which is exactly the cross-entropy loss of lesson 7. Mutual information measures how much knowing one thing (rain) reduces your uncertainty about another (slow).

_Try this._ Compute the surprise −log₂(p) for p = 0.9, 0.5 and 0.05. Notice how fast it grows as p shrinks.

**High school.**

Entropy H(p) = −Σ p log p. Cross-entropy H(p, q) = −Σ p log q is the expected surprise when the truth follows p and you predicted q. KL divergence KL(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p) is the extra surprise from using q instead of p; it is zero only when q = p and it is not symmetric. Minimizing cross-entropy over your model's q is minimizing KL to the truth.

Mutual information I(X; Y) = KL between the joint and the product of marginals; it is zero when independent and captures nonlinear dependence, which correlation misses. Decision trees choose splits by information gain, a drop in entropy.

_Try this._ Estimate the mutual information between each feature (binned) and `y_30` on one month; rank the features and compare the ranking with LightGBM's gain importance.

**Stanford undergrad.**

The source-coding theorem gives entropy its meaning (bits needed on average); cross-entropy is the cost of coding with the wrong distribution. Maximum likelihood equals cross-entropy minimization equals KL minimization. Proper scoring rules and the log score. Differential entropy and its caveats. Mutual information estimation from data is hard in high dimensions; binning and k-NN estimators.

Applications: the information bottleneck as a view of representation learning, entropy regularization, and the variational lower bound (ELBO) which is the KL machinery behind variational autoencoders.

_Try this._ Prove KL(p‖q) ≥ 0 with Jensen's inequality and derive the ELBO for a latent-variable model as a KL identity.

**Stanford grad.**

Information theory in learning theory: mutual-information generalization bounds, minimum description length and Occam, channel capacity as a limit on what noisy features can carry about a target. Rate-distortion as the theory of lossy compression, which is what representation learning does. Estimating mutual information with neural estimators and their pitfalls.

_Try this._ Bound the achievable average precision from the mutual information between the feature set and the target on a synthetic problem, and discuss why the bound is loose for real features.

**PhD at Apple.**

Information-theoretic ideas organize much of modern ML: cross-entropy pretraining of language models, compression as a view of intelligence, and channel-capacity arguments about sensor networks (how much a detector network can tell you about a road). The research frontier includes information-theoretic accounts of generalization in overparameterized models and of what pretraining learns.

_Try this._ Estimate, from data, how much information about a station's speed in 30 minutes is carried by its own history versus by its neighbors versus by the calendar, and what that implies about the horizon at which each source dominates.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why is cross-entropy the loss for classification?</summary>

It is the expected surprise of the truth under the model, which equals the negative log-likelihood; minimizing it moves the model's distribution toward the true one in KL divergence.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does mutual information capture that correlation misses?</summary>

Any dependence, including nonlinear and non-monotone ones; correlation only measures linear association.

</details>

### Read and watch, explained at every level

#### [scikit-learn user guide: Supervised and unsupervised learning](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/supervised_learning.html)

_docs · free · an afternoon · free; one page per method with its pitfalls_

**Age 5.** The manual for a big toolbox of learning methods, with a page for each tool that explains what it is for.

**Middle school.** The scikit-learn user guide has one section per method: nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines, linear models, clustering, principal components, anomaly detection. Each page explains the idea, shows the code, and links an example. Read the page for each method the week you meet it.

**High school.** For the classical-ML phase: the pages on nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, support vector machines, linear models (ridge, lasso, logistic), clustering (k-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical), decomposition (PCA), novelty and outlier detection, and model selection (cross-validation, grid and random search, learning curves). Their examples are runnable on the project's features.

**Stanford undergrad.** The guide is unusually good at stating each method's assumptions, complexity and pitfalls (for instance, k-means's sensitivity to scaling, or the meaning of the SVM's C). Read the 'tips on practical use' sections; they are the accumulated experience of the maintainers.

**Stanford grad.** It is also a reference for evaluation and preprocessing (scalers, encoders, pipelines, `TimeSeriesSplit`). Its consistent API (fit, predict, transform) is the pattern every internal ML library ends up imitating, and the reason to prototype in scikit-learn before writing anything custom.

**PhD at Apple.** scikit-learn's documentation is a public good and a standard; its design decisions (no GPU, no deep learning, stability over novelty) are a deliberate scope that has kept it reliable for fifteen years, which is a lesson in library governance.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Supervised: linear models (OLS, ridge, lasso, elastic net, logistic, quantile, robust), kernel ridge, SVMs, SGD, nearest neighbors, Gaussian processes, naive Bayes, decision trees, ensembles (bagging, forests, boosting, stacking), multiclass and multioutput strategies, feature selection, semi-supervised, isotonic regression, calibration, neural networks. Unsupervised: Gaussian mixtures, manifold learning, clustering (k-means, affinity propagation, mean shift, spectral, hierarchical, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, OPTICS, BIRCH), biclustering, decomposition (PCA, kernel PCA, truncated SVD, dictionary learning, factor analysis, ICA, NMF, LDA), covariance estimation, novelty and outlier detection, density estimation.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Linear models: OLS minimizes ‖Xw − y‖²; ridge adds α‖w‖² (stable under collinearity); lasso adds α‖w‖₁ (sparse); elastic net mixes; `LogisticRegression` with `C` (inverse regularization), solvers and `class_weight`; `QuantileRegressor` with the pinball loss; robust regressors (Huber, RANSAC) for outliers.
2. SVMs: `SVC` with `C` and `kernel` (`linear`, `rbf` with `gamma`, `poly`); the margin, support vectors, and the cost of scaling to many rows (quadratic to cubic); `LinearSVC` for large linear problems; probabilities only via internal calibration.
3. Nearest neighbors: `KNeighborsClassifier` with `n_neighbors` and `weights`; algorithms (brute, KD-tree, ball tree) and when each is efficient; the need for scaling.
4. Naive Bayes: Gaussian, multinomial, Bernoulli, complement variants; fast, good for text, poorly calibrated.
5. Trees and ensembles: `DecisionTreeClassifier` criteria (Gini, entropy), `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, cost-complexity pruning `ccp_alpha`; `RandomForest` with `n_estimators`, `max_features`, out-of-bag score; `HistGradientBoosting` (histogram-based, native NaN and categorical support, early stopping, monotone constraints) as the built-in LightGBM-like learner; `StackingClassifier`.
6. Multiclass and outputs: one-vs-rest and one-vs-one wrappers; `MultiOutputClassifier`; `ClassifierChain`.
7. Feature selection: variance threshold, univariate tests, `SelectFromModel`, recursive feature elimination, sequential selection, all inside pipelines to avoid leakage.
8. Clustering: k-means (inertia, `n_init`, k-means++ initialization, mini-batch), hierarchical (linkage types, dendrograms, connectivity constraints), DBSCAN (`eps`, `min_samples`, noise label −1), HDBSCAN (varying density), spectral (graph Laplacian); evaluation with silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin, and against labels with adjusted Rand and mutual information.
9. Decomposition: PCA (explained variance ratio, whitening, randomized solver), kernel PCA, truncated SVD for sparse data, NMF for non-negative parts, ICA for independent sources; manifold methods (t-SNE, Isomap, UMAP outside sklearn) for visualization only.
10. Outliers and density: `IsolationForest`, `LocalOutlierFactor`, `OneClassSVM`, elliptic envelope; `KernelDensity` with bandwidth; Gaussian mixtures with `n_components`, covariance types and BIC for selection.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
Ridge: min ‖Xw − y‖² + α‖w‖²;  Lasso: min ½‖Xw − y‖² + α‖w‖₁
k-means: min Σ_k Σ_{x∈C_k} ‖x − μ_k‖²
silhouette(i) = (b_i − a_i)/max(a_i, b_i)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- `HistGradientBoosting` is the in-library equivalent of LightGBM and supports NaN, categoricals and monotone constraints.
- Choose clustering by data shape (density, hierarchy, spherical) and judge it by stability and use, not by one score.
- Feature selection belongs inside the pipeline.

**Practice.** Cluster stations by weekly profile with k-means and with hierarchical linkage; compare silhouettes, plot the dendrogram, and check whether the clusters match freeway and direction.

</details>

#### [An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Python (ISLP), chapters 2–4 and 8](https://www.statlearning.com/)

_book · free · three weeks · now chapters 6 (regularization), 9 (SVMs) and 12 (unsupervised)_

**Age 5.** A famous textbook, free, that explains learning machines with pictures and real examples, written by teachers who invented some of the methods.

**Middle school.** Written by statisticians, with Python labs. Chapter 2 explains what learning from data is and why a model can be too simple or too complicated. Chapter 3 is linear regression, chapter 4 is classification including logistic regression, and chapter 8 is trees, forests and boosting. Read a chapter, then do its lab in a notebook.

**High school.** The clearest explanation anywhere of bias versus variance (chapter 2, with figures worth redrawing), of logistic regression as a model of probability (chapter 4), and of why boosting works by fitting small trees to what is left over (chapter 8). Its lab for chapter 8 uses the same scikit-learn calls you will make in stage 9.

**Stanford undergrad.** ISLP is the practical face of The Elements of Statistical Learning. Add chapter 5 on cross-validation and the bootstrap, and chapter 6 on model selection and regularization; together with the core chapters they cover phase 4's theory. Its treatment of the bootstrap is the basis for lesson 6's block bootstrap, with the modification that blocks are days.

**Stanford grad.** After ISLP, go to ESL for proofs and depth. ISLP's boosting section gives the additive-model view; combine it with Friedman's 2001 paper for the gradient view that LightGBM implements. Note where ISLP's examples assume independent rows and how each method's assumptions change under temporal dependence.

**PhD at Apple.** As a citation for standard methods and as a teaching text it is the reference, and its evolution from R to Python editions tracks the field's tooling. For research, its framing of methods as estimators with bias and variance you can reason about is the habit that distinguishes a careful ML engineer from a library user.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Chapter 2, statistical learning: what it is, prediction versus inference, parametric and nonparametric, the bias-variance trade-off, the classification setting and the Bayes classifier, k-nearest neighbors. Chapter 3, linear regression: simple and multiple, coefficient estimates and their accuracy, model fit, qualitative predictors, interactions, nonlinearity, potential problems, comparison with KNN. Chapter 4, classification: logistic regression, multinomial, generative models (LDA, QDA, naive Bayes), comparison, generalized linear models (Poisson regression). Chapter 8, tree-based methods: regression and classification trees, pruning, bagging, random forests, boosting, Bayesian additive regression trees.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. The setup: Y = f(X) + ε; we estimate f for prediction or to understand which inputs matter; reducible versus irreducible error; parametric methods assume a form (linear), nonparametric do not (KNN) and need more data; flexibility versus interpretability.
2. Assessing accuracy: training MSE falls with flexibility but test MSE is U-shaped; expected test error = variance + bias² + irreducible noise; flexible methods have low bias and high variance; cross-validation estimates test error.
3. Classification: the error rate; the Bayes classifier assigns the most probable class and is the lower bound; KNN estimates conditional probabilities locally; small k is flexible (low bias, high variance).
4. Linear regression: least-squares estimates, standard errors and confidence intervals for coefficients, t-tests, R² and residual standard error; multiple regression and the F-test; qualitative predictors as dummies; interaction terms; polynomial terms; diagnostics for nonlinearity, correlated errors (time series!), heteroscedasticity, outliers, high leverage, and collinearity (VIF).
5. Logistic regression: the logit model log(p/(1 − p)) = β₀ + β₁x; maximum likelihood estimation; interpreting coefficients as changes in log odds; multiple logistic regression and confounding; multinomial for several classes.
6. Generative classifiers: model P(X | Y) and the prior, apply Bayes; LDA (shared covariance, linear boundary), QDA (separate covariances), naive Bayes (independent features); ROC curves and the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity; when each method wins.
7. Trees: recursive binary splitting to minimize RSS or Gini/entropy; cost-complexity pruning chosen by cross-validation; trees are interpretable but high variance.
8. Ensembles: bagging averages trees grown on bootstrap samples and out-of-bag error estimates test error; random forests decorrelate trees by sampling m of p predictors at each split; boosting grows trees sequentially on residuals with shrinkage λ, depth d and B trees chosen by cross-validation; variable importance; BART as a Bayesian ensemble.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
E[(y₀ − f̂(x₀))²] = Var(f̂(x₀)) + [Bias(f̂(x₀))]² + Var(ε)
log(p(X)/(1 − p(X))) = β₀ + β₁X
Boosting: f̂ ← f̂ + λ f̂ᵇ, where f̂ᵇ is a depth-d tree fit to the residuals r ← r − λ f̂ᵇ(x)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Test error is U-shaped in flexibility; the bias-variance decomposition says why.
- Logistic coefficients are log odds ratios; generative classifiers model the inputs instead.
- Boosting fits small trees to residuals slowly; shrinkage and the number of trees trade off.

**Practice.** Fit logistic regression, LDA and a random forest to the same traffic features on the chronological split; report AP and a ROC curve for each and explain the ordering using the chapter's arguments about bias and variance.

</details>

#### [Google's Clustering course](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/clustering)

_course · free · a few hours · free; similarity, k-means and how to judge clusters_

**Age 5.** A free short class about sorting things into groups without being told the groups, like putting similar songs together.

**Middle school.** A short free course from Google about clustering: how to measure similarity, the k-means algorithm step by step, how to check whether clusters are any good, and where clustering is used. A few hours. Do it before clustering the stations.

**High school.** Its sections on similarity measures (why scaling matters), on k-means and its failure modes, and on interpreting and evaluating clusters are exactly the unsupervised topic's needs. The section on choosing k with the elbow and silhouette methods is practical.

**Stanford undergrad.** The course is introductory and k-means-centric; pair it with scikit-learn's clustering guide for density-based and hierarchical methods, and with the Gaussian-mixture view for the probabilistic version.

**Stanford grad.** Its emphasis on the similarity measure as the real modelling decision is correct and often skipped; for stations, the choice of profile distance decides the clusters more than the algorithm does.

**PhD at Apple.** A free, focused mini-course; useful as the standard reference when a team disagrees about what a clustering result means.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Clustering overview and workflow; similarity measures (manual and supervised, embeddings); k-means (algorithm, choosing k, advantages and disadvantages); interpreting results and evaluating cluster quality (cardinality, magnitude, downstream performance); and a summary with a worked example.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Uses of clustering: generalization (fill missing values from cluster mates), compression (represent by cluster id), privacy (aggregate), and exploration (structure); clustering is unsupervised, so quality is judged by use.
2. Similarity: prepare data (normalize numerical features, log-transform skewed ones, one-hot or embed categoricals); a manual similarity combines per-feature distances; a supervised similarity learns an embedding (an autoencoder) and measures distance in it; the similarity measure decides the clusters more than the algorithm.
3. k-means: choose k centroids, assign each point to the nearest, recompute centroids as means, repeat until assignments stop changing; it minimizes within-cluster squared distance; initialization matters (k-means++), so run several times; it assumes spherical clusters of similar size and is sensitive to outliers and scale.
4. Choosing k: plot total loss against k and look for the elbow; consider the use case; silhouette as a complementary measure; there is no single right k.
5. Interpreting: check cluster cardinality (sizes) and magnitude (sum of distances) for anomalies; examine features per cluster; verify that similar examples cluster together and dissimilar apart; test clusters in a downstream task.
6. Alternatives: density-based, hierarchical and distribution-based methods for non-spherical or nested structure.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
assign: c_i = argmin_k ‖x_i − μ_k‖²;  update: μ_k = mean{x_i : c_i = k}
```

**Three takeaways.**

- The similarity measure is the modelling decision; the algorithm is secondary.
- Run k-means several times and compare; check cardinality and magnitude for oddities.
- Judge clusters by what they are for.

**Practice.** Cluster stations by their standardized weekly speed profile with k = 3 to 8; plot loss against k, inspect cardinalities, and describe each cluster's typical week in one sentence.

</details>

#### [Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (MacKay)](https://www.inference.org.uk/mackay/itila/)

_book · free · a semester, selectively · free; entropy, coding and learning as one subject_

**Age 5.** A famous free book by a scientist who explained information, coding and learning as one big idea, with puzzles on every page.

**Middle school.** David MacKay's textbook, free online, covers information theory (entropy, coding, compression), probabilistic inference, and machine learning (clustering, neural networks, Gaussian processes) as one subject. It is long; read chapters 1, 2 and 4 for entropy and coding, and the exercises are famously good.

**High school.** Chapters 2 and 4 make entropy and the source-coding theorem concrete; chapter 22 on maximum likelihood and clustering connects to the unsupervised topic; chapter 36 previews decision theory. His writing style, with worked puzzles, rewards patience.

**Stanford undergrad.** The book unifies coding, inference and learning through probability; its chapters on Bayesian inference, on model comparison (Occam's razor as a consequence of marginal likelihood) and on Gaussian processes are a second, deeper take on the Bayesian topic.

**Stanford grad.** MacKay's treatment of the information-theoretic view of learning (chapters on inference and on neural networks as inference) is the intellectual background for variational methods and for the information bottleneck.

**PhD at Apple.** A classic, free, and still one of the best-written technical books in the field; its lectures (also free) are a model of teaching.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Part I, data compression: probability, entropy and inference; the source coding theorem; symbol codes; stream codes. Part II, noisy-channel coding: dependent random variables, the noisy-channel coding theorem, error-correcting codes. Part III, further topics in information theory. Part IV, probabilities and inference: an example inference task (clustering), maximum likelihood and clustering, exact marginalization, Laplace's method, model comparison and Occam's razor, Monte Carlo methods, variational methods, and decision theory. Part V, neural networks: single neurons, capacity, Hopfield networks, Boltzmann machines, supervised learning in multilayer networks, learning as inference, Gaussian processes, deconvolution. Part VI, sparse graph codes.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Probability and inference: the sum and product rules, Bayes' theorem as inference, likelihood, priors, and the argument that all inference is probability; the entropy of a distribution and Gibbs' inequality; information content as −log p.
2. Source coding: a source with entropy H can be compressed to about H bits per symbol and no fewer; Huffman codes for symbols, arithmetic coding for streams; the link to prediction: a good predictive model is a good compressor.
3. Noisy channels: mutual information as the information a received symbol gives about the sent one; channel capacity as the maximum over input distributions; error-correcting codes achieve rates up to capacity; a reading-level pass suffices for this course.
4. Clustering as inference: k-means as a hard assignment, soft k-means with responsibilities, and the connection to Gaussian mixtures and expectation-maximization; maximum likelihood versus Bayesian posteriors over parameters.
5. Model comparison: the evidence (marginal likelihood) automatically penalizes complexity, giving an Occam's razor without ad hoc terms; Laplace's method approximates the evidence with a Gaussian around the mode.
6. Monte Carlo and variational methods: importance sampling, rejection sampling, Metropolis, Gibbs sampling, slice sampling; variational free energy minimization as an alternative to sampling; these are the algorithms behind the Bayesian phase.
7. Neural networks as inference: a neuron as a probabilistic classifier, learning as maximizing a posterior, regularization as priors, error bars on predictions from the posterior, and Gaussian processes as the infinite-width limit of a network with a Bayesian prior.
8. Decision theory: expected utility; the point that a probability model plus a loss function yields the decision, which is exactly the alert threshold rule.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
H(X) = Σ p(x) log₂ (1/p(x));  I(X; Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y)
evidence P(D | M) = ∫ P(D | θ, M) P(θ | M) dθ
soft k-means: r_k(x) ∝ exp(−β ‖x − μ_k‖²)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Prediction and compression are the same problem; cross-entropy measures both.
- The marginal likelihood is a built-in Occam's razor.
- Sampling and variational methods are the two ways to compute Bayesian answers.

**Practice.** Implement soft k-means with a temperature parameter on the daily profiles, watch it become hard k-means as the temperature drops, and relate the responsibilities to a Gaussian mixture's posterior.

</details>

#### [StatQuest with Josh Starmer (YouTube)](https://statquest.org/)

_video · free · hours, as needed · the videos on k-means, PCA, SVMs and regularization_

**Age 5.** Videos with silly songs and simple drawings that explain how learning machines work, one small idea at a time.

**Middle school.** A YouTube channel where each video explains one idea, such as what a decision tree is or how logistic regression works, with drawings and a short song. Watch the videos on decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting and logistic regression during phase 4; they are slow, clear and free.

**High school.** StatQuest's series on gradient boosting (four videos) walks through fitting trees to residuals step by step with numbers, which is exactly lesson 8's mechanism. The videos on ROC and AUC, on cross-validation and on bias and variance give the pictures behind lesson 6. The logistic regression series covers maximum likelihood and the meaning of the coefficients.

**Stanford undergrad.** The channel's strength is tracing a computation with small numbers until it is obvious; use it to check your understanding of a derivation rather than as a source of the derivation. Its XGBoost series covers the second-order split gain, which is the LightGBM math in lesson 8's higher levels.

**Stanford grad.** It stops at intuition and worked examples, which is the right place for a video; the formal accounts are in ISLP and ESL. When you teach, its pattern (a concrete numeric example before any symbol) is worth stealing.

**PhD at Apple.** A reminder that clarity is a research skill; the channel's popularity among practitioners reflects a gap textbooks leave, and it is the resource to hand to a stakeholder who wants to know what a boosted tree actually does.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Hundreds of short videos, each one concept: statistics fundamentals (mean, variance, distributions, p-values, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, maximum likelihood), machine learning fundamentals (bias and variance, cross-validation, confusion matrices, sensitivity and specificity, ROC and AUC), linear models (regression, R², logistic regression series, regularization with ridge, lasso and elastic net), trees (decision trees, regression trees, random forests, AdaBoost, gradient boost series, XGBoost series), support vector machines, PCA and clustering, neural networks and backpropagation, and more.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Maximum likelihood: pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable; for a normal, the sample mean and variance; for logistic regression, the coefficients that maximize the product of predicted probabilities of the observed classes.
2. Logistic regression series: fitting a line to log odds, the S-curve back in probability, maximum likelihood instead of least squares, R² analogues and p-values for coefficients, and the meaning of each coefficient.
3. Bias and variance, cross-validation: bias as inability to capture the true relationship, variance as sensitivity to the training set; k-fold cross-validation to compare methods; the confusion matrix, sensitivity (recall) and specificity, ROC by sweeping thresholds and AUC to compare models.
4. Regularization: ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero to reduce variance; lasso can zero them (feature selection); elastic net mixes; λ chosen by cross-validation.
5. Trees and ensembles: building a classification tree with Gini impurity and a regression tree with squared residuals; random forests with bootstrapping plus random feature subsets and out-of-bag error; AdaBoost's weighted stumps; gradient boost for regression (fit trees to residuals, scale by a learning rate) and for classification (residuals of log odds, leaf values from the sum of residuals over the sum of p(1 − p)); XGBoost's similarity scores, gain, pruning by γ, regularization λ, and the second-order derivation.
6. Support vector machines: the maximal margin classifier, soft margins, and the kernel trick (polynomial, radial) computing high-dimensional dot products cheaply.
7. PCA and clustering: PCA step by step with singular value decomposition, scree plots and loadings; k-means and hierarchical clustering with distance choices.
8. Neural networks: a chain of weighted sums and activations, the chain rule for backpropagation worked with actual numbers, gradient descent step by step.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
Gradient boost (classification): leaf value = Σ residuals / Σ p(1 − p)
XGBoost similarity = (Σ residuals)² / (Σ p(1 − p) + λ);  gain = sim_L + sim_R − sim_root
Ridge: minimize Σ (y − ŷ)² + λ Σ βⱼ²
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Boosting's leaf values come from residuals divided by curvature; XGBoost's gain is the same idea with regularization.
- Regularization trades a little bias for a lot of variance.
- Sensitivity and specificity, precision and recall: know which pairs move together.

**Practice.** Follow the gradient boost classification videos with pencil and paper on eight rows of traffic data: compute the initial log odds, the residuals, one tree's leaf values, and the updated predictions.

</details>

#### [Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization (Bergstra, Bengio, 2012)](https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/bergstra12a.html)

_paper · free · an evening or two · free; why random beats grid_

**Age 5.** A paper that found that trying dial settings at random beats trying them in a neat grid, because only a few dials really matter.

**Middle school.** Bergstra and Bengio showed that random search finds good hyperparameters faster than grid search for the same number of trials. The reason is in one figure: if only one of two dials matters, a grid wastes trials repeating the same values of the important one, while random search tries many different values. Free to read in the Journal of Machine Learning Research.

**High school.** Read the introduction and the figure, then the experiments on neural networks. The lesson generalizes: budget your trials, sample them randomly (or with a smarter method), and look at which parameters actually moved the score.

**Stanford undergrad.** The argument rests on low effective dimensionality of the hyperparameter response surface; the paper also introduces the use of quasi-random sequences. It is the foundation for later Bayesian and multi-fidelity methods, which improve on random search by modelling the response surface.

**Stanford grad.** Compare with Hyperband and Bayesian optimization papers; random search remains the honest baseline that every tuning method must beat, and it parallelizes trivially.

**PhD at Apple.** A rare methodology paper that changed practice immediately; for a lead, its message is that a well-chosen search space and a fixed budget matter more than the search algorithm.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** An empirical and theoretical case that random search over hyperparameters beats grid search for the same number of trials, on neural networks and deep belief networks, with an analysis based on low effective dimensionality and a discussion of quasi-random sequences and of the reproducibility of experiments.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. The problem: hyperparameters (learning rate, layer sizes, regularization) are chosen by trial; grid search evaluates all combinations of a few values per dimension; the number of trials grows exponentially with dimensions.
2. Low effective dimensionality: on most problems, only a few hyperparameters matter, and which ones differ by dataset; a grid with k values per dimension tries only k distinct values of the important one, wasting the rest on repeats.
3. Random search: sample each hyperparameter from its own distribution independently; every trial has a distinct value for every dimension, so the important ones are explored densely; the experiments show equal or better results in a fraction of the trials.
4. Practical benefits: trials are independent and can run in parallel or be stopped and extended; a failed trial does not break the design; adding a new hyperparameter does not require restarting.
5. Quasi-random sequences: low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton) spread points more evenly than pure random, with a small extra gain.
6. Method: define sensible distributions (log-uniform for learning rates and regularization), fix a budget, run, and analyze which hyperparameters actually changed the score.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
learning_rate ~ LogUniform(1e-3, 0.3); num_leaves ~ Uniform{15, …, 255}; min_data_in_leaf ~ LogUniform(20, 2000)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Random search is the honest baseline every tuner should beat.
- Use log-uniform distributions for scale-like parameters.
- Analyze the results to learn which parameters matter; that is more valuable than the best trial.

**Practice.** Run 30 random trials and 30 grid trials over four LightGBM parameters with the same ranges; plot the best validation AP so far against trial number for each.

</details>

#### [Optuna documentation](https://optuna.readthedocs.io/)

_docs · free · an afternoon · free; tuning with pruning in an hour_

**Age 5.** The manual for a helper that tries dial settings for you, learns which ones look promising, and stops the bad tries early.

**Middle school.** Optuna is a free Python library for hyperparameter search. You write a function that trains a model with settings drawn from ranges you define and returns the validation score; Optuna runs trials, favors promising regions, and can stop bad trials early. The tutorial pages get you running in an hour.

**High school.** Read the tutorial (define an objective, create a study, optimize), the pruning page (early stopping of bad trials with LightGBM's callback), and the visualization page (parameter importance, optimization history). Use it to tune four LightGBM parameters with a budget of 30 trials on the chronological validation split.

**Stanford undergrad.** Its default sampler is a tree-structured Parzen estimator, a Bayesian optimization method; the docs explain samplers and pruners so you can choose. Understand how to make trials reproducible (seeds), how to store studies (SQLite) and how to run trials in parallel on the Mac's cores.

**Stanford grad.** Optuna's design (define-by-run search spaces, pluggable samplers) makes it usable for pipeline search, not only parameters; its parameter-importance analysis is a practical functional-ANOVA implementation for pruning the search space of a monthly retrain.

**PhD at Apple.** Tuning libraries are infrastructure; the questions at scale are distributed trials, warm starts across model versions, and integration with experiment tracking, all of which Optuna's docs address at a level worth reading before building your own.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Tutorial: the objective function and trials, samplers (TPE default, random, CMA-ES, grid), pruners (median, successive halving, Hyperband) with integration callbacks, multi-objective optimization, user attributes, saving and resuming studies with storage, distributed optimization, visualization (history, importance, parallel coordinates, slices, contours), and best practices for reproducibility.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Define-by-run: the objective function suggests values inside itself (`trial.suggest_float('lr', 1e-3, 0.3, log=True)`, `suggest_int`, `suggest_categorical`), builds and evaluates the model, and returns the score; conditional search spaces are natural.
2. Studies: `optuna.create_study(direction='maximize', sampler=..., pruner=..., storage='sqlite:///study.db', study_name=...)`; `study.optimize(objective, n_trials=30, timeout=...)`; `study.best_trial`, `best_params`, `trials_dataframe()`.
3. Samplers: TPE models good and bad regions with density estimates and samples where the ratio is favorable; random sampler as baseline; CMA-ES for continuous spaces; grid for exhaustive small spaces.
4. Pruning: report intermediate values (`trial.report(score, step)`) and stop unpromising trials (`trial.should_prune()`); the LightGBM integration callback reports each boosting round; median pruner and Hyperband implement successive halving.
5. Visualization and importance: optimization history, parameter importances (functional ANOVA), slice plots per parameter, parallel coordinates for interactions, and contour plots.
6. Reproducibility and scale: seed the sampler, log every trial's parameters and score, persist the study in a database to resume or to run trials in parallel processes on the Mac's cores.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
def objective(trial):
    params = dict(objective='binary', metric='average_precision', learning_rate=trial.suggest_float('lr', 1e-3, 0.3, log=True),
                  num_leaves=trial.suggest_int('leaves', 15, 255, log=True), min_data_in_leaf=trial.suggest_int('mdl', 20, 2000, log=True),
                  feature_fraction=trial.suggest_float('ff', 0.5, 1.0), num_threads=8, verbose=-1)
    m = lgb.train(params, dtr, 3000, valid_sets=[dva], callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100), optuna.integration.LightGBMPruningCallback(trial, 'average_precision')])
    return m.best_score['valid_0']['average_precision']
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Suggest inside the objective; pruning inside the training loop.
- Persist the study; resume and parallelize for free.
- Read the importance plot before the best parameters.

**Practice.** Tune four LightGBM parameters with TPE and pruning under a 30-trial budget, persist the study, and report parameter importances and the gain over defaults on the chronological validation split.

</details>

#### [Visual Information Theory (Olah)](https://colah.github.io/posts/2015-09-Visual-Information/)

_essay · free · an hour · free; entropy and KL with pictures_

**Age 5.** A web page with pictures that explains what information is, using rectangles whose size shows how surprising something is.

**Middle school.** Chris Olah's essay explains entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence with diagrams of code lengths: rare events need long codes, and using the wrong codebook wastes bits. It makes the cross-entropy loss feel like a real cost. Free, about an hour.

**High school.** Read it before the information-theory topic; its diagrams show why cross-entropy is at least entropy, why KL is not symmetric, and what mutual information measures. Then redo its examples with the traffic label's base rate as the distribution.

**Stanford undergrad.** The essay gives the coding interpretation that makes the theorems intuitive (the source-coding theorem as optimal code lengths); with it, the KL-based derivations in variational inference and the information bottleneck read naturally.

**Stanford grad.** Olah's other essays (on neural network representations, on attention) are of the same quality; his work on interpretability is where the visual method meets research.

**PhD at Apple.** An example of explanation as research communication at its best; when you write for a broad technical audience, this is the standard.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** A visual essay on information theory: optimal codes and code lengths, entropy, cross-entropy and its asymmetry, KL divergence, entropy and multiple variables (joint, conditional, mutual information), and the connection to machine learning.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Codes: to send messages about outcomes, give short codewords to frequent outcomes; a codeword of length L costs a fraction 1/2^L of the code space; the cheapest code assigns length −log₂ p(x) to outcome x.
2. Entropy: the expected code length under the optimal code, H(p) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x); it measures uncertainty in bits; uniform is maximal, certain is zero.
3. Cross-entropy: the expected length when you use a code optimized for q but events follow p, H(p, q) = −Σ p(x) log₂ q(x); always at least H(p); not symmetric, because the wrong code hurts differently in each direction.
4. KL divergence: the extra bits, KL(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p); zero only when the distributions match; the essay's rectangles show why it is asymmetric and why a code that ignores a possible event costs infinitely.
5. Multiple variables: joint entropy H(X, Y); conditional entropy H(Y|X) = H(X, Y) − H(X); mutual information I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X, Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X), the reduction in uncertainty about one from knowing the other; the Venn-like diagram of these quantities.
6. Machine learning: minimizing cross-entropy between labels and predictions minimizes the KL to the truth (the entropy of the truth is fixed); log loss is measured in nats; mutual information as a dependence measure for feature screening.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
H(p) = −Σ p log₂ p;  H(p, q) = −Σ p log₂ q;  KL(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p) ≥ 0
I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) = Σ p(x, y) log [p(x, y)/(p(x)p(y))]
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Cross-entropy is the cost of the wrong codebook; minimizing it moves your model toward the truth.
- KL is not a distance; the direction matters.
- Mutual information is the reduction in surprise one variable gives about another.

**Practice.** Compute the entropy of the slow-episode label per hour of day, the cross-entropy of the LightGBM predictions, and the mutual information between the label and `down1_speed` binned into ten quantiles.

</details>

### Build

_Everything this asks for has been explained above: the lessons and topics for the ideas, the walkthroughs for the code, the books and courses for depth. The page The project, laid out holds the tree, the conventions and the constants every file below refers to; the glossary at the end defines any word that is still new._


Five side studies and one report. Nothing in this phase changes the pipeline; every script lives under `studies/`, reads what phase 4 wrote, and writes `output/studies/<name>.json` and `output/studies/<name>.png`. The report in `docs/reports/phase5.md` is where the numbers are explained and where the decisions that do reach the pipeline are written down (a fault list to exclude before training, a parameter set to adopt or not). The order is by what each study needs: the regression twin and the three-class study reuse phase 4's feature table and split as they are; the clustering study needs only the labels files; the tuning study needs a spare evening of the Mac and comes after the others so the machine is free; the information study needs the saved horizon-30 model and closes the phase by looking back at the feature set.

Write them in this order: `studies/regression_twin.py`, `studies/multiclass_ratio.py`, `studies/station_clusters.py`, `studies/tune_lgbm.py`, `studies/feature_information.py`, then `docs/reports/phase5.md`. Every study takes `--months` (default every month present), uses `split.split_dates()` and `split.frames()` and never scores the test frame; each JSON records `split_used: ["train", "val"]` so that is checkable. Every study seeds its randomness with `--seed 0` and prints one summary line at the end.

#### `studies/regression_twin.py` · study · new

_Purpose._ The regression twin of the classifier: LightGBM regression on the speed itself at 15, 30 and 60 minutes, and quantile models for a 10 to 90 % band at 30 minutes, scored by MAE per hour against persistence and the profile, with the band's coverage measured rather than assumed. Topic 1's "Try this" is this file.

_Reads._ `data/features/YYYY-MM.parquet` (features, `speed_lag_0`, `speed_t30`, `slot`, `daytype`, `station_id`, `timestamp`); `data/labels/YYYY-MM.parquet` for `speed` on the full grid, to build `speed_t15` and `speed_t60` by merging each row with the same station's row `h` minutes later (the feature table has rows dropped, so a `shift` inside it would be wrong); `models/profile_<split>.parquet` for the profile at the target slot, `(slot + steps) % 288` with the row's own day type; `models/categorical_dtypes.joblib`. Asserts `speed_t30` from the merge equals the feature table's `speed_t30` on every row.

_Writes._ `output/studies/regression_twin.json`: `split_used`, `horizons`, per horizon `mae`, `rmse`, `r2` for `model`, `persistence`, `profile`, plus `mase` (model MAE over persistence MAE), `best_iteration`, `mae_by_hour` (24 values per model), `worst_stations` (ten `station_id` with the largest model MAE and the hour of their worst MAE); under `band`: `horizon`, `alphas` (0.1, 0.9), `coverage` overall and per hour, `mean_width_mph`, `coverage_train` for contrast. `output/studies/regression_twin.png`: MAE per hour for the three forecasts at 30 minutes, and coverage per hour with the 0.8 line.

_Run._ `python studies/regression_twin.py [--months ...] [--horizons 15 30 60] [--band-horizon 30] [--objective regression] [--rounds 1000] [--seed 0]`. `--objective` is `regression`, `regression_l1` or `huber`; MAE is reported whichever is trained, and the report says which one won.

_Must contain._

- `add_speed_targets(df, full, horizons) -> pd.DataFrame` · `speed_t{h}` by merging on `(station_id, timestamp + h minutes)` against the full-grid labels frame.
- `profile_at_target(df, profile, steps) -> np.ndarray` · the profile speed at the target slot.
- `reg_params(objective, alpha=None) -> dict` · `common.LGBM_PARAMS` with `objective` replaced, `metric='l1'`, `is_unbalance` removed, and `alpha` set for `objective='quantile'`.
- `fit(tr, va, feats, target, params, rounds) -> lgb.Booster` · early stopping on validation `l1` with `common.LGBM_PATIENCE`.
- `scores(y, yhat) -> dict` · `mae`, `rmse`, `r2` (`sklearn.metrics`); `r2` is always reported beside the baselines' `r2`, never alone.
- `coverage(y, lo, hi) -> float` · share of rows with `lo <= y <= hi`.
- `main()` · per horizon fit and score the three forecasts overall and per local hour; the band at `--band-horizon`; the JSON, the figure, and a printed line per horizon `h=30 mae model=… persistence=… profile=…` plus `band coverage=… (target 0.8)`.

_Skeleton._

_Check._ The printed persistence MAE grows with the horizon and the model's MAE is below it at 30 and 60 minutes; the band coverage on validation is near 0.8 and lower than `coverage_train`. If coverage is 0.95 or more, the quantile models collapsed to wide constants; if the model's MAE is above persistence at 15 minutes, that is the plan's warning about momentum and goes in the report as is.

#### `studies/multiclass_ratio.py` · study · new

_Purpose._ Topic 2's "Try this": the speed ratio 30 minutes ahead as three ordered classes, three classifiers that are not trees (softmax regression, k-nearest neighbors, a linear support vector machine), compared on macro F1, the 3 × 3 confusion matrix and calibration. The point is to see each method's character on the same rows, not to replace the trees.

_Reads._ `data/features/YYYY-MM.parquet`; `models/profile_<split>.parquet` for the profile at the target slot (the same `profile_at_target` idea as the regression twin, reimplemented locally because studies are not imported either). Class of a row: `ratio_t30 = speed_t30 / profile_at_target`; class 0 below `common.SLOW_RATIO`, class 1 from `SLOW_RATIO` to `RATIO_UPPER`, class 2 above, where `RATIO_UPPER = 0.8` is this study's own constant.

_Writes._ `output/studies/multiclass_ratio.json`: `split_used`, `cuts`, `class_shares` on validation, `train_rows`, `val_rows`, and per model (`softmax`, `knn`, `linear_svm`): `macro_f1`, `per_class_f1`, `confusion` (3 × 3 list), `ordinal_mae` (mean absolute class distance), `top_label_ece`, `log_loss`, `fit_seconds`, and for k-NN the `k` chosen on validation among 5, 15, 51. `output/studies/multiclass_ratio.png`: the three confusion matrices side by side, row-normalized.

_Run._ `python studies/multiclass_ratio.py [--months ...] [--train-rows 200000] [--val-rows 100000] [--feats small] [--seed 0]`. `--feats` is `small` (the six numeric columns `15_train_logreg.py` uses) or `all` (every numeric feature); `--train-rows` and `--val-rows` subsample because k-NN's cost is at prediction and a million queries against seven million rows takes hours.

_Must contain._

- `RATIO_UPPER = 0.8` · the study's cut between "slowing" and "free"; `SLOW_RATIO` comes from `common`.
- `make_classes(ratio: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray` · 0, 1, 2 from the two cuts.
- `standardize(tr, va, feats)` · training mean and standard deviation, NaN to 0, float32, as in `15`; k-NN and the SVM are useless without it.
- `fit_softmax(X, y) -> LogisticRegression` · `LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)`, which is multinomial by default.
- `fit_knn(X, y, Xva, yva, ks=(5, 15, 51)) -> KNeighborsClassifier` · the `k` with the best validation macro F1.
- `fit_linear_svm(X, y) -> CalibratedClassifierCV` · `CalibratedClassifierCV(LinearSVC(C=1.0), method='sigmoid', cv=3)` so it has probabilities to calibrate-score.
- `top_label_ece(proba, y, n_bins=10) -> float` · bin rows by their maximum predicted probability and compare that confidence with the accuracy in the bin.
- `ordinal_mae(y, yhat) -> float` · `np.abs(y - yhat).mean()`, which charges a "slow" called "free" twice as much as "slowing".
- `main()` · classes, subsample, three fits, metrics, the figure, the JSON, one printed line per model.

_Skeleton._

def fit_linear_svm(X, y) -> CalibratedClassifierCV: ...
def top_label_ece(proba, y, n_bins: int = 10) -> float:
    """Confidence of the predicted class against its accuracy, per bin."""
    ...
def ordinal_mae(y, yhat) -> float:
    """Mean absolute class distance."""
    ...

def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Three classes from the speed ratio")
    ap.add_argument("--months", nargs="*"); ap.add_argument("--train-rows", type=int, default=200_000)
    ap.add_argument("--val-rows", type=int, default=100_000); ap.add_argument("--feats", default="small")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)

if __name__ == "__main__":

_Check._ The printed class shares sum to 1 with class 2 the largest; the three macro F1 values are all above 1/3 (a constant predictor's score); the SVM's `top_label_ece` before calibration would be meaningless, which is why the wrapper is there, and after it the softmax model usually has the lowest ECE. If k-NN takes more than ten minutes, `--val-rows` is too large.

- `main()` · load, profiles, k-means with stability, PCA, anomalies, figure, JSON, and a printed line: `k=… silhouette=… pc1=…% pc2=…% top anomaly=… on …`.

#### `studies/tune_lgbm.py` · study · new

_Purpose._ Topic 4's "Try this": 30 Optuna trials over four LightGBM parameters on the chronological validation split, every trial logged, the defaults as trial zero, and the gain over defaults reported against the noise of the validation score rather than as a number to believe. Add `optuna>=3.5` to `requirements.txt` under `# phase 5`.

_Reads._ `data/features/YYYY-MM.parquet`, `models/categorical_dtypes.joblib`, `output/baselines.json` (nothing from it but the split check) and `output/evaluation_report.json` for the `ap_ci` of `lightgbm` at the horizon, which is the noise level the gain is compared with.

_Writes._ `output/studies/tune_lgbm.json`: `split_used`, `horizon`, `trials` (a list with `number`, `params`, `val_ap`, `best_iteration`, `seconds`), `defaults` (`params`, `val_ap`), `best` (`params`, `val_ap`, `number`), `gain`, `noise_halfwidth` (half the width of `ap_ci`), `verdict` (`"adopt"` when `gain > noise_halfwidth` and the best trial's `best_iteration` is not at the cap, else `"defaults were fine"`), `total_seconds`. `output/studies/tune_lgbm.png`: validation AP against trial number with the default as a horizontal line and the running best.

_Run._ `python studies/tune_lgbm.py [--months ...] [--horizon 30] [--trials 30] [--rounds 1000] [--train-rows 0] [--seed 0]`. `--rounds` caps each trial (early stopping usually ends it sooner); `--train-rows 0` means every training row, and a positive value subsamples the training frame by row for a faster first pass, which the JSON records. Thirty trials at five to twenty minutes each is a night; start it before bed with nothing else running.

_Must contain._

- `SPACE` · the four parameters and their ranges: `num_leaves` 15 to 255 (int), `learning_rate` 0.01 to 0.2 (log), `min_data_in_leaf` 50 to 1000 (int), `feature_fraction` 0.5 to 1.0; every other key stays at `common.LGBM_PARAMS`.

- `main()` · `optuna.create_study(direction='maximize', sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=args.seed))`, `study.enqueue_trial({the four defaults})` so trial 0 is the baseline, `study.optimize(..., n_trials=args.trials)`, the JSON with the verdict rule above, the figure, and a printed line `default ap=… best ap=… gain=… noise=… verdict=…`.
