</details>

#### [The Little Book of Deep Learning (Fleuret)](https://fleuret.org/francois/lbdl.html)

_book · free · a weekend · free; the whole field in 150 small pages_

**Age 5.** A short free book, made to fit on a phone screen, that explains deep learning from start to finish in plain language.

**Middle school.** François Fleuret's book is about 150 small pages, free, covering machine learning basics, efficient computation, training, the main model components, architectures, and applications. It is dense but readable; use it as a summary after the longer courses.

**High school.** Read the chapters on training (losses, autoregressive models, optimization), on model components (layers, attention, normalization) and on architectures after lesson 9 to consolidate; its figures are precise and its notation consistent.

**Stanford undergrad.** The book is a compact, rigorous map of the field; its chapter on efficient computation (GPUs, memory, batching) is the shortest correct account of why hardware shapes models.

**Stanford grad.** Useful as a reference for definitions and as a checklist of what a current practitioner should know; its brevity makes gaps in your own understanding visible.

**PhD at Apple.** A free, expert summary; the kind of document to hand a strong engineer who needs the whole picture in a weekend.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Part I, foundations: machine learning (learning from data, basis function regression, under and overfitting, categories of models); efficient computation (GPUs, tensors); training (losses, autoregressive models, gradient descent, backpropagation, training protocols, the benefits of scale). Part II, deep models: model components (layers, linear, activations, pooling, dropout, normalizing, skip connections, attention, token embedding, positional encoding); architectures (MLP, convolutional networks, attention models). Part III, applications: prediction (image denoising, classification, detection, segmentation, speech recognition, text-image, reinforcement learning) and synthesis (text generation, image generation). A closing chapter on what is missing.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Foundations: a model is a parametric function; learning minimizes a loss on training data; generalization requires capacity matched to data; the categories of tasks (regression, classification, density modelling, generation).
2. Computation: tensors as the data structure, GPUs as parallel matrix engines, memory bandwidth as the bottleneck, and why batching matters.
3. Training: cross-entropy and its relatives; autoregressive factorization for sequences; stochastic gradient descent with momentum and Adam; backpropagation through the computational graph with stored activations; training protocols (validation, learning-rate schedules, early stopping) and the empirical benefits of scale (more data, more parameters, more compute improve smoothly).
4. Components: linear layers, convolutional layers (1-D and 2-D, stride, padding, dilation, transposed), activations (ReLU, GELU, and others), pooling, dropout, batch and layer normalization with their statistics, skip connections and why they help optimization, attention layers (query, key, value, multi-head, causal masking), token embeddings and positional encodings.
5. Architectures: the MLP; convolutional networks (LeNet, ResNet, and the receptive-field view); attention models (the transformer encoder and decoder, GPT as a decoder-only model, the vision transformer).
6. Applications: how each task is cast as a loss over a network's outputs (denoising as regression, detection with box regression and class heads, segmentation as per-pixel classification, speech with CTC, text-image with contrastive alignment, reinforcement learning with value networks) and how generation works (autoregressive sampling, diffusion).
7. What is missing: recurrent networks, GANs, graph networks, self-supervision, and the training details of large models, with pointers.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
autoregressive: p(x_1..x_T) = Π_t p(x_t | x_{<t})
layer norm: y = γ (x − μ)/σ + β over the feature dimension
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Every architecture is a stack of a dozen component types; know the components and any diagram is legible.
- Autoregressive factorization plus cross-entropy is how sequence generation is trained.
- Skip connections and normalization are what make depth optimizable.

**Practice.** Read the components chapter, then list which components the spatio-temporal net uses and which it could add (layer norm, skip connections, attention over stations), and test one addition.

</details>

#### [A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (Karpathy)](https://karpathy.github.io/2019/04/25/recipe/)

_essay · free · an hour · free; the checklist that prevents silent failures_

**Age 5.** A checklist from an expert about how to train a learning machine without fooling yourself: start simple, look at the data, change one thing at a time.

**Middle school.** A blog post with a step-by-step recipe: inspect the data first, build a tiny end-to-end pipeline, get baselines right, overfit a small batch on purpose, then regularize and tune. It is short, free and practical, and it prevents most beginner mistakes.

**High school.** Apply it to the spatio-temporal net: verify the loss at initialization, overfit two batches, add complexity one piece at a time, and plot everything. Its list of things that silently go wrong (mismatched shapes, wrong learning rates, data leaks) is a debugging checklist.

**Stanford undergrad.** The post's principle, that neural network training fails silently and so must be built incrementally with verification at each step, is the engineering discipline behind every successful training run; its specific checks are cheap and catch real bugs.

**Stanford grad.** Read it with Karpathy's course on activations and gradients statistics; together they are the practical theory of training diagnostics.

**PhD at Apple.** A widely used piece of practitioner wisdom; for a lead, it is the shared protocol to require before anyone reports a result.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** A blog post arguing that neural network training fails silently and must be built incrementally, with a step-by-step recipe: become one with the data; set up an end-to-end skeleton with dumb baselines; overfit; regularize; tune; squeeze out the juice.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Failure is silent: shapes broadcast wrongly, labels are off by one, learning rates are off by orders of magnitude, and the loss still goes down; only a disciplined process catches it.
2. Become one with the data: look at hundreds of examples, find duplicates, corrupt labels, imbalances, biases; think about what features a simple model would use; plot distributions and outliers.
3. Skeleton and baselines: fix the seed; simplify (no augmentation, no fancy schedules); verify the initial loss equals the expected value for random predictions (for binary cross-entropy at prevalence p, −[p log p + (1 − p) log(1 − p)]); initialize the final layer's bias to the base rate; build human and simple baselines; a model that predicts from inputs and one with inputs zeroed should differ; overfit one batch to zero loss; verify decreasing training loss with capacity; visualize exactly what enters the network just before it does; visualize prediction dynamics on a fixed batch; use backpropagation to chart dependencies (a loss on one example should produce gradients only for that example); generalize a special case first.
4. Overfit: get a model large enough to overfit the training set, then regularize; use the standard architecture for the domain; Adam with learning rate 3e-4 is a safe start; add complexity one piece at a time; disable learning-rate decay at first.
5. Regularize: more real data, augmentation, creative augmentation, pretraining, fewer inputs, smaller model, smaller batch, dropout (carefully with batch norm), weight decay, early stopping on validation; a larger model with early stopping often beats a small one.
6. Tune: random search over hyperparameters rather than grid; Bayesian optimization if you like; squeeze: ensembles, and train longer than you think.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
initial BCE ≈ −[p log p + (1 − p) log(1 − p)] for prevalence p;  final bias = log(p/(1 − p))
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Verify the loss at initialization and overfit one batch before anything else.
- Add one thing at a time and keep a fixed batch to watch.
- Regularize after you can overfit, not before.

**Practice.** Apply the recipe to the spatio-temporal net: check the initial loss against the prevalence formula, set the output bias to the base rate, overfit two batches, then add neighbor mixing and early stopping one step at a time with a log of each change and its effect.

</details>

#### [UvA Deep Learning Tutorials](https://uvadlc-notebooks.readthedocs.io/)

_docs · free · an afternoon · free notebooks; initialization, optimization, transformers, graphs_

**Age 5.** A set of free lessons with code you can run that teach how to build learning machines with a popular tool called PyTorch.

**Middle school.** The University of Amsterdam's deep learning course notebooks, free online: PyTorch basics, activation functions, initialization, optimization, transformers, graph neural networks, autoencoders, and more. Each notebook runs and explains as it goes. They fill gaps between the theory and the code.

**High school.** The notebooks on initialization and optimization, on transformers and multi-head attention, and on graph neural networks are directly useful for lesson 9 and lesson 10's advanced levels; run them on the Mac (they are written for GPUs but work on CPU and MPS with smaller settings).

**Stanford undergrad.** Their careful experiments (comparing initializations, optimizers, normalization) are the empirical version of the training material, and their graph neural network notebook implements message passing from scratch.

**Stanford grad.** The tutorials on energy-based models, normalizing flows and autoregressive models are a bridge to the generative-model topic with working code.

**PhD at Apple.** A free, maintained set of reference implementations; useful when reproducing a paper and needing a correct baseline component.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Notebooks: introduction to PyTorch; activation functions; optimization and initialization; inception, ResNet and DenseNet; transformers and multi-head attention; graph neural networks; energy-based models; deep autoencoders; normalizing flows; autoregressive image modelling; vision transformers; meta-learning; self-supervised contrastive learning; plus a JAX track and guides on scaling.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Activation functions: sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, LeakyReLU, ELU, Swish compared by gradient behavior and by training experiments; the vanishing-gradient plots per layer.
2. Optimization and initialization: constant versus random initialization, variance analysis leading to Xavier and Kaiming, the effect of activation choice; SGD, momentum and Adam compared on a small model; learning-rate effects; the notebook's diagnostic plots of gradient norms per layer.
3. ResNets and friends: skip connections, bottlenecks, pre-activation blocks, DenseNet's concatenation, and what each does to optimization.
4. Transformers: scaled dot-product attention implemented from scratch, multi-head attention, the encoder block, positional encoding, learning-rate warmup and why it matters, and experiments on sequence tasks (reversing, set anomaly detection).
5. Graph neural networks: graph convolution as normalized adjacency multiplication, graph attention layers from scratch, node classification on Cora, and PyTorch Geometric usage.
6. Generative and self-supervised: autoencoders with latent visualization, normalizing flows with coupling layers, autoregressive PixelCNN, energy-based models with contrastive divergence, and SimCLR contrastive learning with augmentations and a linear probe.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
attention = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) V;  MultiHead = Concat(head_1..head_h) W^O
GCN layer: H′ = D̂⁻½ Â D̂⁻½ H W with Â = A + I
Kaiming: Var(w) = 2/n_in for ReLU
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Initialization and activation choices are visible in per-layer gradient statistics; plot them.
- Attention and graph convolution are a few lines each when written from scratch.
- Contrastive pretraining plus a linear probe is the standard test of a representation.

**Practice.** Run the optimization notebook's gradient-norm diagnostics on the spatio-temporal net, then reimplement its GCN layer with the registry's adjacency and compare with the two-hop mixing layer.

</details>

#### [The training-recipe papers: Adam (Kingma, Ba, 2014), Batch Normalization (Ioffe, Szegedy, 2015), Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6980)

_paper · free · an evening or two · free; the three tricks behind the standard recipe_

**Age 5.** Three papers that gave learning machines three tricks: a smarter way to take steps, a way to keep numbers in a comfortable range, and a way to make the machine not rely on any one part too much.

**Middle school.** Three research papers behind the standard training recipe. Adam adapts the step size for each weight; batch normalization keeps activations in a stable range so training is faster and more forgiving; dropout randomly switches off neurons during training so the network cannot depend on any one. All free; read the abstracts and the main figures.

**High school.** Read each after using the method: Adam's update rule and its bias correction, batch norm's normalization and its learned scale and shift, dropout's training and test-time behavior. The experiments show the effect sizes; note what each claims and what later work revised.

**Stanford undergrad.** Understand Adam as a combination of momentum and per-parameter scaling; batch norm's effect on optimization (smoothing the loss landscape, later analyses argue) rather than the internal-covariate-shift story; dropout as approximate model averaging. Each has known failure modes worth knowing.

**Stanford grad.** Together with later corrections (AdamW's decoupled weight decay, layer normalization for transformers, batch norm's issues at small batch size) they are the history of the training recipe; reading them teaches how empirical claims in ML get revised.

**PhD at Apple.** Canonical citations; for research, the interesting part is the gap between their stated explanations and the later understanding, which is a lesson in how the field learns.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Adam: an optimizer with per-parameter adaptive learning rates from exponential moving averages of the gradient and its square, with bias correction, convergence analysis and experiments. Batch normalization: normalizing each layer's inputs per mini-batch with learned scale and shift, its effect on training speed and on allowable learning rates, and inference with population statistics. Dropout: randomly dropping units during training to prevent co-adaptation, its interpretation as training an exponential ensemble, the weight-scaling rule at test time, and experiments across domains.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Adam's update: m_t = β₁m_{t−1} + (1 − β₁)g_t; v_t = β₂v_{t−1} + (1 − β₂)g_t²; bias-corrected m̂ = m_t/(1 − β₁ᵗ), v̂ = v_t/(1 − β₂ᵗ); θ ← θ − α m̂/(√v̂ + ε); defaults α = 1e-3, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 1e-8; the effective step is bounded by α and invariant to gradient scale; later AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient.
2. Why Adam: momentum smooths noisy gradients; dividing by the root of the second moment equalizes step sizes across parameters with different gradient scales; bias correction fixes the early steps when the averages start at zero.
3. Batch normalization: for each feature, normalize over the mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, then scale by γ and shift by β (learned); during inference use running averages of mean and variance; place before the nonlinearity; it allows higher learning rates, makes initialization less critical and regularizes slightly; the paper's 'internal covariate shift' explanation was later disputed in favor of loss-landscape smoothing.
4. Batch norm caveats: depends on batch size (small batches give noisy statistics), behaves differently in training and evaluation (`model.eval()` matters), interacts with dropout, and is unsuitable for sequence models where layer normalization is used.
5. Dropout: during training, each unit is kept with probability p (0.5 hidden, 0.8 inputs typical) and dropped otherwise; at test time, all units are kept and weights scaled by p (or inverted dropout scales at training time); the network cannot rely on specific co-adapted units; it approximates averaging over 2ⁿ thinned networks; experiments show consistent gains on vision, speech and text with larger models and longer training.
6. Practical combination: Adam(W) with a learning-rate schedule, normalization appropriate to the architecture, dropout tuned by validation; the three form the default recipe that most models still use in some form.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
Adam: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − α · m̂_t / (√v̂_t + ε)
BatchNorm: y = γ (x − μ_B)/√(σ_B² + ε) + β
Dropout (inverted): h ← h ⊙ mask / p, mask ~ Bernoulli(p)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Adam normalizes step sizes per parameter; its defaults work across most problems.
- Batch norm stabilizes training but ties the model to batch statistics; use layer norm for sequences.
- Dropout is ensemble averaging in disguise; scale correctly at test time.

**Practice.** Train the MLP with SGD, SGD with momentum and Adam at three learning rates each, with and without dropout 0.2, and tabulate validation AP and epochs to early stop.

</details>

### Build

_Everything this asks for has been explained above: the lessons and topics for the ideas, the walkthroughs for the code, the books and courses for depth. The page The project, laid out holds the tree, the conventions and the constants every file below refers to; the glossary at the end defines any word that is still new._


Write `17a_train_mlp.py` first: one hidden layer of 64 units in numpy, a backward pass you wrote, a finite-difference check that says whether it is right, and then the same network in PyTorch on the M1's GPU. It is small enough to hold in your head, and every rule of this phase (float32 on MPS, `model.eval()`, the learning rate, early stopping on validation AP) is learned on it before the bigger network hides them. `tests/test_backprop.py` pins the gradient check so it runs on every `pytest`. Then `stnet.py`, the module: the adjacency from the registry, the windows, the `Mix` and `STNet` classes from the walkthroughs, the masked loss with `pos_weight`, a training step, prediction, save and load. Then `17b_train_stnet.py`, which trains it on MPS and writes the checkpoint and a prediction file for both later splits. `studies/mps_vs_cpu.py` comes after the module exists, because it times the real network. Then the change to `16b_calibrate_select.py`, which reads the net's validation predictions and applies `common.CHALLENGER_MARGIN`, and a rerun of `18_evaluate_lead_time.py --challenger` so the net sits in the report beside the trees. `docs/decisions/challenger.md` is last, with the numbers from `calibration.json` and the report and the data flow drawn from memory. `torch` has been in `requirements.txt` since phase 0; nothing is added.

The order of the two networks is the point of the phase. The MLP sees one station's row and cannot beat the trees; the spatio-temporal net sees every station at once and might, at 30 and 60 minutes. Whether it does is decided by a rule written before the run, not after.

#### `17a_train_mlp.py` · runner · new

_Purpose._ Stage 9's educational network, lesson 9 steps 1 to 4. Three parts in one file: the numpy MLP with a hand-written backward pass; the finite-difference check in float64 over twenty random entries of every parameter; the same network in PyTorch, initialised from the numpy weights, run for one epoch of plain SGD in both to show matching loss curves, then trained properly with AdamW and early stopping on validation AP and saved as `models/mlp_h30.pt`. Trains horizon 30 by default.

_Reads._ `data/features/*.parquet` cut by `split.frames`; `models/gbt_h30_features.json` for the feature list, minus `common.CATEGORICALS`, because this network takes numeric columns only. Asserts no object column remains, standardises with training mean and standard deviation, and after standardising replaces NaN with 0 and adds an `<col>_isna` indicator for every column that had NaN in training, lesson 5's rule for networks.

_Writes._ `models/mlp_h30.pt`: a dict with `state_dict`, `columns`, `mean`, `std`, `horizon`, `best_epoch`, `val_ap`. `output/mlp_h30_curves.png`: left, the per-batch loss of the numpy and torch networks over the SGD epoch on the same batches; right, validation AP by epoch under AdamW. Prints `gradcheck max_abs_diff=<n>`, `curves max_rel_diff=<n>`, one line per epoch, `best validation AP <n>`, and ends with `stage=train_mlp seconds=<n> rss_gb=<n> rows=<n> val_ap=<n> best_epoch=<k> device=<mps|cpu>`.

_Run._ `python 17a_train_mlp.py [--horizon 30] [--rows N] [--epochs 30] [--batch 2048] [--lr 1e-3] [--device mps|cpu] [--seed 0]`. `--rows` keeps the last N training rows for a first pass; `--device` defaults to `mps` when `torch.backends.mps.is_available()`.

_Must contain._
- `H = 64`, `EPS = 1e-4`, `GRADCHECK_TOL = 1e-6`, `N_CHECK = 20`, `SGD_LR = 0.1`, `PATIENCE = 5`: the lesson's numbers; the test imports the tolerance from here, so it is written once.
- `load_matrix(horizon: int, rows: int | None) -> tuple`: `Xtr, ytr, Xva, yva` as float32 arrays, `columns`, `mean`, `std`.
- `init(d: int, H: int = H, seed: int = 0) -> dict`: step 1's initialisation, He for `W1`, the four arrays in one dict `P` with keys `W1`, `b1`, `w2`, `b2`; gathering the walkthrough's four globals into `P` is the one change, so the test can pass its own.
- `forward(P: dict, X: np.ndarray) -> tuple`, `backward(P: dict, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> dict`, `L(P: dict, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float`: step 1 and step 2's loss, otherwise unchanged; `backward` returns `gW1`, `gb1`, `gw2`, `gb2`.
- `gradcheck(P: dict, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, n: int = N_CHECK, eps: float = EPS, seed: int = 0) -> float`: casts everything to float64, draws `n` (parameter, index) pairs across all four parameters, central differences as in step 2, returns the largest absolute difference against `backward`; the caller asserts it is below `GRADCHECK_TOL`.
- `sgd_epoch_numpy(P: dict, X, y, lr: float, batch: int, order: np.ndarray) -> list[float]`: plain SGD on the batches `order` defines, one loss per batch.
- `torch_from_numpy(P: dict, dev) -> torch.nn.Sequential`: step 3's `Linear(d, 64), ReLU, Linear(64, 1)` with the weights copied from `P`.
- `sgd_epoch_torch(net, Xt, yt, lr: float, batch: int, order: np.ndarray) -> list[float]`: `torch.optim.SGD` and `BCEWithLogitsLoss()` without `pos_weight`, the same batches, one loss per batch; the two lists are the curves.
- `train_adamw(net, Xt, yt, Xv, yva, epochs: int, batch: int, lr: float, path) -> tuple[int, float]`: steps 3 and 4 unchanged, `AdamW(lr, weight_decay=1e-4)`, `pos_weight` from the training prevalence, early stopping on validation AP with `PATIENCE`, save on improvement, reload the best weights at the end.
- `main()`: argparse, load, `init`, `gradcheck` on 64 rows with the assert, the two SGD epochs and their comparison, `train_adamw`, the figure, the log line.

_Skeleton._

```python
    a.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=30); a.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=2048)
    a.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=1e-3); a.add_argument("--device", default=None); a.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    args = a.parse_args(); t0 = time.time()
    ...
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

_Check._ `python 17a_train_mlp.py --rows 200000 --epochs 3` prints `gradcheck max_abs_diff=` around 1e-10 and never above 1e-6, and `curves max_rel_diff=` below 1e-3; if the curves differ by 0.1 the two networks are not the same network (a transposed `W1`, or a sigmoid applied twice). The full run writes `models/mlp_h30.pt` and the PNG; write the MLP's validation AP into `docs/stages/17a_train_mlp.md` beside the logistic regression's and LightGBM's phase 4 numbers, wherever it lands.

_Watch for._ The gradient check must run on arrays that never touched the GPU and in float64; the training must run in float32. Keep the two in separate variables (`P64` for the check, `P` for training) instead of casting one dict back and forth, which is how the walkthrough's `astype` lines get lost and a float64 array reaches `torch.tensor(..., device='mps')`.

#### `stnet.py` · module · new

_Purpose._ Stage 9's Model B: the `Mix` module from lesson 9 step 5 and the `STNet` class from lesson 10 step 5, put here unchanged apart from the head, with the adjacency (lesson 10 step 3), the windows (step 4), the masked loss with `pos_weight` per horizon, one training epoch, prediction, save and load. The model's constants live here and `17b`, `16b` and the study import them.

_Reads._ Nothing on its own; `load_model` reads a checkpoint.

_Writes._ Nothing; `save_model` writes the checkpoint the runner names.

_Must contain._
- `CHANNELS = ["speed_ratio", "occ", "flow", "incident_active", "min_sin", "min_cos"]`: the walkthrough's `chan`; the plan's scaled flow is `flow` standardised with training statistics, below. `WINDOW = 12`, `HIDDEN = 64`, `BATCH_TIMESTAMPS = 64`, `EPOCHS = 15`, `PATIENCE = 3`, `LR = 1e-3`, `WEIGHT_DECAY = 1e-4`, `HORIZON_ORDER = (15, 30, 60)`; `MODEL_PATH = common.MODELS / f"stnet_thresh{common.SLOW_RATIO}_win{common.SLOW_WINDOW}.pt"`; `PREDICTIONS_PATH = common.OUTPUT / "predictions_stnet.parquet"`.
- `device() -> torch.device`: `mps` when available, else `cpu`.
- `adjacency(reg: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[list[int], np.ndarray, np.ndarray]`: step 3 unchanged: `ids = sorted(reg.ID)` as ints, `A_up` and `A_down` float32 (N, N) with a 1 where the row's station has that neighbour.
- `channel_stats(df_train: pd.DataFrame) -> dict`: mean and standard deviation of `occ` and `flow` over training rows, stored in the checkpoint so serving scales the same way.
- `make_windows(df: pd.DataFrame, ids: list[int], stats: dict, window: int = WINDOW) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, pd.DatetimeIndex]`: step 4 with its assert that `ids` equals the pivot's station order; the frame is first reindexed onto the full five-minute range × `ids` so a window never spans a gap; `occ` and `flow` standardised, then NaN filled with 1.0 for `speed_ratio` and 0 elsewhere (the walkthrough's `nan_to_num` would turn a missing ratio into a stopped road); `X` is `(T − window, window, C, N)` float32 as a strided view from `np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view` over the `(T, C, N)` array, not the walkthrough's `np.stack` copy, so a year of a hundred stations is about 300 MB instead of about 3 GB and still entirely in memory; `Y` `(T − window, N, 3)` float32 from `y_15`, `y_30`, `y_60` with NaN as 0; `M` the same shape, 1 where the target was known; the timestamps of the window ends.
- `Mix(nn.Module)`: step 5 of lesson 9, unchanged.
- `STNet(nn.Module)`: lesson 10 step 5 with `C = len(CHANNELS)`, `H = HIDDEN`; `head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(H, H), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(H, 3))`, the plan's MLP head in place of the walkthrough's single `Linear`; `forward(x, A_up, A_down)` returns `(B, N, 3)` logits and asserts `x.shape[1:] == (WINDOW, C, N)`.
- `pos_weights(Y: np.ndarray, M: np.ndarray) -> torch.Tensor`: shape `(3,)`, negatives over positives per horizon among masked entries; asserts every horizon has positives.
- `masked_bce(logits, y, m, pos_w) -> torch.Tensor`: `BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_w, reduction='none')` times `m`, summed and divided by `m.sum()`.
- `train_epoch(model, X, Y, M, A_up, A_down, opt, pos_w, dev, rng, batch: int = BATCH_TIMESTAMPS) -> float`: shuffled batches of `batch` window indices, each gathered from the view into a contiguous float32 array and moved with `.to(dev)`, `zero_grad`, loss, `backward`, `step`; returns the mean loss; raises `FloatingPointError` with the batch index the first time a loss is not finite.
- `predict(model, X, A_up, A_down, dev, batch: int = 256) -> np.ndarray`: `model.eval()`, `torch.no_grad()`, sigmoid, `(T, N, 3)` float32 on the CPU.
- `validation_ap(P: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, M: np.ndarray) -> dict[int, float]`: AP per horizon over masked entries.
- `save_model(model, path, stats: dict, ids: list[int]) -> None` and `load_model(path, dev=None) -> tuple[STNet, dict, list[int]]`: a dict with `state_dict`, `stats`, `ids`, `channels`, `window`, `hidden`; `load_model` calls `model.eval()` before returning.
- `predictions_frame(P: np.ndarray, ids: list[int], ts: pd.DatetimeIndex, split_name: str) -> pd.DataFrame`: long format `split`, `station_id`, `timestamp`, `p_15`, `p_30`, `p_60`.

_Skeleton._

```python
"""The spatio-temporal net: adjacency, windows, Mix, STNet, masked loss, train, predict, save."""
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, torch, torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score as ap
import common

CHANNELS = ["speed_ratio", "occ", "flow", "incident_active", "min_sin", "min_cos"]
WINDOW, HIDDEN, BATCH_TIMESTAMPS, EPOCHS, PATIENCE, LR, WEIGHT_DECAY = 12, 64, 64, 15, 3, 1e-3, 1e-4
HORIZON_ORDER = (15, 30, 60)
MODEL_PATH = common.MODELS / f"stnet_thresh{common.SLOW_RATIO}_win{common.SLOW_WINDOW}.pt"
PREDICTIONS_PATH = common.OUTPUT / "predictions_stnet.parquet"

def device() -> torch.device: ...
def adjacency(reg: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[list[int], np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Lesson 10 step 3: sorted ids, A_up, A_down as float32 (N, N)."""
    ...
def channel_stats(df_train: pd.DataFrame) -> dict: ...
def make_windows(df: pd.DataFrame, ids: list[int], stats: dict, window: int = WINDOW):
    """X view (T-window, window, C, N), Y and M (T-window, N, 3), window-end timestamps."""
    ...

class Mix(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, H): super().__init__(); self.Wu = nn.Linear(H, H, bias=False); self.Wd = nn.Linear(H, H, bias=False)
    def forward(self, h, A_up, A_down): return h + self.Wu(A_up @ h) + self.Wd(A_down @ h)

class STNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C: int = len(CHANNELS), H: int = HIDDEN):
        super().__init__(); self.gru = nn.GRU(C, H, batch_first=True); self.mix1 = Mix(H); self.mix2 = Mix(H)
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(H, H), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(H, 3))
    def forward(self, x, A_up, A_down):
        """x (B, 12, C, N) -> (B, N, 3) logits; lesson 10 step 5."""
        ...

def pos_weights(Y: np.ndarray, M: np.ndarray) -> torch.Tensor: ...
def masked_bce(logits, y, m, pos_w) -> torch.Tensor: ...
def train_epoch(model, X, Y, M, A_up, A_down, opt, pos_w, dev, rng, batch: int = BATCH_TIMESTAMPS) -> float: ...
def predict(model, X, A_up, A_down, dev, batch: int = 256) -> np.ndarray: ...
def validation_ap(P: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, M: np.ndarray) -> dict[int, float]: ...
def save_model(model, path, stats: dict, ids: list[int]) -> None: ...
def load_model(path, dev=None) -> tuple[STNet, dict, list[int]]: ...
def predictions_frame(P: np.ndarray, ids: list[int], ts: pd.DatetimeIndex, split_name: str) -> pd.DataFrame: ...
```

_Check._ `python -c "import pandas as pd, torch, stnet; reg = pd.read_parquet('data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet'); ids, Au, Ad = stnet.adjacency(reg); m = stnet.STNet(); print(len(ids), Au.sum(), (Au.T == Ad).all(), m(torch.zeros(2, 12, 6, len(ids)), torch.as_tensor(Au), torch.as_tensor(Ad)).shape, sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()))"` prints the station count, the count minus one route end per (freeway, direction), `True` (i is upstream of j exactly when j is downstream of i), `torch.Size([2, N, 3])`, and about 35 thousand parameters; the plan's 0.1 M is the order of magnitude, not a target.

_Watch for._ `sliding_window_view` returns a read-only view whose window axis comes last; `np.moveaxis` to `(T − window, window, C, N)` is still a view, and indexing a batch of it with an integer array is what makes the copy. Never call `np.ascontiguousarray` on the whole view; that is the 3 GB copy the view exists to avoid.

_Purpose._ Stage 9 item 6: trains `stnet.STNet` on the MPS device with the registry's road graph, batches of 64 timestamps, 15 epochs, early stopping on validation AP, float32 only, the whole windowed dataset in memory. Writes the checkpoint with the label tag in its name and a prediction file for the validation and test blocks that `16b` and `18` read.

_Reads._ `data/features/*.parquet`, only `station_id`, `timestamp`, the six `stnet.CHANNELS`, `y_15`, `y_30`, `y_60`; `data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet`. Splits with `split.frames`. Asserts before training: the station set of the table equals the registry's `ID` set (or prints the stations dropped to reach the intersection and refuses if more than five), no NaN in `X` after filling, `M.sum()` over the training windows is positive for every horizon, and the training block's last window ends before `train_end`.

_Writes._ `models/stnet_thresh0.6_win3.pt` (`stnet.MODEL_PATH`): the checkpoint dict from `stnet.save_model` plus `best_epoch`, `val_ap`, `epochs_run`, `seed`, `device`. `output/predictions_stnet.parquet` (`stnet.PREDICTIONS_PATH`): `split` category (`val`, `test`), `station_id` category, `timestamp` datetime64[ns, UTC], `p_15`, `p_30`, `p_60` float32; the test rows are written and never printed or looked at here. Prints per epoch `epoch=<k> loss=<n> val_ap_15=<n> val_ap_30=<n> val_ap_60=<n> seconds=<n>`, then `early stop at epoch <k>, best epoch <j>`, then `stage=train_stnet seconds=<n> rss_gb=<n> rows=<windows> best_epoch=<j> val_ap_30=<n> device=<mps|cpu>`.

#### `tests/test_backprop.py` · test · new

_Purpose._ The finite-difference check as a test that runs on every `pytest`, at the tolerance `17a` defines, plus the proof that the torch twin is the same network. It loads `17a_train_mlp.py` by path with `importlib`, because a digit-led name cannot be imported and the numpy network lives nowhere else; the runner's work sits under `if __name__ == '__main__'`, so loading runs nothing. Synthetic data only; no `data/` and no GPU.

_Reads._ `17a_train_mlp.py` as a module.

_Must contain._
- `mlp()`: a module-level fixture that loads the runner with `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("mlp17a", common.ROOT / "17a_train_mlp.py")`.
- `toy(d: int = 10, n: int = 64, seed: int = 0) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]`: random float32 `X` and a label made from a fixed linear rule, so about a third of rows are positive.
- `test_backward_matches_finite_differences`: `gradcheck(P, X, y)` is below `mlp.GRADCHECK_TOL` and the check touched all four parameter names (`gradcheck` with `return_names=True`, or a second call per name); the value is printed so `pytest -s` shows it near 1e-10.
- `test_torch_twin_matches_numpy_forward`: `torch_from_numpy(P, 'cpu')` on `X` gives probabilities equal to `forward(P, X)[2]` to 1e-5.
- `test_one_sgd_step_matches`: after one `sgd_epoch_numpy` and one `sgd_epoch_torch` on the same single batch with `SGD_LR`, the torch `W1` equals the numpy `W1` to 1e-5 and the two losses agree to 1e-6.

_Skeleton._

```python
import importlib.util
import numpy as np, pytest, torch
import common

def _load():
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("mlp17a", common.ROOT / "17a_train_mlp.py")
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(mod); return mod

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def mlp():
    return _load()

def toy(d=10, n=64, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)).astype(np.float32)
    y = (X[:, 0] - X[:, 1] > 0.4).astype(np.float32); return X, y

def test_backward_matches_finite_differences(mlp):
    X, y = toy(); P = mlp.init(X.shape[1], seed=0)
    diff = mlp.gradcheck(P, X, y, n=mlp.N_CHECK, eps=mlp.EPS, seed=1)
    print("max_abs_diff", diff)
    assert diff < mlp.GRADCHECK_TOL

def test_torch_twin_matches_numpy_forward(mlp): ...
def test_one_sgd_step_matches(mlp): ...
```

_Check._ `pytest tests/test_backprop.py -q -s` prints `max_abs_diff` around 1e-10 and `3 passed`. Change `(z1 > 0)` to `(z1 >= 0)` in `backward` and the first test still passes (the boundary has measure zero); change `np.outer(e, w2)` to `np.outer(w2, e)` and it fails with a difference near 1. Both facts are worth one line in the notebook page.

#### `16b_calibrate_select.py` · runner · changed

_Purpose._ Stage 10 with the plan's selection rule. Phase 4's version fits an isotonic map per horizon on LightGBM's validation scores and picks `tau_h` at `common.ALERT_PRECISION`. The change: when the net's prediction file exists, read its validation rows, align them to LightGBM's by keys, compute the net's validation AP on the same rows, time its prediction for one timestamp, and ship LightGBM unless the net's AP is at least `common.CHALLENGER_MARGIN` higher and it predicts in under a second. For a horizon the net wins, the isotonic map and `tau_h` are fit on the net's scores. Every number behind the choice is recorded in `calibration.json`.

_Reads._ What phase 4's version reads (the validation block of `data/features/*.parquet`, the three boosters, `models/gbt_h{h}_features.json`, `models/categorical_dtypes.joblib`); `output/predictions_stnet.parquet` rows with `split == 'val'` (`station_id`, `timestamp`, `p_15`, `p_30`, `p_60`); `models/stnet_thresh0.6_win3.pt` and the registry for the timing. Asserts the challenger file has the six columns, that its aligned row count is at least 90 % of the validation rows the net could have windows for, and that no challenger timestamp lies outside the validation block.

_Writes._ `models/calibration.json`: phase 4's keys, unchanged, plus at the top level `margin` (`common.CHALLENGER_MARGIN`), `max_predict_seconds` (1.0), `challenger_file` or null, `challenger_predict_seconds` or null, and per horizon under the keys `"15"`, `"30"`, `"60"`: `val_ap_lightgbm`, `val_ap_stnet` or null, `n_val_aligned`; `chosen` is now `lightgbm` or `stnet`, and `tau`, `recall_at_tau`, `val_ap`, `knots` describe the chosen model. `models/iso_h{h}.joblib`, fit on the chosen model's scores. `19_predict_live.py` keeps reading `cal[str(h)]['tau']` unchanged.

_Run._ `python 16b_calibrate_select.py [--months ...] [--horizons 15 30 60] [--precision 0.5] [--challenger output/predictions_stnet.parquet] [--no-challenger]`; the first three are phase 4's; the challenger path defaults to `stnet.PREDICTIONS_PATH` and is skipped with a printed line when the file is absent. Prints per horizon `h=30 ap_lgbm=<n> ap_stnet=<n> diff=<n> predict_s=<n> chosen=<lightgbm|stnet>` and ends with `stage=calibrate seconds=<n> rss_gb=<n> rows=<n>`.

_Must contain._
- `load_validation(sp, months)`, `predict_raw(va: pd.DataFrame, h: int) -> np.ndarray`, `calibrate(y, p) -> IsotonicRegression`, now with lesson 11 step 1's first-half, second-half check printed, and `choose_tau(y, q, precision) -> tuple[float, float, float]` (step 2 through `evaluate.threshold_at_precision`): phase 4's, unchanged.
- `load_challenger(path, va: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: the `val` rows inner-joined to `va` on `station_id`, `timestamp`; prints `n_val` and `n_val_aligned`.
- `time_challenger(path, reg: pd.DataFrame, n: int = 5) -> float`: `stnet.load_model` on the CPU, the serving device, one window of zeros `(1, 12, 6, N)`, the median of `n` timed calls of `stnet.predict`; the checkpoint load is not timed, because serving loads once.
- `select(ap_lgbm: float, ap_stnet: float | None, seconds: float | None, margin: float = common.CHALLENGER_MARGIN, max_seconds: float = 1.0) -> str`: `stnet` only when `ap_stnet - ap_lgbm >= margin` and `seconds < max_seconds`, else `lightgbm`.
- `main()`: argparse, the phase 4 flow, then per horizon the challenger AP on the aligned rows, `select`, `calibrate` and `choose_tau` on the chosen scores, the JSON with every field above, written atomically.

_Skeleton._

```python
"""Stage 10: isotonic maps, thresholds at the required precision, and the challenger rule."""

import joblib, lightgbm as lgb, numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score as ap, precision_recall_curve
import common, evaluate, features, split, stnet

def load_validation(sp, months) -> pd.DataFrame: ...              # phase 4's four, unchanged
def predict_raw(va: pd.DataFrame, h: int) -> np.ndarray: ...
def calibrate(y, p) -> IsotonicRegression: ...
def choose_tau(y, q, precision: float): ...

def load_challenger(path, va: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The net's validation rows aligned to va by station_id and timestamp."""
    ...

def time_challenger(path, reg: pd.DataFrame, n: int = 5) -> float:
    """Median seconds for one timestamp's prediction on the CPU."""
    ...

def select(ap_lgbm: float, ap_stnet: float | None, seconds: float | None,
           margin: float = common.CHALLENGER_MARGIN, max_seconds: float = 1.0) -> str:
    """'stnet' only when it beats the trees by margin and predicts fast enough, else 'lightgbm'."""
    ...

def main() -> None:
    a = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    a.add_argument("--months", nargs="*"); a.add_argument("--horizons", nargs="*", type=int, default=[15, 30, 60])
    a.add_argument("--precision", type=float, default=common.ALERT_PRECISION)
    a.add_argument("--challenger", default=str(stnet.PREDICTIONS_PATH)); a.add_argument("--no-challenger", action="store_true")
    args = a.parse_args(); t0 = time.time()
    ...
    common.log_stage("calibrate", t0, rows=len(va))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

_Check._ `python 16b_calibrate_select.py` prints three `chosen=` lines and `python -c "import json; c = json.load(open('models/calibration.json')); print(c['margin'], {h: (c[h]['chosen'], round(c[h]['val_ap_lightgbm'], 3), c[h]['val_ap_stnet'] and round(c[h]['val_ap_stnet'], 3)) for h in ('15', '30', '60')})"` prints `0.02` and three triples. Then `python 18_evaluate_lead_time.py --challenger output/predictions_stnet.parquet` and the report's `table` has `stnet` rows beside `lightgbm` at every horizon. `python -c "import json; print(json.load(open('models/calibration.json'))['30']['tau'])"` still works for phase 9.

_Watch for._ A mixed choice, trees at 15 minutes and the net at 60, is allowed by the rule and means the serving loop of phase 9 loads both models and builds both inputs. Write that consequence into `challenger.md` before accepting a mixed result; if the consumer wants one model, say so there and choose per the 30-minute horizon.

#### `docs/decisions/challenger.md` · doc · new

_Purpose._ The written decision on the challenger, with the numbers that made it, the cost of the net, and its data flow drawn from memory and checked against the code.

_Reads._ `models/calibration.json`, `output/evaluation_report.json` (the `--challenger` run), `output/studies/mps_vs_cpu.json`, `logs/pipeline.log` (the `train_stnet` line).

_Must contain._
- The rule: `common.CHALLENGER_MARGIN`, the one-second bar, and the plan's reason, that trees are faster, more stable and easier to debug at 3 am.
- The numbers: one list item per horizon with LightGBM's validation AP, the net's, the difference, the net's prediction seconds and `chosen`, copied from `calibration.json`; then the test-split row for both from the report.
- Cost: `seconds`, `rss_gb`, `best_epoch` and `device` from the log line; the step and epoch timings on both devices from the study.
- Data flow: a text drawing made with `stnet.py` closed, with the shape at every arrow, from the feature Parquet through the pivot `(T, C, N)`, the windows `(T − 12, 12, C, N)`, the per-station sequences `(B·N, 12, C)`, the GRU to `(B, N, H)`, two `Mix` rounds with `A_up` and `A_down`, the head to `(B, N, 3)`, the masked loss with `pos_weight`, AdamW, early stopping on validation AP, the checkpoint, the predictions Parquet and `16b`; then the shapes printed by the module's check, and a list of every arrow the drawing had wrong. A picture at `docs/decisions/stnet_dataflow.png` may sit beside the drawing but does not replace it.
- What the net sees that the trees do not, in the plan's words, and what it does not see: the calendar beyond sin and cos, the incident columns beyond the flag, rain, the static columns.
- Decision: one sentence per horizon naming the shipped model, matching `chosen`, and what the serving loop will load.
- What would change it: a second seed's spread, more months, a third hop; the number that would have to move and by how much.
- Date, data window, commit of `17b` and `16b`.

_Check._ `grep -c 'chosen\|lgbm\|stnet' docs/decisions/challenger.md` is above 5; the per-horizon decisions on the page equal `calibration.json`'s `chosen`; the data-flow section lists its mistakes, and a blank list means the drawing was made with the file open.

### Done when

- `pytest tests/test_backprop.py -q -s` prints `max_abs_diff` below 1e-6 (it should be near 1e-10) and `3 passed`; flipping `np.outer(e, w2)` in `backward` makes the first test fail.
- `python 17a_train_mlp.py --rows 200000 --epochs 3` prints `gradcheck max_abs_diff=` below 1e-6 and `curves max_rel_diff=` below 1e-3; the full run writes `models/mlp_h30.pt` and `output/mlp_h30_curves.png`, and `docs/stages/17a_train_mlp.md` shows the MLP's validation AP beside the logistic regression's and LightGBM's.
- `python 17b_train_stnet.py --epochs 1 --max-windows 2000` ends with a finite, lower loss and a checkpoint; the full run's log line has `rss_gb` under 4, every epoch line finite, and an `early stop at epoch` line or, if it ran all 15, a `best_epoch` in the log line; the net trained without a NaN.
- `python -c "import pandas as pd; p = pd.read_parquet('output/predictions_stnet.parquet'); print(sorted(p.split.unique()), p.isna().sum().sum(), float(p.p_30.min()) >= 0 and float(p.p_30.max()) <= 1)"` prints `['test', 'val'] 0 True`.
- `python studies/mps_vs_cpu.py` writes `output/studies/mps_vs_cpu.json` with rows for both devices and a `stnet_speedup_mps_over_cpu` between 0.5 and 3; the table is in `challenger.md` under cost.
- `python 16b_calibrate_select.py` prints three `chosen=` lines; `calibration.json` has `margin` 0.02, `chosen` per horizon and `tau` per horizon; `python 18_evaluate_lead_time.py --challenger output/predictions_stnet.parquet` puts `stnet` rows beside `lightgbm` in the report's `table` at every horizon, which is the net sitting next to the trees.
- `docs/decisions/challenger.md` exists with all eight sections; its data-flow drawing was made with `stnet.py` closed, its shapes match the ones the module's check prints, and its per-horizon decision equals `chosen` in `calibration.json`.
- `git status --short` shows the four new code files, the test, the study, the two docs and the stage pages, and nothing under `models/` or `output/`.

### Pitfalls

- `TypeError: Cannot convert a MPS Tensor to float64 dtype` or a run that is ten times slower than the CPU. A float64 array reached the device: pandas gives float64 from any column that was upcast, and the gradient check works in float64 on purpose. Cast with `.astype(np.float32)` before every `torch.tensor(..., device=dev)`, keep the float64 arrays of `gradcheck` in their own variables, and let `stnet.make_windows` assert float32; there is no float64 on MPS and there never will be.
- Predictions at serving time differ from the ones `17b` wrote, or memory climbs while predicting. The model was left in training mode and prediction ran with autograd on; today the net has no dropout so the numbers only drift when you add one, but the memory cost is there now. `stnet.predict` calls `model.eval()` inside `torch.no_grad()`, `stnet.load_model` calls `eval()` before returning, and nothing else predicts.
- The loss rises after the first epoch, or is NaN by the second, and validation AP sits at the prevalence. The learning rate is ten times too high: 1e-2 with AdamW on standardised inputs diverges on this network. `stnet.LR` is 1e-3, `17a` starts there too, and the tiny-subset rule holds: `--max-windows 2000` must show the loss falling within one epoch before the full run.
- The net won by 0.03 on the third seed and you ship it. Selection on noise: three seeds is three draws and the rule was written for one. The rule in `16b` is fixed before the run, one seed is the run, and if you want a second seed its spread goes into `challenger.md` and the margin applies to the mean. The plan says the deep model may not beat the trees on a hundred stations and a year, and that is a normal outcome, not a failure of the phase.
- `FloatingPointError` from `stnet.train_epoch` at a random batch. A NaN in `X` (a station whose `speed_ratio` was NaN and did not get the 1.0 fill, or a channel standardised with a zero standard deviation) or an infinite `pos_weight` because a horizon had no positive training window. `make_windows` fills and asserts; `pos_weights` asserts positives per horizon; the error names the batch so you can index into `X` and find the station.
- The adjacency assert in `make_windows` fires, or worse, does not, and the net learns nothing from its neighbours. `station_id` is a category of strings in the feature table and `reg.ID` is integers, so the two sorted orders differ (`'1000' < '999'`). Sort both as integers, and compare `ids` against `sorted(df.station_id.astype(int).unique())`.
- `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for @: 'numpy.ndarray' and 'Tensor'` inside `Mix`. `A_up` was passed as the numpy array `adjacency` returns. `torch.as_tensor(A_up, device=dev)` once, before the loop, as lesson 10 step 5 does, and never inside `forward`.
- MPS appears fifty times faster than the CPU in the timing study. The clock stopped when the kernel was queued, not when it finished. `torch.mps.synchronize()` before every `perf_counter()` read; the honest ratio is near 1 for this network at batch 64.
- An op fails with `NotImplementedError: The operator ... is not currently implemented for the MPS device`. `PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1` was set after `import torch`, which is too late. The first line of `17b` and of the study sets it before the import; setting it in the shell works as well.
- The net's validation AP is higher than LightGBM's until you look at the rows. The two were scored on different row sets: the net has no window for the first hour of the validation block and skips masked targets. `16b.load_challenger` inner-joins on the keys and writes `n_val` and `n_val_aligned`; compare APs only on the aligned rows.
- The gradient check fails at 1e-6 with differences near 1e-4 and the backward pass is right. The check ran in float32, where rounding swamps a central difference at ε = 1e-4; lesson 9 step 2 casts to float64 for exactly this reason. `gradcheck` casts internally; if you rewrote it, cast.
- Validation windows contain training rows. The windows were built on the whole table and then cut by timestamp, so the first eleven validation windows reach back across the gap day. `17b.windows_for` builds each split's windows from that split's rows only, and the assert on the last training window's end catches the other direction.

## Phase 8: Deep learning across domains

_weeks 42–54 · ≈100 h · builds a headline classifier, a local LLM extractor, a profile generator_

**Goal.** Vision, language, large language models, generative models and transfer learning: the parts of deep learning the traffic data cannot carry, learned on small public data that fits the Mac mini.

### What you need to learn

- Convolutions, pooling, feature hierarchies, residual networks; classification, detection, segmentation; transfer from pretrained vision models.
- Tokens, embeddings, self-attention, transformers; encoder and decoder models; fine-tuning a text classifier.
- Large language models: pretraining, fine-tuning, preference tuning, prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use; evaluation and its traps; running a quantized model locally.
- Autoencoders, variational autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models; what they are for beyond images.
- Transfer learning, self-supervised objectives, foundation models, parameter-efficient adaptation; when training from scratch still wins.

### Topic: Convolutional networks and computer vision

**Goal.** Understand how networks see: convolutions, pooling, feature hierarchies, and the tasks built on them.

**Age 5.**

A picture is a grid of tiny colored dots. A computer can slide a small window over the grid looking for edges, then corners, then eyes and wheels, and finally decide 'that is a car'.

_Try this._ Look at a photo through a paper tube. Move it around. You see edges and small parts before you can tell what the whole thing is.

**Middle school.**

A convolution slides a small filter (say 3 × 3 numbers) across the image and computes a weighted sum at each spot, so one filter finds one pattern everywhere. Stacking layers of filters finds bigger patterns; pooling shrinks the image so later layers see more of it at once.

Convolutional networks classify images, find objects with boxes, and label every pixel. They can also read a traffic camera and count cars, which is another way to measure a road.

_Try this._ Draw a 5 × 5 grid of zeros with a vertical line of ones, and slide a 3 × 3 filter [−1, 0, 1] across each row. Where does the output light up?

**High school.**

Layers: convolution (filters, stride, padding), nonlinearity, pooling, batch normalization, then fully connected layers or global pooling. Why convolutions: weight sharing and locality make them data-efficient and translation-equivariant. Classic architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet with skip connections) and what each added.

Tasks: classification, detection (boxes), segmentation (pixels); transfer learning from ImageNet-pretrained models; data augmentation. A 1-D convolution over time is the same idea and is what temporal convolutions in traffic models do.

_Try this._ Train a small convolutional network on a public digits dataset in PyTorch on MPS, then replace the classifier head and fine-tune a pretrained ResNet on a tiny dataset of your own photos.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Convolution as a linear operator with structure (Toeplitz), receptive fields, dilations, depthwise separable convolutions and their cost, normalization variants, and residual connections as a fix for optimization depth. Detection pipelines (region proposals, anchor-free methods), segmentation with encoder-decoders, and the metrics (mAP, IoU).

Vision transformers as an alternative inductive bias, and when convolutions still win (small data, efficiency). Self-supervised pretraining for vision.

_Try this._ Implement a 2-D convolution in numpy with padding and stride, verify against PyTorch, and count the multiplications for a 3 × 3 convolution on a 224 × 224 × 64 tensor.

**Stanford grad.**

Equivariance and invariance as design principles (group-equivariant networks); the interplay of architecture and data scale (ConvNets versus ViTs as data grows); efficient architectures for edge devices (MobileNet, quantization); robustness to distribution shift and adversarial examples; explaining vision models (saliency, concept methods). For transport: camera-based traffic counting and incident detection as complementary sensors.

_Try this._ Design a camera-based vehicle counter for one Fremont on-ramp: architecture, training data, evaluation, and how you would fuse it with loop-detector counts.

**PhD at Apple.**

Vision on device (phones, cameras, cars) is an engineering discipline of its own: latency and energy budgets, hardware-aware architecture search, quantization-aware training, and privacy (on-device processing of imagery). Research threads: multimodal models linking vision and language, 3-D and video understanding, and foundation models for perception.

_Try this._ Sketch a privacy-preserving on-device pipeline that turns roadside camera video into aggregate counts without storing images, and list the failure modes you would monitor.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why share the same filter across the whole image?</summary>

A pattern is a pattern wherever it appears; sharing makes the network data-efficient and lets it recognize a car in any corner.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does pooling buy?</summary>

A larger receptive field for later layers and some tolerance to small shifts, at the cost of resolution.

</details>

### Topic: Language: tokens, embeddings, attention and transformers

**Goal.** Understand how text becomes numbers and how attention lets a model relate every word to every other.

**Age 5.**

A computer cannot read letters, so it turns words into lists of numbers. Words that mean similar things get similar numbers.

Then, to understand a sentence, it lets each word look at the other words and decide which ones matter for it. That looking is called attention.

_Try this._ In the sentence 'the road near the school was slow because of a crash', which words tell you why it was slow? Point at them. That is attention.

**Middle school.**

Tokens are pieces of text (words or word parts); each token gets an embedding, a vector learned so that related tokens sit near each other. Attention computes, for each token, how much to weigh every other token, then mixes their vectors accordingly. A transformer stacks attention and small networks many times.

The same machinery reads 511 incident headlines: 'Injury collision on I-880 N' can be turned into features, or classified by severity, by a small language model.

_Try this._ Take three incident headlines and list which words in each would help decide whether it is serious. Then guess which words a model would attend to.

**High school.**

Tokenization (byte-pair encoding), embeddings (word2vec's idea: predict neighbors), positional information, self-attention as softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V, multi-head attention, feed-forward blocks, residuals and layer normalization. Encoder models (BERT) for understanding, decoder models (GPT) for generation.

Older sequence models (RNNs, LSTMs) processed words in order and struggled with long range; attention sees everything at once, which is why transformers won. Evaluation: perplexity for language modelling, accuracy or F1 for classification.

_Try this._ Implement single-head self-attention in numpy for a sentence of six tokens with random embeddings, print the attention matrix, and explain what a row means.

**Stanford undergrad.**

The transformer in full: scaled dot-product attention and its quadratic cost, causal masking, positional encodings (sinusoidal, learned, rotary), training with teacher forcing, and the compute and memory of a layer. Pretraining objectives (masked language modelling, next-token prediction), fine-tuning for classification, and embeddings from encoders for retrieval.

Practical NLP: text preprocessing pitfalls, class imbalance in text classification, and using a small pretrained encoder on the 511 headlines for severity when the field is missing.

_Try this._ Fine-tune a small pretrained encoder to predict incident severity from headlines and compare with a bag-of-words logistic regression; report macro F1 and calibration.

**Stanford grad.**

Efficient attention (linear, sparse, flash), long-context methods, mixture of experts, and the interpretability of attention (attention is not explanation). Multilingual and multimodal models. Sequence models for non-text data: transformers over time steps and over stations in spatio-temporal forecasting, and their inductive-bias trade-offs against graph convolutions.

_Try this._ Replace the GRU in the spatio-temporal net with a small temporal transformer and the neighbor mixing with spatial attention; compare validation AP and training time on the M1.

**PhD at Apple.**

Language models are now general-purpose components: embeddings for retrieval, classifiers with no labels, and interfaces to systems. The research frontier spans scaling, alignment, efficiency, and evaluation. For a transport product the relevant questions are extracting structured facts from free-text reports reliably and cheaply, and doing it on device where privacy demands.

_Try this._ Design an evaluation for a model that extracts route, direction and severity from free-text incident reports, including how you would build a labelled set and measure calibration of its confidence.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>What is an embedding?</summary>

A learned vector for a token, arranged so that tokens used in similar ways end up near each other.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why did attention replace recurrence?</summary>

It relates every position to every other in one step, trains in parallel, and handles long-range dependencies that recurrent models forget.

</details>

### Topic: Large language models: pretraining, fine-tuning, prompting, retrieval and evaluation

**Goal.** Know what a large language model is, how it is trained and adapted, how to use one responsibly in a system, and how to evaluate it.

**Age 5.**

A large language model has read a huge amount of writing and learned to guess the next word so well that it can answer questions and write stories.

It is not always right, so people check its answers, and they give it the right documents to read when they want facts.

_Try this._ Ask an adult to ask a chatbot what time it is. It probably cannot know. Why not? Because it has no clock unless someone gives it one.

**Middle school.**

Pretraining: the model reads billions of words and learns to predict the next token. Fine-tuning: it is trained a little more on examples of the behavior you want. Prompting: you write instructions and examples in the input. Retrieval-augmented generation: you search your documents and put the relevant ones in the prompt so the model answers from them.

Models can be confidently wrong (hallucinate), so evaluation matters: test on questions with known answers and measure how often the model is right.

_Try this._ Write a prompt asking a model to turn 'Injury collision on I-880 N at Mission Blvd' into route, direction and location fields. Try three headlines. Where does it guess?

**High school.**

The training pipeline: pretraining on web-scale text, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, preference tuning (reinforcement learning from human feedback or direct preference optimization). Scaling laws: loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute. Inference: sampling, temperature, context windows, cost per token.

Adaptation: prompting (instructions, few-shot examples, structured output), parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), retrieval (embeddings, a vector index, chunking), and tool use. Evaluation: held-out benchmarks, task-specific test sets, and human review. On a 16 GB Mac mini, a quantized 3 to 8 billion-parameter model runs locally but competes with training for memory.

_Try this._ Run a small quantized open model locally, ask it to extract structured fields from 50 incident headlines, and measure exact-match accuracy against fields you labelled by hand.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Architecture and training at scale: decoder-only transformers, tokenizer design, data curation and deduplication, mixed precision, distributed training. Alignment methods and their failure modes; hallucination as a calibration problem; retrieval as grounding. Evaluation science: contamination, benchmark saturation, LLM-as-judge and its biases, and why task-specific evaluation sets beat leaderboards.

Systems: latency and cost, caching, batching, structured decoding, guardrails, and observability for model calls. For this project: an LLM could parse free-text reports or draft the weekly monitoring summary, never decide alerts.

_Try this._ Build a small retrieval-augmented question answerer over the repository's documentation with a local embedding model, and write a 30-question evaluation set with exact answers to score it.

**Stanford grad.**

Research threads: scaling and data efficiency, reasoning and tool use, long context, interpretability (probing, circuits), safety and alignment, efficient inference (quantization, speculative decoding, distillation), and evaluation methodology. The open scientific question of what capabilities emerge from next-token prediction and why.

_Try this._ Design an experiment measuring whether an LLM's extracted incident severity improves the traffic model's average precision over the raw feed's field, controlling for the cases where the feed's field is missing.

**PhD at Apple.**

Deploying LLMs in products is a discipline of evaluation, cost and risk: task-specific evals with regression tests, human review loops, privacy of prompts, on-device versus server inference, and clear boundaries on what the model may decide. The research frontier includes reliable structured extraction, calibrated abstention, and agents that act through tools with verifiable behavior.

_Try this._ Write the evaluation and safety plan for using an on-device language model to summarize the weekly monitoring report for a traffic operations team, including what it must never assert.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>What is retrieval-augmented generation for?</summary>

Grounding answers in your documents so the model reads facts instead of recalling them, which cuts hallucination and keeps knowledge current.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why evaluate on your own test set rather than a public benchmark?</summary>

Public benchmarks may be in the training data and rarely match your task; a held-out set of your own questions measures what you will ship.

</details>

### Topic: Generative models: autoencoders, variational autoencoders, GANs and diffusion

**Goal.** Understand models that learn to produce data, the ideas behind each family, and what they are for beyond pictures.

**Age 5.**

Some learning machines do not sort things; they make new things, like drawing a car that has never existed, by learning what cars usually look like.

_Try this._ Draw a car from memory. You are using what you learned about cars to make a new one. A generative model does the same with numbers.

**Middle school.**

An autoencoder squeezes data through a narrow middle and learns to rebuild it; the middle becomes a compact summary. A variational autoencoder makes that middle a probability so you can sample new data. A GAN trains a forger against a detective until the forgeries look real. A diffusion model learns to remove noise step by step, so starting from pure noise it can produce a realistic sample.

For traffic, generative models can produce realistic fake days for testing or fill in missing sensor data.

_Try this._ Take a daily speed profile, add random noise to it, and try to guess the original. That guessing, repeated many times, is what a diffusion model learns.

**High school.**

Autoencoders and reconstruction error as an anomaly score; VAEs with a latent Gaussian and a loss of reconstruction plus a KL term; GANs with a generator and discriminator and their training instability; diffusion models as learned denoising over many steps with a simple noise-prediction loss. Evaluation is hard: likelihood is not quality; sample-quality scores exist for images.

Uses: synthetic data, imputation, compression, and learning representations that transfer.

_Try this._ Train a small autoencoder on daily speed profiles in PyTorch; use reconstruction error to rank days by strangeness and inspect the top five.

**Stanford undergrad.**

The ELBO and amortized variational inference behind VAEs; the reparameterization trick; posterior collapse. GANs as a minimax game, mode collapse, Wasserstein formulations. Diffusion: forward noising process, reverse process, score matching, the connection to stochastic differential equations, classifier-free guidance. Normalizing flows as exact-likelihood models.

Time-series generation and imputation with these families; conditional generation (a day given weather and calendar) as a simulator for evaluation.

_Try this._ Derive the VAE loss from the ELBO and implement a conditional VAE that generates daily profiles given weekday and rain; compare generated and real distributions of the 5 pm speed.

**Stanford grad.**

Diffusion models' dominance in images and their extension to audio, video, molecules and time series; latent diffusion for efficiency; evaluation via distribution metrics and downstream utility. Generative models for scientific simulation and for data augmentation under distribution shift. Privacy risks (memorization) and the synthetic-data trade-offs.

_Try this._ Train a small diffusion model on daily station profiles and test whether augmenting training with its samples improves the classifier's average precision on rare rainy-day episodes.

**PhD at Apple.**

Generative modelling is now infrastructure for media, science and simulation. The research frontier includes fast sampling, controllability, evaluation, and world models that couple generation with dynamics. For transport, generative simulators of traffic conditioned on interventions are a path to counterfactual evaluation of alerts and routing.

_Try this._ Propose a generative traffic simulator conditioned on incidents and weather, trained on PeMS history, and the validation that would let you trust its counterfactuals.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>What does the KL term in a VAE do?</summary>

It keeps the learned latent distribution close to a simple prior so that sampling from the prior produces sensible outputs.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is likelihood a poor measure of sample quality?</summary>

A model can assign high likelihood to data while producing blurry or degenerate samples; likelihood and perceptual quality measure different things.

</details>

### Topic: Transfer learning, self-supervision and foundation models

**Goal.** Reuse what a model learned elsewhere, learn from unlabeled data, and know when a pretrained model beats training from scratch.

**Age 5.**

If you already know how to ride a bicycle, learning a scooter is faster. Learning machines can also start from something they already learned instead of starting from zero.

_Try this._ Name one thing you learned that made a new thing easier. That is transfer.

**Middle school.**

Transfer learning takes a model trained on a big dataset and adapts it to a small one: keep the early layers, retrain the last part. Self-supervised learning makes its own labels from unlabeled data, like predicting a hidden word or a missing patch, so it can learn from everything. Foundation models are big models pretrained this way that many tasks reuse.

For traffic, a model pretrained on all of California's PeMS could be fine-tuned for Fremont with less data.

_Try this._ Cover part of a sentence with your hand and guess the missing word. You just made a label with no teacher.

**High school.**

Feature extraction versus fine-tuning; learning rates for pretrained layers; catastrophic forgetting. Self-supervised objectives: masked prediction, contrastive learning (pull similar views together), next-step prediction. Foundation models in vision, language and now time series; zero-shot and few-shot use.

Practical rule: with little labelled data, start pretrained; with lots of in-domain data and a narrow task, training from scratch on tabular features still wins, which is why LightGBM is this project's production model.

_Try this._ Pretrain a small network on all Fremont stations with a masked-step objective, then fine-tune it on one station's classification task and compare with training that station's model from scratch on the same data.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Why transfer works (shared low-level features, representations as inductive bias), negative transfer, domain adaptation and domain shift; contrastive learning theory (InfoNCE as a mutual-information bound); masked autoencoders; scaling behavior of pretraining. Time-series foundation models and their mixed evidence against tuned task-specific models.

Evaluating transfer honestly: matched compute and data budgets, and the leakage risk when pretraining data overlaps the test period.

_Try this._ Implement a contrastive pretraining on station-day windows (two augmented views of the same window as positives), then a linear probe for the slow-episode label; report linear-probe AP against raw features.

**Stanford grad.**

Representation quality and its measurement (probes, transfer suites), the role of data curation in pretraining, parameter-efficient adaptation (adapters, LoRA), continual pretraining, and model merging. Foundation models for spatio-temporal data and the open question of whether traffic dynamics transfer across cities.

_Try this._ Design an experiment testing whether pretraining on PeMS District 4 improves 60-minute skill in Fremont, with a leakage-safe split in time and space.

**PhD at Apple.**

The economics of pretraining (one large cost amortized over many tasks) reshaped ML organizations; the research frontier includes what pretraining learns, how to adapt safely, and how to evaluate foundation models on tasks they were not built for. For transport, a state-wide pretrained traffic model served to many cities is a plausible product and a research program.

_Try this._ Write the research plan for a California-wide traffic foundation model: data, objective, evaluation across cities, and the failure modes you would expect.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>When does training from scratch beat a pretrained model?</summary>

With plenty of in-domain data and a narrow task, especially tabular problems where boosted trees on engineered features remain strongest.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What makes self-supervision possible?</summary>

The data contain their own supervision: hide part of an input and predict it from the rest.

</details>

### Read and watch, explained at every level

#### [Understanding Deep Learning (Prince)](https://udlbook.github.io/udlbook/)

_book · free · reference, chapters as needed · now chapters 10 to 18: convolutions, transformers, graphs, generative models_

**Age 5.** A newer big book about deep learning, free to read, with lots of clear pictures that show what each part of a network does.

**Middle school.** Simon Prince's textbook (2023), free as a PDF with notebooks. It covers supervised learning, networks, training, measuring performance, regularization, convolutional and recurrent and transformer networks, graph networks, and generative models. It is more modern and more visual than the older Deep Learning book. Read the early chapters after phase 6.

**High school.** Chapters 1 to 9 are the modern version of lesson 9: networks, loss functions, fitting, gradients and initialization, measuring performance, and regularization, each with figures that make the idea visible. Chapter 13 on graph neural networks covers the neighbor mixing of the spatio-temporal net. The notebooks let you run every figure.

**Stanford undergrad.** Prince's treatment of why deep networks generalize, of the loss landscape, and of the transformer architecture is the clearest current textbook account, and it includes the recent empirical findings (double descent, scaling) that Goodfellow predates. Chapter 12 on transformers is the reading before lesson 8's attention material.

**Stanford grad.** The chapters on generative models (VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion) are a compact, correct introduction with the math intact, and the chapter on ethics is unusually careful for a technical text. Use it as the reference when reading current papers.

**PhD at Apple.** A free, modern, rigorous textbook is a public good; it is the one to recommend to a new graduate student and the one to cite for standard architectures in the current idiom. Its figures are also the model for how to draw a network in a paper.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Chapters: introduction; supervised learning; shallow networks; deep networks; loss functions; fitting models; gradients and initialization; measuring performance; regularization; convolutional networks; residual networks; transformers; graph neural networks; unsupervised learning; generative adversarial networks; normalizing flows; variational autoencoders; diffusion models; reinforcement learning; why does deep learning work; deep learning and ethics.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Shallow and deep networks: a shallow network is a linear combination of ReLU-transformed linear functions, producing piecewise linear maps with regions; depth composes such maps and creates exponentially many regions per parameter; universal approximation with width, efficiency with depth.
2. Losses from maximum likelihood: choose a distribution over outputs (Gaussian gives least squares, Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy, categorical gives softmax cross-entropy, others give robust or heteroscedastic losses); the network predicts the distribution's parameters.
3. Fitting: gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, momentum, Adam; learning-rate schedules and warmup; backpropagation derived for the general case with the forward pass storing activations; initialization that preserves variance (He), and the analysis of exploding and vanishing signals.
4. Measuring performance: noise, bias and variance; the double-descent curve; hyperparameter search; the importance of test sets; the curse of dimensionality and how real data lie on lower-dimensional manifolds.
5. Regularization: explicit (L2, early stopping), implicit (SGD's noise, larger learning rates), heuristic (ensembling, dropout, augmentation, transfer learning, multi-task, self-supervision), and the general picture of why regularized deep networks generalize.
6. Architectures: convolutions (invariance, equivariance, pooling, receptive fields, classic networks), residual connections (why depth trained poorly before them, batch and layer norm), transformers (dot-product attention, positional information, encoder and decoder, scaling, vision transformers), graph networks (adjacency, node embeddings, message passing, graph-level and node-level tasks, spectral and spatial views).
7. Generative models: GANs (minimax, mode collapse, Wasserstein), normalizing flows (invertible transformations and exact likelihoods), VAEs (the ELBO, reparameterization, posterior collapse), diffusion (forward noising, reverse denoising, the training objective, conditioning and guidance).
8. Reinforcement learning basics, the chapter on why deep learning works (loss landscapes, overparameterization, lottery tickets, adversarial examples) and the ethics chapter (bias, explainability, misuse, environmental cost).

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
deep network: y = φ_K ∘ … ∘ φ_1(x), each φ = ReLU(W h + b)
ELBO = E_q[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z))
attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Every loss is a negative log-likelihood of some output distribution.
- Depth buys expressive piecewise-linear maps; normalization and residuals make depth trainable.
- Generative families differ in how they make likelihood tractable: flows exactly, VAEs by bounds, diffusion by denoising, GANs not at all.
