#### `launchd/com.traffic1.predict.plist` · plist · new

_Purpose._ The predictor's launchd job: one replay cycle every `common.PREDICT_SECONDS` seconds, whether or not a terminal is open, surviving reboots and, unlike cron, running the missed job when the machine wakes. The plist from lesson 12 step 4 is the template; the only change is that the four hard-coded paths become `__ROOT__`, rendered with `TRAFFIC1_ROOT` at install time, because launchd cannot read `.env` and a plist with someone else's home folder in it runs nothing.

_Reads._ Nothing itself; the job it starts reads what `19_predict_live.py` reads.

_Writes._ `logs/predict.log` and `logs/predict.err` through `StandardOutPath` and `StandardErrorPath`.

_Run._ Render and load all four: `set -a; source .env; set +a; for j in poll predict monitor retrain; do sed "s#__ROOT__#$TRAFFIC1_ROOT#g" launchd/com.traffic1.$j.plist > ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.traffic1.$j.plist; launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.traffic1.$j.plist; done`. Check: `launchctl list | grep traffic1` shows four labels, `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.traffic1.predict | grep -E 'state|last exit'` shows the state and the last exit code. Unload one: `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.traffic1.predict`. Reload after editing: bootout, then bootstrap again.

_Must contain._

- `Label` `com.traffic1.predict`; `ProgramArguments` `__ROOT__/.venv/bin/python`, `__ROOT__/19_predict_live.py`, `--replay`, `--once`; `StartInterval` 300 (the value of `common.PREDICT_SECONDS`, written as a number here because a plist cannot import); `WorkingDirectory` `__ROOT__`; `StandardOutPath` and `StandardErrorPath` under `__ROOT__/logs/`; `RunAtLoad` true so the first cycle runs the moment the job loads; `EnvironmentVariables` with `OMP_NUM_THREADS` `8`, the plan's house rule, and `PATH` set to `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/bin:/opt/homebrew/bin`, because launchd jobs do not get your shell's `PATH` and `libomp` lives under Homebrew.

_Skeleton._

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>com.traffic1.predict</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array>
    <string>__ROOT__/.venv/bin/python</string><string>__ROOT__/19_predict_live.py</string>
    <string>--replay</string><string>--once</string>
  </array>
  <key>StartInterval</key><integer>300</integer>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key><string>__ROOT__</string>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>__ROOT__/logs/predict.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>__ROOT__/logs/predict.err</string>
  <key>EnvironmentVariables</key><dict>
    <key>OMP_NUM_THREADS</key><string>8</string>
    <key>PATH</key><string>/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/bin:/opt/homebrew/bin</string>
  </dict>
</dict></plist>
```

_Check._ `plutil -lint launchd/com.traffic1.predict.plist` prints `OK`. Ten minutes after loading, `grep -c '^stage=predict' logs/predict.log` prints 2 or 3, and `stat -f %m output/predictions_latest.json` changes every five minutes. `logs/predict.err` is empty; if it names `libomp`, the `PATH` line is missing.

#### `launchd/com.traffic1.monitor.plist` · plist · new

_Purpose._ The weekly monitor. Same template with the label `com.traffic1.monitor`, `ProgramArguments` `__ROOT__/.venv/bin/python __ROOT__/20_monitor.py --retrain-if-due`, and instead of `StartInterval` a `StartCalendarInterval` dict with `Weekday` 1, `Hour` 4, `Minute` 0 (Monday 04:00 local, after Sunday's PeMS file has been cleaned by the retrain job's `features` step or by hand); logs `logs/monitor.log` and `logs/monitor.err`; no `RunAtLoad`. launchd runs a missed calendar job once at the next wake, which is why it and not cron carries the weekly job on a machine that may have slept.

_Check._ `plutil -lint` prints `OK`; `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.traffic1.monitor | grep -A3 'calendar'` shows the Monday entry; the first Monday after loading, `ls output/monitor/` has a new file.

#### `launchd/com.traffic1.retrain.plist` · plist · new

_Purpose._ The monthly retrain by schedule. Label `com.traffic1.retrain`, `ProgramArguments` `/usr/bin/caffeinate`, `-i`, `/usr/bin/make`, `retrain`, so the Mac cannot idle-sleep during the hour the job takes; `StartCalendarInterval` with `Day` 2, `Hour` 3, `Minute` 0 (the second of the month at 03:00, after the first's file has posted); `WorkingDirectory` `__ROOT__`; logs `logs/retrain.log` and `logs/retrain.err`; `EnvironmentVariables` as the predictor's, plus `TRAFFIC1_ROOT` `__ROOT__`. It runs `make retrain`, which is `20_monitor.py --stash`, then `features` for the newest month, `train`, `calibrate`, `evaluate`, then `20_monitor.py --promote`; the promote step refuses a worse model and restores the previous set, which is the canary the lesson's last question asks for. The house rule stands: this job and the download never overlap, and the monitor never runs while this does; the schedule keeps them a day and an hour apart, and `make retrain` starts by checking that no `09_collect_pems_selenium.py` or `20_monitor.py` process is running (`pgrep -f`) and exits 1 if one is.

_Check._ `plutil -lint` prints `OK`. Run it once by hand, `launchctl kickstart gui/$(id -u)/com.traffic1.retrain`, on a month you already have: `tail -1 logs/retrain.log` shows `promote` or `refused` and `models/manifest.json`'s `history` grew by one; `make rollback` then restores the previous hashes.

#### `Makefile` · config · changed

_Purpose._ Finished: phase 0's `setup`, `check` and `test` stay as written, and phase 9 adds every target LAYOUT lists, so the whole pipeline is `make all` and the operations are one word each. Recipes are indented with a tab; `MONTHS` defaults to every month present and can be given on the command line.

_Must contain._

- `MONTHS ?= $(shell ls data/pems_processed 2>/dev/null | sed 's/.parquet//')` at the top; `PY = .venv/bin/python`; `RUNNERS = $(basename $(wildcard [0-9]*_*.py))`, the fifteen runner stems, for the stage-page check; the newest month for `retrain` is `$(lastword $(sort $(MONTHS)))`.
- `setup`, `check`, `test` · phase 0's targets; the skeleton below abbreviates their recipes to fit, so keep the full ones phase 0 wrote.
- `collect` · one poll. `pems` · `09_collect_pems_selenium.py` for `MONTHS`, newest first, under `caffeinate -i`.
- `clean`, `labels`, `incidents`, `features` · runners 10 to 13 over `MONTHS`, each target depending on the one before.
- `baselines`, `train`, `calibrate`, `evaluate` · runners 14, 16 (and 15 inside `train`), 16b, 18.
- `all` · depends on the pipeline targets, then fails naming the first runner without a page under `docs/stages/`.
- `predict`, `monitor`, `retrain`, `rollback`, `serve`, and `.PHONY` listing every target.

_Skeleton._

```make
MONTHS ?= $(shell ls data/pems_processed 2>/dev/null | sed 's/.parquet//')
PY      = .venv/bin/python
RUNNERS = $(basename $(wildcard [0-9]*_*.py))
.PHONY: setup check test collect pems clean labels incidents features baselines train calibrate evaluate all predict monitor retrain rollback serve
setup:
	test -d .venv || python3 -m venv .venv
	$(PY) -m pip install --upgrade pip && $(PY) -m pip install -r requirements.txt
	command -v brew >/dev/null && { brew list libomp >/dev/null 2>&1 || brew install libomp; } || true
check:
	$(PY) -c "import platform, torch, lightgbm, pandas; print(platform.machine(), torch.__version__, lightgbm.__version__, pandas.__version__, 'mps', torch.backends.mps.is_available())"
test:
	$(PY) -m pytest -q
collect:
	$(PY) 02_collect_events.py
pems:
	caffeinate -i $(PY) 09_collect_pems_selenium.py $(foreach m,$(sort $(MONTHS)),--month $(m))
clean:
	for m in $(MONTHS); do $(PY) 10_clean_pems.py --month $$m || exit 1; done
labels: clean
	for m in $(MONTHS); do $(PY) 11_build_labels.py --month $$m || exit 1; done
incidents: labels
	for m in $(MONTHS); do $(PY) 12_join_incidents.py --month $$m || exit 1; done
features: incidents
	for m in $(MONTHS); do $(PY) 13_feature_engineering.py --month $$m || exit 1; done
baselines: features
	$(PY) 14_train_baselines.py
train: baselines
	$(PY) 15_train_logreg.py && $(PY) 16_train_lgbm.py
calibrate: train
	$(PY) 16b_calibrate_select.py
evaluate: calibrate
	$(PY) 18_evaluate_lead_time.py
all: evaluate
	for r in $(RUNNERS); do test -f docs/stages/$$r.md || { echo "missing docs/stages/$$r.md"; exit 1; }; done
predict:
	$(PY) 19_predict_live.py --replay --once
monitor:
	$(PY) 20_monitor.py
retrain:
	! pgrep -f '09_collect_pems_selenium.py|20_monitor.py' >/dev/null || { echo "another heavy job is running"; exit 1; }
	$(PY) 20_monitor.py --stash && $(MAKE) features MONTHS=$(lastword $(sort $(MONTHS))) && $(MAKE) train calibrate evaluate && $(PY) 20_monitor.py --promote
rollback:
	$(PY) 20_monitor.py --rollback
serve:
	.venv/bin/uvicorn serve.app:app --port 8000
```

_Check._ `make -n all MONTHS=2026-03` prints the nine commands in order without running them; `make all` on a tree with one page deleted ends with `missing docs/stages/<runner>.md` and exit code 1; `cat -A Makefile | grep -c '^\^I'` prints the number of recipe lines, all tabs. From a fresh clone, `make setup && make all` runs to `output/evaluation_report.json`, which is the first Done-when check.

_Watch for._ `MONTHS` is evaluated when `make` starts, so `make clean` on a fresh clone sees no months in `data/pems_processed/` and does nothing; run `make pems MONTHS=2026-03` first, or pass `MONTHS` explicitly. And `$$m` inside a recipe is the shell's `$m`; a single dollar is `make`'s and silently expands to nothing.

#### `tests/test_golden_features.py` · test · new

_Purpose._ The proof that serving features equal training features: one stored day's input rows and the feature rows `13_feature_engineering.py` produced for it live under `data/golden/YYYY-MM-DD/`; the test runs `features.build_features` on the stored input and compares with the stored output bit for bit. It runs under `make test` (alone: `pytest -q tests/test_golden_features.py`), and skips with a clear message when no golden day exists, so `make test` still passes on a fresh clone. The file also holds the maker, `write_golden(day)`, so the fixture and its test cannot drift apart.

_Reads._ `data/golden/YYYY-MM-DD/input.parquet`, `expected.parquet`, `registry.parquet`, `weather.parquet`, `meta.json` (below); `features.build_features(input, registry, weather_hourly=weather)`, the call `13_feature_engineering.py` makes.

_Must contain._

- `GOLDEN = common.DATA / 'golden'`; `LEAD_IN = max(common.LAGS + tuple(common.ROLL_STEPS.values()))` · the steps before midnight the input must carry so the first rows' lags and rolling windows are defined (12).
- `golden_days() -> list[Path]`; the module skips when empty.
- `write_golden(day: str) -> Path` · slices the day plus `LEAD_IN` steps before its local midnight from the month's `data/pems_processed/`, `data/labels/` and `data/incidents/` files joined on `station_id` and `timestamp` (the rows `13_feature_engineering.py` hands to `build_features`), saves them as `input.parquet`; saves the day's rows of `data/features/YYYY-MM.parquet` restricted to the feature columns in `models/gbt_h30_features.json` plus the keys as `expected.parquet`; copies the registry and the weather rows for the day; writes `meta.json` with `day`, `columns`, the sha256 of each file, and `git rev-parse HEAD` at creation. Invoked once as `python -c "from tests.test_golden_features import write_golden; write_golden('2026-03-15')"` on a weekday with a rush hour.
- `test_golden_day_exists()` · the folder has the five files and `meta.json`'s hashes match.
- `test_features_bit_for_bit()` · for every golden day: `build_features(input, registry, weather_hourly=weather)` on the stored frames, keep the day's timestamps, align to `expected.parquet` on `station_id` and `timestamp`, and `pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(got[cols], exp[cols], check_exact=True, check_dtype=True)`; NaN equals NaN.
- `test_no_target_in_features()` · none of `y_15`, `y_30`, `y_60`, `speed_t30`, `label`, `label_abs` is among `meta.json`'s `columns`.
- `test_serving_slice_matches()` · the 13-step slice the loop uses: `build_features` on the rows of the 13 slots ending at 17:00 local only, newest row per station, equals the same rows of `expected.parquet`; this is the exact code path `19_predict_live.py` runs, and it fails when a feature needs more history than the buffer carries.

_Skeleton._

```python
"""Golden-file test: build_features on a stored day equals the feature table 13 wrote for it, bit for bit."""
import json, hashlib
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd, pytest
import common
from features import build_features

GOLDEN = common.DATA / "golden"
LEAD_IN = max(common.LAGS + tuple(common.ROLL_STEPS.values()))
DAYS = sorted(p for p in GOLDEN.glob("????-??-??") if (p / "meta.json").exists()) if GOLDEN.exists() else []
pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not DAYS, reason="no data/golden/<day>/ yet; run write_golden() once")

def write_golden(day):
    """Store one day's input rows, expected feature rows, registry, weather and hashes under data/golden/<day>/."""
    ...

def _load(p):
    meta = json.load(open(p / "meta.json"))
    return (pd.read_parquet(p / "input.parquet"), pd.read_parquet(p / "expected.parquet"),
            pd.read_parquet(p / "registry.parquet"), pd.read_parquet(p / "weather.parquet"), meta)

@pytest.mark.parametrize("p", DAYS, ids=[p.name for p in DAYS])
def test_features_bit_for_bit(p):
    inp, exp, reg, hourly, meta = _load(p)
    got = build_features(inp, reg, weather_hourly=hourly)    # the exact call 13_feature_engineering.py makes
    day = pd.Timestamp(meta["day"], tz=common.TZ)
    got = got[(got.timestamp >= day) & (got.timestamp < day + pd.Timedelta(days=1))]
    key = ["station_id", "timestamp"]
    got = got.sort_values(key).set_index(key); exp = exp.sort_values(key).set_index(key)
    assert len(got) == len(exp), (len(got), len(exp))
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(got[meta["columns"]], exp[meta["columns"]], check_exact=True, check_dtype=True)

def test_golden_day_exists(): ...
def test_no_target_in_features(): ...
def test_serving_slice_matches(): ...
```

_Check._ `pytest -q tests/test_golden_features.py` prints `4 passed` per golden day. Change one constant in `features.py` (a `min_periods`, a lag) and run it again: `test_features_bit_for_bit` fails naming the first differing column, which is the test doing its job; revert. After a retrain the test still passes, because features do not depend on the model; after an intended change to `features.py`, rebuild the month with `make features MONTHS=<month>` and regenerate the golden day, and say so in the commit message.

#### `data/golden/YYYY-MM-DD/` · fixture · new

_Purpose._ One stored day, chosen for a weekday with a visible rush hour and no detector outage, kept under `data/` because it is 40 MB of derived data and git must not carry it; `meta.json` records where it came from and the hashes so a regenerated folder can be told from the original. Made by `write_golden()` above; never edited by hand.

_Writes._ `input.parquet` (the day plus 12 lead-in steps: `station_id`, `timestamp`, `speed`, `occ`, `flow`, `observed_frac`, `samples`, then every column `11_build_labels.py` adds, `slot`, `daytype`, `profile_speed`, `free_flow_85`, `speed_ratio`, `ratio_ff`, `profile_label_rate`, `label`, `label_known`, `label_abs`, then the six incident columns, the dtypes the monthly files have); `expected.parquet` (the day's feature rows: `station_id`, `timestamp` and every column in `models/gbt_h30_features.json`, float32 and categorical as `13_feature_engineering.py` wrote them); `registry.parquet`; `weather.parquet` (the day's hours of `precip_mm`); `meta.json` with `day`, `month_file`, `columns`, `sha256` per file, `created_at`, `git_head`.

_Check._ `python -c "import pandas as pd; e=pd.read_parquet('data/golden/2026-03-15/expected.parquet'); print(e.shape, e.station_id.nunique(), e.timestamp.min(), e.timestamp.max())"` prints 288 rows per station, the station count, and timestamps spanning the local day; the input has 300 rows per station.
#### `serve/app.py` · module · new

_Purpose._ A door on the predictions: a FastAPI service that answers `GET /health`, `GET /predictions` (the current `output/predictions_latest.json`) and `GET /predictions/{station_id}` (one station's three horizons). It reads the file the loop writes and computes nothing, which keeps it stateless: any number of copies can answer, and the loop stays the one place predictions are made. Add `fastapi>=0.110`, `uvicorn>=0.27` and `httpx>=0.27` to `requirements.txt` under `# phase 9`.

_Reads._ `output/predictions_latest.json`, every key; the folder comes from `TRAFFIC1_OUTPUT` when set (the container sets it to `/app/output`), else `common.OUTPUT`. The file is read on every request, not cached, so a container that mounts `output/` sees each five-minute rewrite.

_Writes._ Nothing on disk. Responses: `/health` → `{"status": "ok", "generated_at", "set_id", "latest_age_s": float, "stale": bool}` with `stale` true past 3 × `common.PREDICT_SECONDS`, status 503 with `{"status": "no predictions"}` when the file is missing; `/predictions` → the file's object unchanged; `/predictions/{station_id}` → `{"station_id", "generated_at", "input_ts", "rows": [three objects]}`, 404 with `{"detail": "unknown station"}` otherwise. Every response carries the header `X-Traffic1-Set` with the `set_id`.

_Run._ `make serve`, which is `uvicorn serve.app:app --port 8000`; then `curl -s localhost:8000/health` and `curl -s localhost:8000/predictions/$(python -c "import json; print(json.load(open('output/predictions_latest.json'))['rows'][0]['station_id'])")`. The interactive documentation is at `localhost:8000/docs`.

_Must contain._

- `PRED_PATH: Path` from the rule above; `STALE_AFTER_S = 3 * common.PREDICT_SECONDS`.
- `class Row(BaseModel)` · `station_id: int`, `fwy: int`, `dir: str`, `abs_pm: float`, `h: int`, `p: float`, `alert: bool`. `class Predictions(BaseModel)` · `generated_at: str`, `input_ts: str`, `mode: str`, `set_id: str`, `rows: list[Row]`. `class StationPredictions(BaseModel)`, `class Health(BaseModel)`.
- `load_latest() -> Predictions` · reads and validates the file; raises `HTTPException(503)` when missing or unparsable.
- `app = FastAPI(title='Traffic1 predictions', version='1')` and the three route functions `health()`, `predictions()`, `station(station_id: int)`, each with a `response_model`.
- A middleware or dependency that sets `X-Traffic1-Set`.

_Skeleton._

```python
"""FastAPI door on output/predictions_latest.json: /health, /predictions, /predictions/{station_id}."""
import json, os, time
from pathlib import Path
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Response
from pydantic import BaseModel
import common

PRED_PATH = Path(os.environ.get("TRAFFIC1_OUTPUT", common.OUTPUT)) / "predictions_latest.json"
STALE_AFTER_S = 3 * common.PREDICT_SECONDS

class Row(BaseModel):
    station_id: int; fwy: int; dir: str; abs_pm: float; h: int; p: float; alert: bool

class Predictions(BaseModel):
    generated_at: str; input_ts: str; mode: str; set_id: str; rows: list[Row]

class StationPredictions(BaseModel):
    station_id: int; generated_at: str; input_ts: str; rows: list[Row]

class Health(BaseModel):
    status: str; generated_at: str; set_id: str; latest_age_s: float; stale: bool

def load_latest():
    """Parse the loop's file; 503 when it is missing."""
    ...

app = FastAPI(title="Traffic1 predictions", version="1")

@app.get("/health", response_model=Health)
def health(response: Response): ...

@app.get("/predictions", response_model=Predictions)
def predictions(response: Response): ...

@app.get("/predictions/{station_id}", response_model=StationPredictions)
def station(station_id: int, response: Response): ...
```

_Check._ With the loop's file present, `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost:8000/predictions` prints `200`; move the file away and `/health` prints `503`; an unknown id prints `404`. `curl -sI localhost:8000/health | grep X-Traffic1-Set` shows the manifest's `set_id`.

#### `serve/Dockerfile` · config · new

_Purpose._ The service in a box: the interpreter, the packages and `serve/app.py` travel together, so the same image runs on the Mac, a server or a cloud VM. The walkthrough's three lines are the core: `COPY requirements.txt`, `pip install`, `CMD`. The predictions come in through a volume, not the image, because a file that changes every five minutes does not belong in an image.

_Must contain._

- `FROM python:3.11-slim`; `WORKDIR /app`; `COPY requirements.txt .`; `RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`; `COPY common.py .` and `COPY serve/ serve/`; `ENV TRAFFIC1_OUTPUT=/app/output`; `EXPOSE 8000`; `CMD ["uvicorn", "serve.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]`.
- A `.dockerignore` at the repository root with `data/`, `models/`, `output/`, `logs/`, `.venv/`, `.git/`, `__pycache__/`, so `docker build` does not ship 16 GB of raw PeMS to the daemon as build context; without it the build takes an hour before the first line runs.

_Skeleton._

```text
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY common.py .
COPY serve/ serve/
ENV TRAFFIC1_OUTPUT=/app/output
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "serve.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

_Check._ `docker build -f serve/Dockerfile -t traffic1-serve .` finishes; `docker run --rm -d -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD/output:/app/output" --name traffic1 traffic1-serve` then `curl -s localhost:8000/health` prints `ok`; `docker stop traffic1`. `docker image ls traffic1-serve` shows the size; it is a few gigabytes because `requirements.txt` carries torch, and the report may note that a service-only requirements list would make it a tenth of that.

_Watch for._ Docker Desktop on the M1 builds arm64 images; a server that is x86 needs `docker build --platform linux/amd64`, which is slow under emulation but works. `common.py` must import without `.env` present: `common.env()` returns defaults when the file is missing, and the service never needs a secret.

#### `tests/test_serve.py` · test · new

_Purpose._ The golden test through the endpoint, and latency measured. It replays the golden day's 5 pm slot with `19_predict_live.py --at`, so `output/predictions_latest.json` holds a known cycle, then asks the service for it, in process by default (FastAPI's `TestClient`, which is httpx underneath) or over HTTP when `SERVE_URL` is set, which is how the container is tested.

_Reads._ `data/golden/YYYY-MM-DD/meta.json` and, when present and made under the live `set_id`, `predictions.json`; `models/manifest.json`; `models/calibration.json` for `tau`; the running service or `serve.app`.

_Must contain._

- `client()` fixture · `httpx.Client(base_url=os.environ['SERVE_URL'])` when set, else `fastapi.testclient.TestClient(app)`; skips when no golden day exists.
- `golden_cycle()` fixture (module scope) · `subprocess.run([sys.executable, '19_predict_live.py', '--replay', '--once', '--at', slot], check=True)` where `slot` is the golden day at 17:00 local converted to UTC; yields the parsed `output/predictions_latest.json`.
- `test_health_ok(client)` · 200, `status == 'ok'`, `latest_age_s < 60`.
- `test_predictions_match_file(client, golden_cycle)` · `/predictions` equals the file's object exactly.
- `test_station_rows(client, golden_cycle)` · for every station in the registry: 200, three rows with `h` in {15, 30, 60}, `p` in [0, 1], `alert == (p >= tau[h])`; an unknown id gives 404.
- `test_golden_predictions(client, golden_cycle)` · when `predictions.json` exists and its `set_id` equals the manifest's live `set_id`, every `p` matches to 1e-6; otherwise skips with the reason.
- `test_latency(client)` · 100 `GET /predictions` and 100 `GET /predictions/{station_id}`; prints median and p95 in ms; asserts the p95 of the station call is under 100 ms in process and under 250 ms over HTTP. The two numbers go into `docs/stages/19_predict_live.md`.

_Skeleton._

```python
"""Golden test through the endpoint, and latency for 100 requests."""
import json, os, subprocess, sys, time
import httpx, numpy as np, pandas as pd, pytest
import common

GOLDEN = sorted(common.DATA.glob("golden/????-??-??"))
pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not GOLDEN, reason="no golden day")

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def client():
    if os.environ.get("SERVE_URL"):
        return httpx.Client(base_url=os.environ["SERVE_URL"], timeout=5)
    from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
    from serve.app import app
    return TestClient(app)

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def golden_cycle():
    meta = json.load(open(GOLDEN[-1] / "meta.json"))
    slot = pd.Timestamp(meta["day"] + " 17:00", tz=common.TZ).tz_convert("UTC").strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M")
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "19_predict_live.py", "--replay", "--once", "--at", slot], check=True, cwd=common.ROOT)
    return json.load(open(common.OUTPUT / "predictions_latest.json"))

def test_predictions_match_file(client, golden_cycle):
    r = client.get("/predictions"); assert r.status_code == 200
    assert r.json() == golden_cycle

def test_latency(client, golden_cycle):
    sid = golden_cycle["rows"][0]["station_id"]; t = []
    for _ in range(100):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); assert client.get(f"/predictions/{sid}").status_code == 200; t.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    med, p95 = np.median(t) * 1e3, np.percentile(t, 95) * 1e3
    print(f"latency ms median={med:.1f} p95={p95:.1f}")
    assert p95 < (250 if os.environ.get("SERVE_URL") else 100)

def test_health_ok(client, golden_cycle): ...
def test_station_rows(client, golden_cycle): ...
def test_golden_predictions(client, golden_cycle): ...
```

_Check._ `pytest -q tests/test_serve.py -s` prints `latency ms median=... p95=...` and `5 passed` (or one skip for the golden predictions when the set changed). Against the container: `SERVE_URL=http://localhost:8000 pytest -q tests/test_serve.py -s` passes the same way, with larger latencies; both pairs of numbers go into the stage page.

#### `studies/profile_stnet_step.py` · study · new

_Purpose._ Profile one training step of the spatio-temporal net on the M1 with the PyTorch profiler and with timers around data movement, forward, backward and optimizer, name the largest cost, apply one fix, and measure again; the JSON carries before and after. Optimizing before profiling is the phase's fourth pitfall, and this study is the habit that prevents it.

_Reads._ `stnet.py`'s `STNet`, `Mix` and its window builder; the windows for one training month built exactly as `17b_train_stnet.py` builds them; `data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet` for the adjacency.

_Writes._ `output/studies/profile_stnet_step.json` with `device`, `batch` (int), `n_stations` (int), `params` (int), and `before` and `after`, each an object with `ms_per_step` (float, mean of 20 timed steps after 3 warm-up steps), `share` (an object `data`, `forward`, `backward`, `optimizer`, fractions summing to 1), `top_ops` (a list of `[name, ms]` for the ten largest from `prof.key_averages()`), plus `fix` (str) and `speedup` (float, before over after). `output/studies/profile_stnet_step.png`: two stacked bars, before and after, one colour per section.

_Run._ `python studies/profile_stnet_step.py --month 2026-03 --batch 64 --fix resident --steps 20 --seed 0 --device mps`. `--fix` is one of `resident` (keep the whole windowed tensor on the device and index it there instead of moving each batch), `batch128` (double the batch), `none` (measure twice, which shows the noise floor); the default is `resident` because on unified memory the per-batch upload is the usual winner, but the JSON must show it, not this sentence.

_Must contain._

- `WARMUP = 3`, `STEPS = 20`.
- `timed_step(net, opt, lossf, X, y, A_up, A_down, dev, resident: bool) -> dict` · one step with `torch.mps.synchronize()` (or `torch.cuda.synchronize`, or nothing on CPU) after each of the four sections, returning their milliseconds.
- `profile_step(...) -> list[tuple[str, float]]` · the same step inside `torch.profiler.profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU], record_shapes=True)`; MPS kernels show as CPU-side dispatch time, and the table still ranks the operators.
- `run(config) -> dict` · warm-up, the timed steps, the profile, the `share`.
- `main()` · `before = run(fix='none')`, `after = run(fix=args.fix)`, the figure, the JSON, `common.log_stage('study_profile_stnet_step', t0, rows=n_windows)`.

_Skeleton._

```python

from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
import common, stnet

WARMUP, STEPS = 3, 20

def sync(dev):

def timed_step(net, opt, lossf, X, y, A_up, A_down, dev, resident):

    ...

def profile_step(net, opt, lossf, X, y, A_up, A_down, dev):
    """Top ten operators by CPU time from the PyTorch profiler."""
    ...

def run(month, batch, fix, steps, dev, seed):
    """Warm-up, timed steps, profile; returns the before/after object."""
    ...

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--month", required=True); ap.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=64)
    ap.add_argument("--fix", choices=["resident", "batch128", "none"], default="resident")
    ap.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=STEPS); ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
```

_Check._ `before.share` sums to 1 and its largest entry is the cost the report names; `after.ms_per_step` is below `before.ms_per_step` and `speedup` is above 1, or the JSON says the fix did nothing and the report says which section was really the largest. `--fix none` twice gives `speedup` within 0.95 to 1.05, which is the noise you must beat.

#### `docs/compute_budget.md` · doc · new

_Purpose._ A compute budget for a statewide model, built from the numbers this pipeline measured on the M1 and nothing else: the `stage=` lines in `logs/pipeline.log`, the training times in `output/evaluation_report.json`, and `output/studies/profile_stnet_step.json`. It answers what a model for every PeMS mainline station in California would need, where one machine breaks first, and what it would cost.

_Must contain._

- `Measured on the M1` · a list of the numbers used, each with the log line it came from: rows per second in `10_clean_pems.py` and `13_feature_engineering.py`, seconds per horizon and peak `rss_gb` in `16_train_lgbm.py`, milliseconds per step and windows per month in `17b_train_stnet.py`, bytes per row of the feature table, seconds per prediction cycle.
- `The statewide problem` · station count from the meta files (count every district's `d??_text_meta` file, or the number PeMS documents, stated as which), rows per year, feature-table gigabytes, and the download at one file per `PEMS_GAP_SECONDS` per district-day.
- `Scaling arithmetic` · stages 5 to 8 and LightGBM scale with rows; LightGBM memory scales with rows × features at one byte per histogram cell; the net scales with stations per step and with steps per epoch; the arithmetic intensity of the net's matrix products and where they sit on the M1's roofline, from the Try-this, with the sentence on why small batches are bandwidth-bound.
- `What breaks first` · in order: disk for raw files, then LightGBM's memory at the full row count, then wall-clock for the download; with the row count at which each happens.
- `Options` · one model per district with the same code (embarrassingly parallel), a single large VM, per-route models; what each does to the numbers above.
- `Cost` · hours from the arithmetic times an hourly VM price you looked up on the day, with the date and the instance type, for a first training and for a monthly retrain; storage per year.
- `What to re-measure` · the three numbers the budget is most sensitive to and how to measure them on a second district.

_Check._ Every number in the page has a source line or a formula beside it; `grep -c 'logs/pipeline.log\|evaluation_report.json\|profile_stnet_step.json' docs/compute_budget.md` is at least 3. A second reader can recompute the statewide hours from the page alone.

#### `docs/ml_test_score.md` · doc · new

_Purpose._ Score the pipeline against the ML Test Score rubric (Breck et al., 2017): its 28 tests in four sections, each scored 0 (not done), 0.5 (done by hand, once) or 1 (automated and run regularly), with the file or test that is the evidence; the final score is the minimum of the four section totals, as the paper defines it; the gaps become a `tests/` plan with a file name, what each test asserts and when it will be written.

_Must contain._

- `How to read this` · the three scores and the minimum rule, in two sentences.
- `Data tests` · the seven, each with score and evidence (`tests/test_clean_pems.py`, `tests/test_features.py`, the golden test, `20_monitor.py`'s PSI, and so on).
- `Model tests` · the seven (baselines beaten, calibration, the leakage experiment, the challenger rule, and the rest), score and evidence.
- `Infrastructure tests` · the seven (reproducible training, the golden serving test, `--rollback`, the atomic write, the integration test that is `make all`), score and evidence.
- `Monitoring tests` · the seven (freshness, drift, decay, the retrain rule, alerting when no file lands), score and evidence.
- `Score` · the four totals and the minimum, and one paragraph on what the minimum means for this project.
- `The tests/ plan` · a list, one line per gap: the test file, the test function's name, what it asserts, the phase or week it is due; at least five entries; every entry that lands in phase 10 or 11 is named there.

_Check._ 28 scored items are on the page (`grep -c 'score: ' docs/ml_test_score.md` prints `28`); the plan has at least five entries; every evidence path exists.

#### `docs/stages/19_predict_live.md` · page · new

_Purpose._ The stage page for the loop: what it reads, what it writes with the field list above, how to run it and how it is scheduled, the numbers from the last run, and what surprised you. It must also hold the two incident windows side by side, archive `[created, max(updated, created + INCIDENT_MIN_MINUTES)]` against live `[first_seen_at, last_seen_at + POLL_SECONDS]`, and the latency chain in minutes from detector to delivered alert.

_Must contain._ `Reads`, `Writes` (fields and dtypes), `Run` (the command, the plist, load and unload), `Last run` (seconds, `rss_gb`, rows, alert count, the latency numbers from `tests/test_serve.py`), `The two incident windows`, `Latency chain`, `Surprises`.

_Check._ `make all`'s page check passes; the page's `Last run` numbers match the newest `stage=predict` line in `logs/pipeline.log`.

#### `docs/stages/20_monitor.md` · page · new

_Purpose._ The stage page for the monitor: reads, writes with the JSON keys, how to run it, the PSI unit check (0.25 σ, 0.5 σ, 1.0 σ and the PSI each gave), the retrain and rollback procedure step by step with the manifest before and after, the numbers from the last weekly file, and surprises. Every other runner without a page under `docs/stages/` gets one in this phase with the same headings, because `make all` fails until the folder is complete.

_Must contain._ `Reads`, `Writes` (keys), `Run`, `PSI unit check`, `Retrain and rollback` (the exact commands and what the manifest shows at each step), `Last run`, `Surprises`.

_Check._ `make all`'s page check passes with every runner's page present; the retrain section's commands were run once and their output pasted.

### Done when

- From a fresh clone, `make setup && make all` produces the evaluation report: `git clone <your fork> t1 && cd t1 && make setup && make pems MONTHS=2026-03 && make all MONTHS=2026-03` ends with `output/evaluation_report.json` written and its page check silent, with a page for all fifteen runners.
- `pytest -q tests/test_golden_features.py` prints `4 passed` on the stored day, and after changing one lag in `features.py` it fails naming the column, then passes again after reverting.
- `make predict` prints `stage=predict seconds=<under 1> rss_gb=<under 0.2> rows=<3 × stations> ... mode=replay`, and every runner's last line is in the log: `awk '{print $1}' logs/pipeline.log | sort -u` lists a `stage=` name for each runner in `RUNNERS`, every line carrying `seconds=` and `rss_gb=`.
- The four jobs are loaded and the Mac cannot sleep: `launchctl list | grep -c traffic1` prints `4`, `plutil -lint launchd/*.plist` prints four `OK`, and `pmset -g | grep -E '^ *(sleep|disksleep)'` shows `0` for both.
- The replay loop has run unattended for a week: `grep -c '^stage=predict' logs/predict.log` is at least 1900 (seven days at 288 cycles, allowing a few restarts), `ls output/predictions_log.parquet/ | wc -l` is at least 7, and `logs/predict.err` is empty.
- The monitor has written four weekly files: `ls output/monitor/*.json | wc -l` prints `4`, each with `scoring.30.ap` beside its `prevalence`, a `drift.alerts` list and `retrain.due`.
- The containerized service answers the golden test: `docker build -f serve/Dockerfile -t traffic1-serve .`, `docker run --rm -d -p 8000:8000 -v "$PWD/output:/app/output" --name traffic1 traffic1-serve`, then `SERVE_URL=http://localhost:8000 pytest -q tests/test_serve.py -s` passes and prints the latency line, whose numbers are in `docs/stages/19_predict_live.md`.
- `make retrain` on an existing month ends in `promote` or `refused` in `logs/pipeline.log`, and `make rollback` restores the previous hashes, `models/manifest.json`'s `history` showing both actions.
- `output/studies/profile_stnet_step.json` names the largest cost and has `speedup` above 1 or a sentence in the report on why not; `docs/compute_budget.md` and `docs/ml_test_score.md` exist with every section above, the score page's `grep -c 'score: '` printing `28` and its plan holding at least five tests.

### Pitfalls

- The golden test passes, yet the served alerts disagree with the evaluation report within weeks, or a feature in the loop is 'the same but faster'. A second copy of the feature code: any arithmetic in `19_predict_live.py`'s `assemble()` is a second implementation, and it drifts the first time `features.py` changes. `assemble()` only joins and calls `build_features`; `test_serving_slice_matches` runs the loop's exact 13-step path against the training table and fails when they part.
- `logs/predict.log` has a gap every night and the weekly file is missing after a reboot. cron instead of launchd on a Mac that sleeps: cron does not run a job the machine slept through and dies with a login session. The four plists in `launchd/`, loaded with `launchctl bootstrap`, plus `pmset` sleep 0 and `caffeinate -i` around the download and the retrain, are the fix; `launchctl print` shows the last exit code when a job ran and failed.
- Monday's monitor shows the 30-minute AP halved after Sunday's retrain, and the old model files are gone. No way to roll back a bad model: `make train` by hand overwrites `models/` in place. `make retrain` starts with `20_monitor.py --stash`, `--promote` refuses a set that lost more than `RETRAIN_DROP` on validation, and `make rollback` restores `models/previous/` file by file; never run `16_train_lgbm.py` alone on a machine whose loop is live.
- A week went into the `Mix` layer and the step is no faster. Optimizing before profiling: the largest cost was the per-batch copy to the device or a Python loop, which `studies/profile_stnet_step.py`'s `before.share` would have shown in a minute. Run the profile first, change one thing, and keep the JSON that proves it.
- The predictor job runs every five minutes and writes nothing; `logs/predict.err` says `libomp` or `No such file`. launchd gives a job neither your shell's `PATH` nor your `.env`, and a plist rendered with `/Users/you` runs on nobody's machine. The `EnvironmentVariables` dict with `PATH` and the `sed` render from `TRAFFIC1_ROOT` are the fix; if `data/` is on an external drive, grant the venv's `python` Full Disk Access in System Settings, the permission that silently blocks scheduled jobs.
- `19_predict_live.py` refuses to start with a hash mismatch right after you trained by hand. That is the manifest doing its job: the files under `models/` are not the set the manifest promoted. Run `make retrain` properly, or, when the by-hand model is the one you want, `20_monitor.py --promote` to record it; never edit the hashes.
- `docker build` sits for an hour before the first step. The build context is the repository root, and without `.dockerignore` Docker copies `data/` and `.venv/` to the daemon first. The ignore file listed under `serve/Dockerfile` cuts the context to kilobytes.
- The weekly AP is `nan` or the scored row count is a few hundred. The window's labels have not posted, or the monitor read the cleaned Parquet, which has no `label` column. `score_week()` joins `data/labels/`, reports `days` per horizon, and a Monday run scores through Saturday; wait, or run `make features MONTHS=<month>` and `make labels` for the new days first.

## Phase 10: Beyond supervised learning

_weeks 60–70 · ≈70 h · builds an alert-policy analysis, a fairness audit, a dashboard ranker_

**Goal.** What changes when a model's output is a decision: reinforcement learning, causal inference, fairness, privacy and ranking.

### What you need to learn

- Markov decision processes, value functions, Q-learning and policy gradients; bandits; off-policy evaluation from logged data; where RL fits in traffic control.
- Potential outcomes, confounding, causal diagrams, randomization; adjustment, instruments, difference-in-differences; interference; performative prediction.
- Fairness definitions and their conflicts; measuring disparity by slice; differential privacy; documentation (model cards, datasheets); governance.
- Recommenders and ranking: collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, learning to rank, ranking metrics, exposure bias and feedback loops.

### Topic: Reinforcement learning: agents, rewards, bandits and policies

**Goal.** Understand learning by acting: the setup, the core algorithms, and where it fits (and does not fit) in a traffic system.

**Age 5.**

Some learning happens by trying things and seeing what happens: touch the hot stove once and you learn. A computer can learn a game the same way, getting points for good moves and losing points for bad ones.

_Try this._ Teach a friend a simple game only by saying 'good' or 'bad' after each move, never explaining the rules. Do they figure it out?

**Middle school.**

In reinforcement learning an agent sees a state, picks an action, gets a reward, and the world moves to a new state. It learns a policy, a rule for choosing actions, that collects the most reward over time. The hard part is that rewards may come late, and that trying new actions (exploration) costs something.

A bandit is the simplest case: one decision, repeated, like which of three alert messages drivers respond to most. Traffic lights and ramp meters can be controlled by reinforcement learning.

_Try this._ Play with a bandit on paper: three slot machines with hidden payout rates; keep choosing, track averages, and decide when to stop exploring.

**High school.**

Markov decision processes: states, actions, transitions, rewards, discounting. Value functions and the Bellman equation; Q-learning and policy gradients as the two families; exploration versus exploitation; deep RL (a network for the value or policy). Bandits: epsilon-greedy, upper confidence bound, Thompson sampling. Simulators are usually required because trying actions in the real world is expensive or unsafe.

For traffic: ramp metering and signal timing are natural RL problems; alerting is closer to a bandit with delayed feedback.

_Try this._ Implement Q-learning on a small grid world in numpy, then Thompson sampling for a three-arm bandit; plot regret over time.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Dynamic programming (value and policy iteration), temporal-difference learning, function approximation and its instability (the deadly triad), policy gradient theorem and actor-critic methods, off-policy evaluation from logged data (importance sampling), and the sample-inefficiency problem. Contextual bandits as the practical middle ground for decisions with immediate feedback.

Offline RL and off-policy evaluation are what a system with logged alerts and outcomes could actually use; online RL on live traffic is rarely acceptable.

_Try this._ Formulate the alerting policy as a contextual bandit with delayed reward, propose an off-policy estimator for a new policy from logged data, and state its assumptions.

**Stanford grad.**

Model-based RL with learned or physical simulators (traffic microsimulation as an environment), multi-agent RL for networks of intersections, safe RL with constraints, and the evaluation problem (simulator-to-real gap). Connections to control theory and to causal inference (policies as interventions).

_Try this._ Design a ramp-metering controller for one Fremont on-ramp trained in a traffic simulator, and the validation that would justify a field trial.

**PhD at Apple.**

RL in products is mostly bandits and offline evaluation; full RL succeeds where a faithful simulator exists (games, some control). The research frontier includes sample efficiency, offline RL with guarantees, RL from human feedback for language models, and safe deployment. For transport, learned control of signals and meters is an active applied area with real deployments.

_Try this._ Write the evaluation protocol for an RL-controlled corridor: metrics, baselines (fixed-time, actuated), safety constraints, and how you would attribute changes to the controller rather than to demand shifts.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>What distinguishes RL from supervised learning?</summary>

There are no correct labels, only rewards, and the agent's actions change the data it sees.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Why are bandits the practical case?</summary>

Immediate feedback and no state transitions make evaluation and safety tractable; most product decisions look like that.

</details>

### Topic: Causal inference: from correlation to intervention

**Goal.** Ask what would happen if you acted, and know what data can and cannot tell you about it.

**Age 5.**

Ice cream sales and sunburns go up together, but ice cream does not cause sunburn; the sun causes both. Finding the real cause is harder than noticing things go together.

_Try this._ Think of two things that happen together in your life but where one does not cause the other. What causes both?

**Middle school.**

Correlation is when two things move together; causation is when changing one changes the other. Confounders are hidden causes of both. The cleanest way to find a cause is an experiment: randomly do the thing to some and not others, then compare. When you cannot experiment, you need assumptions and careful methods.

For traffic: incidents and slowdowns go together, but reporting an incident also depends on congestion; and an alert that changes driver behavior changes the outcome it predicted.

_Try this._ Design a fair test of whether an alert makes drivers reroute: who gets the alert, who does not, and how you decide.

**High school.**

Potential outcomes: each unit has an outcome with and without treatment; the effect is the difference; you only ever see one. Randomization makes the groups comparable. Without it: adjust for confounders (regression, matching, weighting), use natural experiments (instruments, discontinuities, differences-in-differences), and draw the causal diagram (DAG) to decide what to adjust for and what not to (colliders).

A/B tests are randomized experiments; interference (one driver's reroute affects others) breaks the usual analysis.

_Try this._ Draw the DAG for incident, congestion, reporting, rain and alert. Which variables should you adjust for to estimate the effect of an incident on speed, and which must you not?

**Stanford undergrad.**

Identification conditions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency), the back-door and front-door criteria, do-calculus at a reading level, estimators (outcome regression, inverse probability weighting, doubly robust), instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences and synthetic controls. Causal machine learning: double machine learning and causal forests for heterogeneous effects.

Interference and spillovers, which are the rule in traffic; cluster-randomized and switchback designs.

_Try this._ Estimate the effect of rain on the probability of a slow episode with inverse probability weighting on hour and weekday, and compare with a naive difference; explain the gap.

**Stanford grad.**

Time-varying treatments and g-methods for sequential policies (alerting is one); mediation; sensitivity analysis to unmeasured confounding; causal discovery and its limits; causal representation learning. Performative prediction as a bridge between causal inference and ML deployment.

_Try this._ Design a switchback experiment for alerts across days and routes that respects interference, and the analysis that estimates the effect on travel time.

**PhD at Apple.**

Products that act on predictions are causal systems, and evaluating them requires experimental design or credible quasi-experiments; the research frontier includes experimentation under interference, off-policy evaluation, and causal effects of algorithmic systems on populations. Traffic is an unusually good testbed because interventions are visible and physical.

_Try this._ Write the causal question, identification strategy and analysis plan for 'do alerts reduce total delay on I-880 in the evening peak?'

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why does adjusting for a collider cause bias?</summary>

Conditioning on a common effect of two variables induces an association between them that does not exist causally.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does randomization buy?</summary>

Treated and untreated groups are comparable on everything, measured or not, so the difference in outcomes is the causal effect on average.

</details>

### Topic: Fairness, privacy and ethics: what a model owes people

**Goal.** See where a traffic model can treat people unequally or expose them, and know the tools and the limits of technical fixes.

**Age 5.**

A helper should be fair: it should not warn some neighborhoods and forget others. And it should not tell anyone where a particular person drove.

_Try this._ If a helper only worked for one street, who would be left out? How would they feel?

**Middle school.**

Fairness: a model's mistakes can fall more on some groups, for example if detectors are worse in some neighborhoods, alerts there are worse. Privacy: data about where people go is sensitive; even aggregated speeds can reveal a single car at 3 am. Ethics also covers being honest about what the model can do and who is accountable when it is wrong.

_Try this._ Look at the station map. Which parts of Fremont have few detectors? What does that mean for whom the alerts help?

**High school.**

Fairness definitions and why they conflict: equal error rates across groups, calibration within groups, demographic parity; you cannot have all at once. Measuring: slice every metric by area and time. Privacy: anonymization fails against linkage; differential privacy adds calibrated noise with a provable guarantee; aggregation thresholds and k-anonymity are weaker but common. Ethics in practice: documentation (datasheets, model cards), stating limits, and a person accountable for decisions.

For this project: detector coverage is uneven; probe data would raise privacy questions the loop data do not.

_Try this._ Compute recall and false-alarm rate per station and plot them on the map. Which areas get worse service, and why?

**Stanford undergrad.**

Formal fairness criteria (independence, separation, sufficiency) and impossibility results; sources of disparity (measurement, representation, label, deployment); mitigation methods (reweighting, constraints, post-processing) and their costs. Differential privacy: definition, composition, the privacy budget, DP-SGD; federated learning and its limits. Governance: impact assessments, audits, and regulation as constraints on design.

Prediction versus decision: fairness lives in the policy (who gets alerts) as much as in the model.

_Try this._ Implement a DP release of hourly average speeds per station with Laplace noise; plot utility against epsilon and decide the smallest epsilon the product could tolerate.

**Stanford grad.**

The limits of technical fairness (measurement of groups, contested definitions, distributional versus procedural justice); long-term dynamics of fair decisions; privacy attacks on models (membership inference, extraction) and defenses; the tension between transparency and gaming. Participatory design and the role of affected communities in defining harms.

_Try this._ Audit the alert policy for disparate impact across neighborhoods under two fairness definitions, show they conflict on this data, and write the memo that explains the choice to a city council.

**PhD at Apple.**

Responsible ML at scale is organizational: review processes, documentation, red-teaming, monitoring for disparate impact after deployment, and legal compliance. The research frontier includes fairness under distribution shift and feedback, privacy-preserving learning with useful guarantees, and evaluation of societal impact. Transport systems allocate a public good, which raises the stakes.

_Try this._ Design the governance for a public traffic-alert system: what is measured, who reviews it, what triggers a pause, and how the public can contest a decision.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why can a model be calibrated for every group and still have unequal error rates?</summary>

Calibration and equal error rates are different criteria, and when base rates differ across groups they cannot all hold at once.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does differential privacy guarantee?</summary>

That any single person's data changes the released output's distribution by at most a bounded factor, whatever else an attacker knows.

</details>

### Topic: Recommender systems and ranking

**Goal.** Rank things for people from their behavior, evaluate a ranking, and see the feedback loops that ranking creates.

**Age 5.**

When a video app shows you what to watch next, it guessed from what you and people like you watched before. That guessing is a recommender.

Our helper ranks roads too: the ones most likely to jam go to the top of the list.

_Try this._ Make a list of your friend's favorite games ranked from most to least. What did you use to guess?

**Middle school.**

Recommenders learn from clicks, plays and ratings. Collaborative filtering says: people who liked what you liked will like this; matrix factorization learns a few hidden traits per person and per item. Content-based methods use item features. Ranking systems score candidates and order them; evaluation asks whether the good items are near the top.

Ranking the top-risk segments per route for a dashboard is a small ranking problem with the same metrics.

_Try this._ Rank ten stations by predicted probability of a slow episode. If only three actually became slow, how many were in your top three? That is precision at 3.

**High school.**

Matrix factorization with implicit feedback, nearest-neighbor methods, and modern two-tower models that embed users and items; candidate generation then ranking; ranking losses (pointwise, pairwise, listwise). Metrics: precision at k, recall at k, mean average precision, NDCG. Offline evaluation is biased by what was shown (exposure), which is the central difficulty.

Feedback loops: what is recommended gets clicked, which trains the next model; popularity bias and filter bubbles follow.

_Try this._ Implement matrix factorization by alternating least squares on a small public ratings dataset and report NDCG at 10 against a popularity baseline.

**Stanford undergrad.**

Learning to rank (LambdaMART, which is gradient boosting for ranking), embedding retrieval with approximate nearest neighbors, position bias and unbiased learning to rank, off-policy evaluation of rankers from logged data (inverse propensity scoring), and exploration in recommendation. Cold start and side information. Multi-objective ranking (relevance, diversity, freshness).

For the dashboard: rank segments by calibrated risk times exposure (traffic volume), and evaluate with NDCG against realized episodes.

_Try this._ Train a LightGBM ranker (lambdarank) to order stations by risk each 5 minutes using the classifier's features, and compare NDCG at 5 with sorting by calibrated probability.

**Stanford grad.**

Recommendation as a causal and sequential problem: exposure bias, interference between users, long-term effects, and the alignment of optimization targets with user welfare. Large-scale systems (retrieval, ranking, re-ranking stages) and their latency budgets. Evaluation through online experiments and interleaving.

_Try this._ Propose an off-policy evaluation of a new segment-ranking policy for the dashboard from logged views and outcomes, and the propensity model it needs.

**PhD at Apple.**

Recommenders are the most deployed ML systems and the most studied for societal effects; research spans sequential recommendation, causal recommendation, fairness of exposure, and generative retrieval. The methodological core, ranking under partial feedback, transfers to any system that shows people a prioritized list, including a traffic dashboard.

_Try this._ Design the ranking objective for a public traffic dashboard that balances predicted delay, number of affected drivers and fairness of coverage, and say how you would evaluate it.

**Check yourself.**

<details>
<summary>Why is offline evaluation of a recommender biased?</summary>

Logged feedback exists only for items that were shown; items never shown have no data, and the log reflects the old policy's choices.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What does NDCG reward?</summary>

Putting relevant items near the top, with a discount that makes the first positions count most.

</details>

### Read and watch, explained at every level

#### [Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (Sutton, Barto)](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html)

_book · free · a semester · free; the standard first book_

**Age 5.** The classic free book about learning by trial and reward, by two of the people who invented the field.

**Middle school.** Sutton and Barto's textbook, free online, explains reinforcement learning from bandits through Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference methods, to function approximation and policy gradients. Part 1 is readable with basic probability. It is the standard first book.

**High school.** Read chapters 1 to 6 (bandits, MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning) and implement the small examples (grid worlds, the cliff walk). Chapter 13 on policy gradients is the bridge to deep RL. The exercises are excellent and the answers are checkable by simulation.

**Stanford undergrad.** The book's careful treatment of the Bellman equations, of on-policy versus off-policy learning, and of the deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy) is what you need to read deep RL papers critically. Chapter 11 on off-policy methods with approximation is the relevant one for learning from logged alert data.

**Stanford grad.** Its coverage of eligibility traces, of planning with learned models, and of the psychology and neuroscience connections gives the field's intellectual context; the second edition's case studies show what worked and why.

**PhD at Apple.** The canonical reference; its authors' later essays on the field's direction are worth reading alongside. For a lead, it is the book to require before anyone proposes RL for a control problem.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Part I, tabular methods: the k-armed bandit (action values, epsilon-greedy, optimistic initial values, UCB, gradient bandits); finite Markov decision processes (agent-environment interface, returns, policies, value functions, Bellman equations, optimality); dynamic programming (policy evaluation, policy improvement, policy iteration, value iteration, generalized policy iteration); Monte Carlo methods (prediction, estimation of action values, control, off-policy with importance sampling); temporal-difference learning (TD(0), Sarsa, Q-learning, expected Sarsa, double learning); n-step bootstrapping; planning and learning with tabular models (Dyna, prioritized sweeping, MCTS). Part II, approximate methods: on-policy prediction with function approximation (gradient MC, semi-gradient TD, linear methods, feature construction), on-policy control (semi-gradient Sarsa, average reward), off-policy methods and the deadly triad, eligibility traces (TD(lambda)), policy gradient (REINFORCE, actor-critic). Part III: psychology, neuroscience, applications (TD-Gammon, Atari, AlphaGo), frontiers.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. The problem: an agent chooses actions, receives rewards and new states, and seeks to maximise expected discounted return; learning from evaluative (not instructive) feedback creates the exploration-exploitation trade-off.
2. MDPs and Bellman equations: the state value v_pi(s) is the expected return from s under policy pi; it satisfies a recursive consistency equation; the optimal value v* satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, and a greedy policy with respect to v* is optimal.
3. Dynamic programming assumes a known model: policy evaluation iterates the Bellman equation to a fixed point; policy improvement acts greedily; alternating them (generalized policy iteration) is the pattern behind almost every RL algorithm.
4. Monte Carlo learns from complete episodes without a model by averaging returns; off-policy learning reweights returns from a behaviour policy with importance-sampling ratios, at the price of variance.
5. Temporal difference learns from incomplete episodes by bootstrapping: update the estimate toward reward plus discounted estimate of the next state. Sarsa is on-policy (uses the action actually taken); Q-learning is off-policy (uses the max); double Q-learning removes maximisation bias.
6. n-step methods and eligibility traces interpolate between MC (high variance, no bias) and TD(0) (low variance, bias); TD(lambda) averages all n-step returns with weights (1-lambda) lambda^(n-1).
7. Planning uses a model to simulate experience; Dyna interleaves real and simulated updates; MCTS builds a search tree from rollouts guided by value estimates.
8. Function approximation: with large state spaces, values are parameterised (linear in features, or a network) and updated by semi-gradient TD; combining bootstrapping, off-policy learning and function approximation (the deadly triad) can diverge.
9. Policy gradient methods parameterise the policy directly; the policy gradient theorem gives an unbiased gradient estimate from sampled returns (REINFORCE); a learned baseline or critic reduces variance (actor-critic).

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
return: G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma R_{t+2} + gamma^2 R_{t+3} + ...
Bellman: v_pi(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) sum_{s',r} p(s',r|s,a) [r + gamma v_pi(s')]
TD(0): V(S_t) <- V(S_t) + alpha [R_{t+1} + gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)]
Q-learning: Q(S,A) <- Q(S,A) + alpha [R + gamma max_a Q(S',a) - Q(S,A)]
policy gradient: grad J(theta) = E_pi[ G_t grad log pi(A_t|S_t, theta) ]
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Generalized policy iteration (evaluate, then improve) is the skeleton of every RL method.
- TD learning bootstraps; MC does not; the choice trades bias for variance.
- Function approximation plus off-policy plus bootstrapping can diverge, so read Chapter 11 before trusting a deep RL result.

**Practice.** Implement tabular Q-learning and Sarsa on a small gridworld and on a signal-timing toy (a queue that grows with arrivals and drains when the light is green); plot learning curves and show that Q-learning finds the shorter but riskier path in the cliff-walking example.

</details>

#### [David Silver's Reinforcement Learning course (UCL, DeepMind)](https://www.davidsilver.uk/teaching/)

_video · free · ten lectures, two weeks · free lectures alongside the book_

**Age 5.** Video lectures by a scientist who helped build a computer that beat the best human at the board game Go, explaining how machines learn from rewards.

**Middle school.** Ten free lectures that follow Sutton and Barto: Markov decision processes, planning, learning without a model, function approximation, policy gradients, and games. Watch them alongside the book; the lectures make the equations feel inevitable.

**High school.** Lectures 1 to 5 cover the foundations used in the RL topic; lecture 6 on value function approximation and lecture 7 on policy gradients are the bridge to deep RL. Do the book's exercises after each lecture.

**Stanford undergrad.** Silver's derivations (the Bellman equations, the policy gradient theorem) are clear and complete; his lecture on exploration and on integrating learning and planning is a compact treatment of the ideas behind model-based RL.

**Stanford grad.** The course predates much of deep RL; pair it with Spinning Up for algorithms and with recent surveys for offline RL. Its value is conceptual clarity.

**PhD at Apple.** A widely used lecture series that defines the shared vocabulary of the field; useful as a common reference when a team discusses control problems.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Ten lectures: introduction to RL; Markov decision processes; planning by dynamic programming; model-free prediction (MC and TD); model-free control (on-policy and off-policy); value function approximation (incremental methods, batch methods, DQN); policy gradient methods (finite difference, Monte Carlo policy gradient, actor-critic, natural gradient); integrating learning and planning (model-based RL, Dyna, simulation-based search, MCTS); exploration and exploitation (bandits, optimism, Thompson sampling, information state search); case study of classic games (Backgammon, checkers, chess, Go, poker).

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. The RL problem is framed by reward hypothesis, history and state, the Markov property, and the three agent components (policy, value function, model); the distinction between prediction (evaluate a policy) and control (find the best one) organises the course.
2. MDP lecture: Markov processes, reward processes, decision processes; the Bellman expectation and optimality equations in matrix and recursive form; the existence of a deterministic optimal policy.
3. Dynamic programming: iterative policy evaluation, policy iteration and value iteration are contraction mappings, so they converge; asynchronous and prioritised sweeps.
4. Model-free prediction: MC averages returns, TD bootstraps; the bias-variance argument; TD(lambda) with forward (lambda-return) and backward (eligibility trace) views, which are equivalent for offline updates.
5. Model-free control: on-policy MC and Sarsa with GLIE exploration; off-policy Q-learning; the role of importance sampling and why Q-learning avoids it.
6. Function approximation: incremental gradient methods with linear and nonlinear features; batch methods (least-squares, experience replay with fixed targets as in DQN) stabilise learning.
7. Policy gradient: score function, the policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE, reducing variance with a critic and with baselines, compatible function approximation, natural policy gradient.
8. Model-based RL and search: learn a model from experience, plan with it; Dyna; forward search; MCTS with UCT and its success in Go.
9. Exploration: regret, optimism in the face of uncertainty (UCB), probability matching (Thompson sampling), information-state MDPs; contextual bandits.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
UCB: A_t = argmax_a [ Q_t(a) + c sqrt( ln t / N_t(a) ) ]
lambda-return: G_t^lambda = (1-lambda) sum_n lambda^(n-1) G_t^(n)
actor-critic update: theta <- theta + alpha grad log pi(a|s) Q_w(s,a)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Prediction and control are separate problems and every algorithm is a pairing of one evaluation method with one improvement rule.
- Off-policy learning lets one dataset evaluate many policies, which is why Q-learning and DQN are so widely used.
- Exploration is a statistical problem (regret) with principled solutions (UCB, Thompson) that beat epsilon-greedy.

**Practice.** Watch lectures 1 to 5 alongside Sutton and Barto chapters 1 to 6, then reproduce the lecture's gridworld DP demo in NumPy, and implement UCB and Thompson sampling on a bandit that chooses which of three ramp-meter rates to use.

</details>

#### [Spinning Up in Deep RL (OpenAI)](https://spinningup.openai.com/)

_docs · free · a week · free; clean algorithms and a reading list_

**Age 5.** A free website that teaches modern trial-and-reward learning with clear notes and code you can run.

**Middle school.** Spinning Up is an educational site with an introduction to deep reinforcement learning, a list of key papers, and clean implementations of the main algorithms. It was written for people who know some deep learning and want to do RL properly. Read the introduction and run one algorithm on a simple simulated task.

**High school.** Read the three-part introduction (key concepts, kinds of algorithms, the policy-gradient derivation) and study the code for one algorithm (PPO or DQN). The exercises and the 'spinning up as a researcher' essay are practical advice.

**Stanford undergrad.** Its implementations are readable references for the standard algorithms and their tricks; the key-papers list is a curated syllabus for the field. Use it to reproduce a result on a simulated control task before attempting a traffic-control simulator.

**Stanford grad.** It reflects the state of deep RL around its writing; later methods (offline RL, RL from human feedback) are covered elsewhere. Its clarity about what makes RL hard (sample efficiency, instability, reward design) remains accurate.

**PhD at Apple.** A useful teaching resource and a reminder that reproducible baselines were a problem the field had to solve deliberately.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** An introduction (key concepts and terminology; kinds of RL algorithms; intro to policy optimization with derivations), a list of key papers by topic (model-free, exploration, transfer, hierarchy, memory, model-based, meta-RL, scaling, safety, imitation, reproducibility), and clean, single-file implementations with documentation of VPG, TRPO, PPO, DDPG, TD3 and SAC, plus exercises and advice on doing RL research.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Terminology: states and observations, action spaces, policies (deterministic and stochastic, with log-probability computation for categorical and diagonal Gaussian policies), trajectories, reward and return, the RL objective, value functions and advantage functions.
2. Taxonomy: model-free versus model-based; within model-free, policy optimisation (on-policy, stable) versus Q-learning (off-policy, sample-efficient but less stable); hybrids (DDPG, SAC).
3. Policy gradient derivation: the log-derivative trick turns the gradient of an expectation into an expectation of gradients; reward-to-go and baselines reduce variance without bias; the general form with advantage estimates.
4. Vanilla policy gradient: collect trajectories, estimate advantages with a value network (generalized advantage estimation), take one gradient step; simple and on-policy.
5. Trust region and PPO: limit each policy update so performance does not collapse; TRPO by a KL constraint solved with conjugate gradient; PPO by a clipped surrogate objective that is simpler and works nearly as well.
6. Off-policy actor-critic: DDPG learns a deterministic policy and Q function with replay and target networks; TD3 adds twin critics, target smoothing and delayed policy updates; SAC maximises entropy-regularised return with a stochastic policy.
7. Research advice: read for breadth, reproduce results, run many seeds, measure with learning curves, and tune one thing at a time; RL results are noisy and easy to fool yourself with.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
log-derivative: grad E[R(tau)] = E[ sum_t grad log pi(a_t|s_t) R(tau) ]
PPO clip: L = E[ min( r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t ) ], r_t = pi_theta(a|s)/pi_old(a|s)
GAE: A_t = sum_l (gamma lambda)^l delta_{t+l}, delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Policy gradient is one derivation; every on-policy algorithm is that derivation plus a variance-reduction and a step-size control.
- PPO's clipped objective is the practical default for on-policy learning; SAC for continuous control off-policy.
- Run several seeds; a single learning curve in deep RL proves nothing.

**Practice.** Implement VPG from the pseudocode on CartPole with a value baseline, then swap in the PPO clip, and plot five-seed learning curves for each; write one paragraph on what the clip changed.

</details>

#### [Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Cunningham)](https://mixtape.scunning.com/)

_book · free · selected chapters, two weeks · free; applied causal methods with code_

**Age 5.** A free book about telling causes from coincidences, written in a friendly voice with lots of examples from real life.

**Middle school.** Scott Cunningham's book, free online, teaches the methods economists use to find causes in data without experiments: comparing groups over time, using cut-offs, using instruments, and matching. It explains directed graphs (pictures of cause and effect) early and uses them throughout. Code is included.

**High school.** Read the chapters on directed acyclic graphs, on potential outcomes, on matching, and on difference-in-differences. Then draw the DAG for incidents, congestion and reporting and decide what you can estimate from the archive.

**Stanford undergrad.** The Mixtape is the applied-economics complement to Hernán and Robins: more on quasi-experimental designs (instruments, regression discontinuity, synthetic control), less on time-varying treatments. Its worked examples with code are the fastest way to see each method fail and succeed.

**Stanford grad.** Its treatment of difference-in-differences includes the recent literature on staggered adoption, which is relevant to evaluating roadwork or policy changes across corridors. Read it alongside the causal machine-learning literature.

**PhD at Apple.** A free, current, applied causal-inference text; for a product team asking what an alert causes, it is the accessible primer before the formal one.

<details>
<summary><b>Study guide: learn it here</b></summary>

**What it covers.** Chapters: introduction; probability and regression review; directed acyclic graphs; potential outcomes causal model (physical randomisation, randomisation inference, Fisher's sharp null); matching and subclassification (exact matching, approximate matching, propensity scores, coarsened exact matching); regression discontinuity (sharp, fuzzy, bandwidth, density tests, placebo tests); instrumental variables (LATE, weak instruments, heterogeneous effects); panel data (fixed effects); difference-in-differences (the 2x2, parallel trends, event studies, staggered adoption and the Bacon decomposition, Callaway-Sant'Anna); synthetic control; with Stata, R and Python code throughout.

**Key ideas, in order.**

1. Potential outcomes: each unit has Y(1) and Y(0); the individual effect is their difference and is never observed; the average treatment effect requires assumptions (SUTVA, ignorability) to identify from data; randomisation makes treatment independent of potential outcomes.
2. DAGs: draw the assumed causal structure; the backdoor criterion says which variables to condition on to block confounding paths; conditioning on a collider opens a path and creates bias (selection bias).
3. Matching and propensity scores: under conditional independence given X, compare treated to similar controls; the propensity score p(X) = P(D=1|X) reduces dimensionality; check overlap (common support) and balance; inverse probability weighting.
4. Regression discontinuity: when treatment is assigned by a cutoff on a running variable, units just above and below are comparable; estimate with local linear regression on each side, test for manipulation with a density test at the cutoff, run placebo cutoffs.
5. Instrumental variables: an instrument affects treatment but affects the outcome only through treatment; two-stage least squares; the estimate is a local average treatment effect for compliers; weak instruments bias toward OLS.
6. Difference-in-differences: compare the change in the treated group to the change in the control group; parallel trends is the identifying assumption; event-study plots check pre-trends; with staggered adoption the two-way fixed effects estimator can be badly biased because it uses already-treated units as controls.
7. Synthetic control: build a weighted combination of untreated units that matches the treated unit's pre-period trajectory; inference by placebo permutation across donor units.

**Formulas and commands to remember.**

```
ATE = E[Y(1) - Y(0)];  naive difference = ATE + selection bias + heterogeneity bias
DiD: (E[Y_T,post] - E[Y_T,pre]) - (E[Y_C,post] - E[Y_C,pre])
2SLS: first stage D = pi Z + X gamma + v, second stage Y = beta D_hat + X delta + u
propensity weighting: E[Y(1)] = E[ D Y / p(X) ]
```

**Three takeaways.**

- Identification comes from assumptions and design, not from the size of the dataset.
- Draw the DAG before the regression; it says what to control for and what never to control for.
- For policy questions about roads (a new ramp meter, a lane closure), difference-in-differences on nearby untreated segments is the natural design.

**Practice.** Take a real or simulated change on one Fremont segment (a new signal timing), pick control segments, run a difference-in-differences with an event-study plot, and test the parallel-trends assumption with pre-period leads.

</details>

#### [Causal Inference: What If (Hernán, Robins)](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

_book · free · part 1, three weeks · free; the rigorous base, part 1 now_

**Age 5.** A free book about telling the difference between 'these two things happen together' and 'this one causes that one', which is harder than it sounds.

**Middle school.** A textbook by two epidemiologists, free as a PDF, about answering causal questions from data: what would have happened if we had done something else. Part 1 is readable with basic statistics and uses simple examples. Read it in the final phase when you ask what an alert actually causes.

**High school.** Part 1 introduces counterfactuals, randomized experiments, confounding, and the diagrams (DAGs) that make assumptions explicit. Apply it to the project: does an incident cause the slowdown, or does congestion cause the incident to be reported? The book gives the tools to state that question precisely.

**Stanford undergrad.** Its treatment of exchangeability, positivity and consistency as the conditions for causal identification, and of methods (standardization, inverse probability weighting, g-methods), is the rigorous base for causal questions in ML. Part 2 covers models; part 3 covers time-varying treatments, which is where traffic interventions live.
